phy_edx.9.0.summary: Every atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged **nucleus** made of **protons** (relative charge +1, relative mass 1) and **neutrons** (relative charge 0, relative mass 1), surrounded by **electrons** (relative charge -1, very small relative mass of about 1/1836) arranged in shells. Because an atom has **equal numbers of protons and electrons** it has **no overall charge**. Almost all the mass is in the nucleus, while the electrons on the outside are the particles that can move from atom to atom, which is the basis of electric current in metals and of static electricity.

core.p: Edexcel 10.1 asks you to **describe the structure of the atom**, limited to the **position, mass and charge** of protons, neutrons and electrons. That means for each particle you must know three things: where it is, how heavy it is compared with the others, and what charge it carries.
bullets: Position: protons and neutrons in the **nucleus**; electrons **orbit the nucleus** in shells (energy levels).
Relative mass: proton **1**, neutron **1**, electron about **1/1836** (very small, often written as 'negligible' or 0.0005).
Relative charge: proton **+1**, neutron **0**, electron **-1**.
The atom as a whole is **neutral** because number of protons = number of electrons.

callouts.p: This three-by-three table is worth easy marks every year. Practise writing it out from memory.

core.h: The nuclear model of the atom
core.p: An atom is made of a very small central **nucleus** with electrons moving around it. The nucleus contains the protons and neutrons, so it is **positively charged**. The electrons are arranged in **shells** (energy levels) at different distances from the nucleus.
bullets: Nucleus = protons + neutrons (together called **nucleons**).
The nucleus is **positive** because protons are positive and neutrons have no charge.
Electrons are **negative** and are found outside the nucleus.
The negative electrons are held in the atom by **electrostatic attraction** to the positive nucleus.

callouts.p: The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, containing protons and neutrons.

fig.cap: A lithium atom (lithium-7): the nucleus contains 3 protons and 4 neutrons, and 3 electrons are arranged in shells around it. The drawing is not to scale: the real nucleus is far smaller compared with the atom.

core.p: Charges are given as **relative charges**, comparing each particle with the proton. A proton and an electron carry charges of the **same size but opposite sign**, which is why equal numbers of them cancel out exactly.
bullets: Proton: **+1** (positive).
Electron: **-1** (negative).
Neutron: **0** (neutral, hence the name).
The actual size of the charge on a proton or electron is very small (1.6 x 10^-19 C), but at GCSE you mainly use relative values.

callouts.p: Protons and electrons have the same size of charge but very different masses. Do not mix these up.

core.p: Masses are also given as **relative masses**, compared with a proton. Protons and neutrons have almost exactly the same mass, so both are given relative mass 1. An electron is about **1836 times lighter** than a proton, so its mass is tiny in comparison.
bullets: Proton: relative mass **1**.
Neutron: relative mass **1**.
Electron: relative mass about **1/1836** (about 0.0005).
So **almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus**.

callouts.p: For the mass of an electron, mark schemes accept 'very small', 'negligible', '1/1836' or '0.0005'. Do not write 0 on its own.

core.p: In a neutral atom the number of electrons **equals** the number of protons. Each proton's +1 is cancelled by an electron's -1, so the total charge is zero. Neutrons do not affect the charge at all.
bullets: Total charge = (number of protons x +1) + (number of electrons x -1).
Equal numbers -> total charge 0.
The number of neutrons can be different from the number of protons without changing the charge.
Example: carbon has 6 protons, 6 electrons (and usually 6 neutrons) -> neutral.

callouts.p: Atoms have no overall charge because they contain equal numbers of positive protons and negative electrons.

core.h: Size of the atom and nucleus
core.p: Atoms are tiny, with a radius of about **1 x 10^-10 m**. The nucleus is much smaller still, tens of thousands of times smaller across than the atom. So an atom is **mostly empty space**, with nearly all its mass packed into the tiny nucleus.
bullets: Atom radius: about 1 x 10^-10 m (0.1 nm).
Nucleus: tens of thousands of times smaller across than the atom.
If the nucleus were the size of a pea, the atom would be about the size of a football stadium.
The nucleus is therefore **extremely dense**.

fig.cap: Sizes compared: the atom has a radius of about 1 x 10^-10 m, while the nucleus at the centre is tens of thousands of times smaller across, so most of the atom is empty space. Even this drawing exaggerates the size of the nucleus.

core.p: Two numbers describe the make-up of an atom's nucleus. The **atomic number** (proton number) is the number of protons, which decides which element it is. The **mass number** (nucleon number) is the total number of protons plus neutrons.
bullets: Atomic number Z = number of protons (= number of electrons in a neutral atom).
Mass number A = number of protons + number of neutrons.
Number of neutrons = A - Z.
Electrons are not counted in the mass number because their mass is negligible.

callouts.p: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

core.p: Electrons are on the outside of the atom and are less tightly held than the protons in the nucleus, so they can be **gained or lost**. An atom that has gained or lost electrons is an **ion** and has an overall charge.
bullets: **Lose** electrons -> more protons than electrons -> **positive ion**.
**Gain** electrons -> more electrons than protons -> **negative ion**.
The number of protons does **not** change when an ion forms, so it is still the same element.
Protons cannot be moved by rubbing or by a circuit because they are locked in the nucleus.

callouts.p: Objects become charged by transfer of electrons only. Answers that say protons move score zero.

fig.cap: A lithium atom has 3 protons and 3 electrons, so no overall charge. If it loses one electron it becomes a Li+ ion with 3 protons but only 2 electrons, giving an overall charge of +1.

core.p: This spec point opens the electricity topic because **electric current is a flow of charge**, and in metals the moving charges are **electrons**. Some electrons in metals are free to move between atoms (delocalised or free electrons), so metals are good electrical conductors.
bullets: In a metal wire, the charge carriers are **free electrons** (negative).
Electrons flow from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal of a cell.
Conventional current is shown from + to -, the opposite direction to electron flow.
In insulators, electrons are not free to move, so no current flows.
Static electricity is also caused by electrons being transferred between objects.

callouts.p: In metals, current is a flow of negatively charged electrons, because they are the only particles free to move.

core.p: Opposite charges attract and like charges repel. The negatively charged electrons are attracted towards the positively charged nucleus, which keeps them in the atom. Electrons in the outer shells are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are the easiest to remove.
bullets: Electron (-) and nucleus (+): **attract**.
Electron and electron: repel.
Outer electrons are held most weakly -> lost first.
This is why it is always electrons, not protons, that move in circuits and in charging.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare two particles. Always compare the same property directly, using comparative words.
bullets: Proton vs neutron: **same mass**, but proton is positive and neutron is neutral; both in the nucleus.
Proton vs electron: **equal and opposite charge**, but the electron is much lighter and is outside the nucleus.
Neutron vs electron: neutron is much heavier and uncharged; electron is negative and outside the nucleus.

head: Comparison
Similarity
Difference
rows: Same relative mass (1); both in nucleus
Opposite sign; electron about 1/1836 of the mass; different positions
Neutron mass 1 and neutral; electron negligible mass and -1

callouts.p: Use phrases like 'much smaller mass than' and 'opposite charge to' to earn comparison marks.

core.p: Questions on atomic structure are usually short recall items, but they can be combined with electricity questions. Be precise about which particle you mean.
bullets: Always name the particle: say 'electrons', not 'charges' or 'particles'.
Give relative values with signs: +1, 0, -1.
Say 'in the nucleus' or 'in shells around the nucleus' for position.
For neutral atoms, explain using equal numbers of protons and electrons.

callouts.p: Electrons are outside the nucleus. Writing that electrons are in the nucleus is a common lost mark.

analogy.t: A stadium with a marble in the middle
analogy.p: Picture a huge football stadium with a heavy marble on the centre spot. The marble is the nucleus: tiny but holding nearly all the mass and all the positive charge. Specks of dust flying around the stands are the electrons: almost weightless, negative, and far from the centre, with the rest of the stadium empty space. Where it breaks down: electrons do not fly around in neat paths like dust or planets; they are held by electrostatic attraction, not by walls, and the real nucleus is even smaller relative to the atom than a marble in a stadium.

terms.d: The smallest part of an element, made of a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it.
The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and relative charge +1.
A particle in the nucleus with relative mass 1 and no charge.
A particle in shells around the nucleus with relative charge -1 and a very small relative mass (about 1/1836).
A proton or a neutron, the particles found in the nucleus.
A region at a set distance from the nucleus where electrons are found.
The mass of a particle compared with the mass of a proton.
The charge of a particle compared with the charge on a proton.
The number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Having no overall charge because positive and negative charges are equal.
An atom (or group of atoms) that has gained or lost electrons, so it has an overall charge.
An electron in a metal that is not bound to one atom and can move through the metal, carrying current.
The force of attraction between opposite charges, which holds electrons in an atom.

mistakes.w: Electrons are found in the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Electrons are in shells (energy levels) around/outside the nucleus; only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.

mistakes.w: The mass of an electron is 0.
mistakes.r: The electron has a very small (negligible) relative mass of about 1/1836, not zero.

mistakes.w: Neutrons are negative.
mistakes.r: Neutrons have no charge (relative charge 0).

mistakes.w: An atom is neutral because it has equal protons and neutrons.
mistakes.r: An atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

mistakes.w: A positive ion has gained protons.
mistakes.r: A positive ion has lost electrons; the number of protons does not change.

mistakes.w: Protons are heavier than neutrons.
mistakes.r: Protons and neutrons both have relative mass 1.

mistakes.w: The nucleus is negative.
mistakes.r: The nucleus is positive because it contains positive protons and neutral neutrons.

mistakes.w: Current in a wire is a flow of protons.
mistakes.r: Current in a metal is a flow of (free) electrons; protons stay in the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Mass number = protons + electrons.
mistakes.r: Mass number = protons + neutrons.

exam.q: State the relative charge of a neutron.
model: 0 / zero / no charge.
exam.tip: Write 0, not 'neutral charge of 1'.

exam.q: Name the particle in an atom that has the smallest mass.
model: Electron.
exam.tip: Just the name is needed.

exam.q: State where protons are found in an atom.
model: In the nucleus.
exam.tip: One word answer: nucleus.

exam.q: Complete the table showing the relative mass and relative charge of a proton and an electron.
model: Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
Electron: relative mass 1/1836 (negligible), relative charge -1.
exam.tip: Signs on charges are needed for the mark.

exam.q: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
model: The number of protons equals the number of electrons.
Protons are positive and electrons are negative with the same size of charge, so they cancel.
exam.tip: Mention both equal numbers and opposite charges.

exam.q: Compare a proton with an electron. Refer to mass, charge and position.
model: Proton has much larger mass (relative mass 1) than electron (about 1/1836).
Proton charge +1, electron charge -1 (same size, opposite sign).
Proton is in the nucleus; electron is in shells around the nucleus.
exam.tip: One mark per property; compare directly.

exam.q: An atom of sodium has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons.
model: 11 protons.
12 neutrons (23 - 11).
11 electrons.
exam.tip: Neutral atom: electrons = protons.

exam.q: Explain why almost all the mass of an atom is in its nucleus.
model: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, each of relative mass 1.
Electrons have a negligible / very small mass (about 1/1836).
exam.tip: Link location to mass.

exam.q: A neutral atom loses two electrons. State and explain the overall charge on the particle formed.
model: It now has two more protons than electrons (protons unchanged).
exam.tip: Charge sign plus reason.

exam.q: Describe the structure of an atom. Your answer should include the position, relative mass and relative charge of each particle, and explain why atoms are neutral and why electrons, not protons, are the particles that move in a metal wire.
model: Atom has a small central nucleus surrounded by electrons in shells.
Nucleus contains protons and neutrons.
Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
Neutron: relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
Electron: very small relative mass (about 1/1836), relative charge -1.
Atom is neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.
Protons are held in the nucleus and cannot move between atoms.
Some electrons in metals are free / outer electrons are held weakly, so electrons carry the current.
exam.tip: Cover all three particles fully, then the two explanations.

worked.q: An atom of aluminium has 13 protons and 14 neutrons. Find its atomic number, mass number and number of electrons, and state its overall charge.
worked.ans: Atomic number 13, mass number 27, 13 electrons, overall charge 0.

worked.q: A chlorine atom (17 protons, 18 neutrons) gains one electron. Calculate the relative charge of the particle and its relative mass to the nearest whole number.
steps: Electron mass is negligible, so relative mass is about 35.
worked.ans: Charge -1 (a negative ion); relative mass about 35.

worked.q: How many electrons have the same total mass as one proton? Use this to explain why electrons are left out of the mass number.
steps: Even a large atom has far fewer than 1836 electrons, so their total mass is a tiny fraction of the nucleus mass.
So mass number counts only protons and neutrons.
worked.ans: About 1836 electrons; their mass is negligible compared with the nucleus.

phy_edx.9.1.summary: Circuit diagrams use **standard symbols** so that anyone can read and build a circuit; you must be able to draw and recognise the symbols for cells, batteries, switches, voltmeters, ammeters, resistors, variable resistors, lamps, motors, diodes, thermistors, LDRs and LEDs. Components can be joined in **series** (one single loop, so the **same current** passes through every component and the supply p.d. is **shared**) or in **parallel** (separate branches, so each branch has the **same p.d.** as the supply and the current **splits**). A **voltmeter** measures potential difference in **volts (V)** and must always be connected **in parallel** across the component.

core.p: Edexcel 10.2 to 10.4 ask you to **draw and use circuit diagrams** with the correct symbols and the conventions for positive and negative terminals, to **describe the differences between series and parallel circuits**, and to **recall that a voltmeter is connected in parallel** with a component to measure the potential difference across it, in volts.
bullets: Draw symbols neatly with a ruler; wires are **straight lines** with no gaps.
Show the **positive terminal** of a cell as the **longer line**.
Know the series and parallel rules for current and potential difference.
Voltmeter: **in parallel**, measures p.d. in **volts (V)**.

callouts.p: Symbols, series vs parallel, voltmeter in parallel. Every Paper 2 electricity question builds on these.

core.p: A circuit diagram is a simplified map of a real circuit. Standard symbols mean the diagram can be understood by anyone in any country, and it shows clearly how the components are **connected**, which is what really matters, not what they look like.
bullets: Wires are drawn as straight lines, usually forming rectangles.
A **dot** at a junction shows that wires are joined.
There must be a **complete circuit** (closed loop) for a current to flow.
The layout on paper does not need to match the real positions of components.

callouts.p: In 'complete the circuit' questions, make sure every line meets the next with no gaps, or the circuit is not complete.

core.p: The energy source in most circuits is a **cell** or a **battery**. A battery is **two or more cells** joined together. The **long thin line** is the positive (+) terminal and the **short thick line** is the negative (-) terminal. A **switch** opens or closes a gap in the circuit.
bullets: **Cell**: one long line and one short line.
**Battery**: two or more cells joined in series (sometimes drawn with a dashed line between).
**Open switch**: gap in the circuit, so no current flows.
**Closed switch**: complete path, so current can flow.
Conventional current flows out of the **positive** terminal, round the circuit, and back to the negative terminal.

callouts.p: The longer line of a cell is positive. Students often get this backwards when drawing diodes the right way round.

core.p: Lamps, motors and resistors are the components that transfer energy or control the current. Learn each symbol exactly, because similar-looking symbols mean very different things.
bullets: **Lamp**: circle with a cross inside; transfers energy by light (and heating).
**Resistor**: rectangle; a fixed resistance that limits the current.
**Variable resistor**: rectangle with a diagonal arrow through it; resistance can be changed to vary the current.
**Motor**: circle with an M; transfers energy to a kinetic store.

head: Component

Job
rows: Gives out light, one way only

core.p: Meters are drawn as circles with a letter: **A** for an ammeter and **V** for a voltmeter. Diodes, LEDs, LDRs and thermistors are made from semiconductors. Their symbols are all based on either the diode triangle or the resistor rectangle.
bullets: **Diode**: triangle pointing in the direction current can flow, against a bar; current flows only one way.
**LED** (light-emitting diode): diode symbol with two arrows pointing **away**, because it gives out light.
**LDR** (light-dependent resistor): resistor inside a circle with two arrows pointing **in**, because light falls on it.
**Thermistor**: resistor with a diagonal line with a short flat tail, its resistance depends on temperature.

callouts.p: Arrows pointing out = light goes out (LED). Arrows pointing in = light comes in (LDR).

core.p: In a **series circuit** all the components are connected **one after another in a single loop**. There is only one path, so the charge has to pass through every component in turn.
bullets: **Current is the same** at every point in a series circuit.
The **p.d. of the supply is shared** between the components: V_total = V1 + V2 + ...
The **total resistance is the sum** of the individual resistances: R_total = R1 + R2.
If one component breaks or is removed, the circuit is broken and **everything stops**.
Adding more lamps in series makes each lamp **dimmer**, because the total resistance increases and the current decreases.

callouts.p: Components connected end to end in a single loop, so there is only one path for the current.

core.p: In a **parallel circuit** the components are on **separate branches**, each connected directly across the supply. Charge can take different paths, splitting at a **junction** and rejoining later.
bullets: The **p.d. across each branch is the same** as the supply p.d.
The **current splits** at junctions: total current = sum of the branch currents (I = I1 + I2).
Each branch can be **switched on and off independently**.
If one lamp breaks, the others **stay on**.
Adding another branch **reduces the total resistance**, so the total current from the supply **increases**.

callouts.p: Components connected on separate branches, each across the same two points, so there is more than one path for the current.

fig.cap: A parallel circuit: the two lamps are on separate branches. The current splits at the junction, and each lamp has the full supply p.d. across it, so each lamp is as bright as it would be on its own and can work independently.

core.p: The 'describe the differences' part of the spec is a favourite comparison question. Compare **current**, **potential difference**, **resistance** and **what happens if a component fails**.
bullets: Series: one path; parallel: more than one path.
Series: same current everywhere; parallel: current splits between branches.
Series: p.d. shared; parallel: same p.d. across each branch.
Series: adding resistors increases total resistance; parallel: adding resistors decreases total resistance.
Series: one fault stops everything; parallel: other branches keep working.

head: Feature
Series
Parallel
rows: Splits; branch currents add to total
Sum of resistances; increases when more added
Less than smallest branch resistance; decreases when more added
Each branch can have its own switch

callouts.p: Household lights and sockets are wired in parallel, so each gets the full mains p.d. and can be switched on and off independently.

core.p: A **voltmeter** measures the **potential difference (p.d.)**, also called voltage, across a component, in **volts (V)**. P.d. is a difference between two points, so the voltmeter must be connected **across** the component, **in parallel** with it, with one lead on each side.
bullets: Connect one terminal to each end of the component.
Do **not** break the circuit to add a voltmeter; add it on afterwards across the component.
A voltmeter has a **very high resistance**, so almost no current flows through it and it does not change the circuit.
If wrongly connected in series, its very high resistance would stop almost all the current.
The reading is in **volts (V)**.

callouts.p: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference, in volts, across it.

core.p: Although ammeters are covered in more detail in 10.7, exam questions often mix them up with voltmeters. An **ammeter** measures **current** in **amperes (A)** and is connected **in series**, so all the current passes through it.
bullets: Ammeter: in **series**, very **low resistance**, measures current in A.
Voltmeter: in **parallel**, very **high resistance**, measures p.d. in V.
Memory aid: 'Ammeters in A line, Voltmeters on the Verge (beside)'.

callouts.p: Saying a voltmeter is in series, or an ammeter in parallel, loses the mark every time.

core.h: Drawing circuit diagrams in the exam
core.p: Many questions ask you to draw a circuit to carry out an investigation, for example to find how the current through a lamp changes with p.d. Use a clear, standard layout.
bullets: Draw the supply (cell or battery), then a **single loop** containing the component, an ammeter and a variable resistor (to change the current).
Add the **voltmeter in parallel** across the component last.
Use a ruler and draw symbols the right size; label if unsure.
Check: complete loop, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel, correct symbols.

callouts.p: Typically 1 mark for correct symbols, 1 for ammeter in series, 1 for voltmeter in parallel across the component, 1 for a way to vary the p.d. (variable resistor or variable supply).

core.p: Grade 9 answers explain **why** the rules are true using charge and energy. In series there is only one path, so the same charge must pass through each component (same current), and the energy each coulomb gets from the supply is shared between the components (p.d. shared). In parallel each coulomb goes through only one branch, so it transfers all its energy in that branch (same p.d. across each branch).
bullets: Same current in series: charge is not used up, and there is nowhere else for it to go.
Current splits in parallel: charge is conserved at junctions, so branch currents add up to the total.
P.d. shared in series: energy per coulomb supplied is divided between the components.
Same p.d. in parallel: each branch is connected directly across the supply.

analogy.p: A series circuit is like a single-lane road through several towns: every car (charge) must pass through every town, so the traffic flow (current) is the same everywhere, and if one bridge closes, the whole route stops. A parallel circuit is like a motorway that splits into several separate roads: cars choose one road, the traffic divides at the junction and rejoins later, and a closed road does not stop traffic on the others. A voltmeter is like a surveyor comparing the height of the road before and after a hill: they stand beside the road and do not block it. Where it breaks down: cars use up fuel and can park, but charge is never used up and current in a series circuit is the same everywhere instantly; also the height-difference idea of p.d. is only a model of energy per unit charge.

terms.d: A drawing of a circuit using standard symbols to show how components are connected.
A single source of potential difference; the long line of its symbol is the positive terminal.
Two or more cells connected together.
A component that opens or closes a gap in a circuit to stop or allow a current.
A component that limits (reduces) the current in a circuit.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed, used to vary the current.
A component that allows current to flow in one direction only.
Light-emitting diode: a diode that gives out light when a current flows through it in the forward direction.
Light-dependent resistor: a resistor whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases.
A resistor whose resistance changes with temperature (for the common type, resistance decreases as temperature increases).
A circuit with all components in a single loop, so there is only one path for the current.
A circuit in which components are on separate branches connected across the same two points.
A point in a circuit where the current splits or joins.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts (V).
A meter connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference across it, in volts.
A meter connected in series to measure the current, in amperes.

mistakes.w: A voltmeter is connected in series with the component.
mistakes.r: A voltmeter is connected in parallel (across) the component.

mistakes.w: Voltmeter measures the current through the lamp.
mistakes.r: A voltmeter measures the potential difference across the component, in volts.

mistakes.w: Current is used up as it goes round a series circuit, so it is smaller after each lamp.
mistakes.r: Current is the same at all points in a series circuit; charge is not used up.

mistakes.w: In a parallel circuit the p.d. is shared between the branches.
mistakes.r: Each branch has the same p.d. as the supply; it is the current that splits.

mistakes.w: Drawing the LDR with arrows pointing out (or LED with arrows in).
mistakes.r: LDR arrows point in (light received); LED arrows point out (light emitted).

mistakes.w: Adding more resistors in parallel increases the total resistance.
mistakes.r: Adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance, because there are more paths for the charge.

mistakes.w: The short thick line of a cell is positive.
mistakes.r: The long thin line is the positive terminal; the short thick line is negative.

mistakes.w: A battery is the same as a cell.
mistakes.r: A battery is two or more cells joined together.

mistakes.w: Drawing a variable resistor as a resistor with an arrow touching it from the side.
mistakes.r: A variable resistor has a diagonal arrow drawn through the rectangle.

exam.q: Draw the circuit symbol for a light-dependent resistor (LDR).
model: Rectangle (resistor) inside a circle with two arrows pointing towards it.
exam.tip: Arrows must point in.

exam.q: State the unit of potential difference.
model: Volt (V).
exam.tip: Do not write 'voltage' as the unit.

exam.q: State how a voltmeter should be connected to measure the potential difference across a lamp.
model: In parallel with / across the lamp.
exam.tip: 'Across' and 'in parallel' are both accepted.

exam.q: Name the component whose symbol is a circle with a cross inside it.
model: (Filament) lamp.
exam.tip: Not 'bulb' if the question asks for the component name; 'lamp' is safest.

exam.q: Describe two differences between a series circuit and a parallel circuit.
model: Series has one path; parallel has more than one path / branches.
Current same everywhere in series but splits in parallel / p.d. shared in series but same across each branch in parallel / one fault stops all in series but not in parallel.
exam.tip: Each difference must mention both types of circuit.

exam.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series to a 6 V battery. State the p.d. across each lamp and explain your answer.
model: The supply p.d. is shared between components in series, and identical lamps share it equally.
exam.tip: Equal sharing only works for identical components.

exam.q: The same two lamps are now connected in parallel to the 6 V battery. State the p.d. across each lamp.
model: 6 V (each).
exam.tip: Parallel branches each get the full supply p.d.

exam.q: Explain why the lights in a house are connected in parallel rather than in series.
model: Each light gets the full (mains) p.d.
Each light can be switched on and off independently.
If one light fails, the others keep working.
exam.tip: Three separate advantages for three marks.

exam.q: Draw a circuit that could be used to measure the current through and the potential difference across a fixed resistor, with a way of changing the current.
model: Correct symbols for cell/battery and resistor in a complete loop.
Ammeter in series with the resistor.
Voltmeter in parallel across the resistor.
Variable resistor in series (or variable power supply).
exam.tip: Check each meter's position before you finish.

exam.q: A student builds a circuit with a battery, a switch, and three identical lamps. Lamp X is in the main circuit and lamps Y and Z are in parallel with each other. Explain what happens to the brightness of the lamps when lamp Z is removed. Use ideas about current, potential difference and resistance, and comment on how the circuit shows the differences between series and parallel connections.
model: Y and Z are in parallel, so removing Z leaves only one path for that part of the circuit.
The resistance of the parallel section increases (one branch instead of two).
So the total resistance of the circuit increases.
So the current from the battery (through X) decreases, and X gets dimmer.
The p.d. across X decreases, so the p.d. across Y increases (supply p.d. shared in series).
So Y gets brighter; X is in series, so all current passes through it, whereas Y and Z shared the current.
exam.tip: Work step by step: resistance first, then current, then the p.d. shares, then brightness.

worked.q: A 9 V battery is connected to a lamp and a resistor in series. A voltmeter across the resistor reads 5.5 V. What would a voltmeter across the lamp read?
steps: In series the supply p.d. is shared: V_supply = V_lamp + V_resistor.
worked.ans: 3.5 V across the lamp.

worked.q: A 12 V supply is connected to three lamps in parallel. The branch currents are 0.5 A, 0.5 A and 1.0 A. Find the p.d. across each lamp and the current from the supply.
steps: In parallel, each branch has the same p.d. as the supply, so each lamp has 12 V across it.
Current splits at the junctions, so total current = sum of branch currents.
worked.ans: 12 V across each lamp; 2.0 A from the supply.

worked.q: Model answer: a student connects a voltmeter in series with a lamp and a cell. The lamp does not light and the voltmeter reads almost the full cell p.d. Explain why.
steps: A voltmeter has a very high resistance.
In series, all the current must pass through the voltmeter, so the current becomes almost zero.
With almost no current the lamp cannot light.
Almost all of the supply p.d. is across the very high resistance of the voltmeter, so it reads close to the cell p.d.
The voltmeter should be connected in parallel across the lamp instead.
worked.ans: The voltmeter's very high resistance in series stops the current; it must be connected in parallel.

phy_edx.9.10.summary: The heating effect of an electric current has both **advantages** and **disadvantages**. It is **useful** whenever we want heating: kettles, electric heaters, toasters, irons, hair dryers, electric showers and the **fuse**, which melts to protect a circuit. It is a **disadvantage** whenever heating is not wanted: it **wastes energy** (lowering efficiency), can **damage components**, and overheated wires can melt insulation and cause **fires**. Grade 9 answers explain the reasoning: heating comes from electrons doing work against resistance, so it can be designed in (high resistance elements) or designed out (low resistance wires).

core.p: You must **describe the advantages and disadvantages of the heating effect of an electric current**. Expect short 'give one advantage' questions and longer evaluate or discuss questions with appliances.
bullets: **Advantage**: the heating is the useful output of the appliance (or is used for safety).
**Disadvantage**: the heating is unwanted, wastes energy or causes harm.
The same physics causes both: electrons collide with lattice ions and transfer energy to the thermal store.
Always link your answer to a **named example**.

callouts.p: Whether heating is an advantage or disadvantage depends on **whether it is the job the device is meant to do**.

core.h: Reminder: where the heating comes from
core.p: When there is a current in a resistor, work is done against resistance. Electrons collide with the ions in the metal lattice, the ions vibrate more and the resistor gets hotter, transferring energy to the surroundings.
bullets: More current -> more heating.
More resistance -> more heating for the same current.
So heating devices use **high resistance** elements, and cables use **low resistance** wires.
This background (10.22 to 10.25) is what lets you explain each advantage and disadvantage.

core.p: Many appliances exist purely to make use of the heating effect. Their **heating element** is a coil or strip of high resistance metal wire which gets hot when a current passes.
bullets: **Electric kettles** and **electric showers**: heat water.
**Electric fires / heaters** and **storage heaters**: heat rooms.
**Toasters** and **electric ovens/hobs**: cook food.
**Irons** and **hair dryers**: heat cloth or air.
**Immersion heaters**: heat a tank of water.
In these appliances, nearly all the electrical energy goes to the thermal store, which is exactly what we want.

fig.cap: An electric kettle uses the heating effect: a current in the high resistance heating element transfers energy to the thermal store of the element and then the water.

core.p: Because all of the electrical energy ends up as thermal energy, an electric heater can be described as transferring essentially **all** of its input energy into heating. The 'waste' heat of other devices is the useful output here.
bullets: Heating is easy to **control**: switch on and off instantly, use a thermostat.
**Clean at the point of use**: no fumes, smoke or flames in the home.
Heating can be placed exactly where needed (e.g. underfloor heating, a small heater).
Electric heaters are simple and need little maintenance.

callouts.p: An electric heater may transfer almost all its energy to heating, but electricity can be **more expensive** per unit of energy than gas, and power stations may waste energy and release CO2 generating it.

core.p: A **fuse** uses the heating effect to protect a circuit. It contains a thin wire with a low melting point. If the current becomes too large, the fuse wire heats up and **melts**, breaking the circuit.
bullets: Melting stops the current, preventing cables overheating and catching fire.
It protects the appliance and the wiring; with an earth wire it protects the user from electric shock.
The fuse rating should be just above the normal operating current.
Fuse details and choosing ratings belong to 10.37 to 10.41; here, recognise the fuse as a **useful application of the heating effect**.

fig.cap: A cartridge fuse: if the current is too large, the thin fuse wire heats up enough to melt, breaking the circuit. This is a safety advantage of the heating effect.

core.p: Historically, the heating effect made **filament lamps** work: the filament gets so hot it glows and gives out light.
bullets: The filament is a thin coil of high melting point metal (tungsten).
It is heated to a very high temperature so it emits visible light.
However, most of the energy is still transferred by heating, which is wasted (see disadvantages).

core.p: In any device that is not meant to heat things, heating is **unwanted energy transfer**: the energy is **dissipated** to the surroundings and is not useful.
bullets: Wasted thermal energy in **wires and cables** (including power transmission lines).
**Filament lamps** waste most of their input energy as heat, which is why they have been replaced by LEDs.
Computers, phones, TVs, chargers and motors all get warm: wasted energy.
Wasted energy lowers **efficiency** and increases the cost of electricity bills.
More wasted energy means more electricity generated, often from fossil fuels, so more environmental impact.

callouts.p: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input (can be given as a decimal or percentage).

fig.cap: Comparing an electric heater and a filament lamp, each with 100 J input. For the heater all the thermal energy is useful; for the lamp most of it is wasted heating and only a little becomes useful light.

core.p: If too much current flows, or wires have too high a resistance, wires can get dangerously hot.
bullets: Hot wires can **melt the plastic insulation**, exposing live wires and causing shocks or short circuits.
Overheated wiring can start **fires**.
Overloading a socket with many appliances increases current and heating.
This is why fuses and circuit breakers are needed and why high-current appliances use thick cables.

core.h: Disadvantage 3: damage and reduced lifespan of components
core.p: Heat can damage electronic components and change how circuits behave.
bullets: Overheating can damage microchips and batteries, shortening their life.
Rising temperature changes the **resistance** of components (metals' resistance increases), changing currents.
Devices need **fans, heat sinks or vents** to remove heat, adding cost, size and noise.
Filament lamps eventually fail when the hot filament breaks.

core.p: Engineers reduce unwanted heating in the places it is a problem.
bullets: Use **low resistance** (thick, short, copper) wires.
Keep currents low (e.g. transmit at high voltage in the National Grid).
Use more efficient devices, e.g. **LEDs** instead of filament lamps.
Add cooling (heat sinks, fans) to electronics.
Use fuses and circuit breakers to cut the current if it becomes dangerous.

core.p: Use this table to build balanced answers. In 'discuss' or 'evaluate' questions, give points on both sides and a conclusion.
bullets: Pair each point with an example and a reason.
In a 6-mark answer aim for at least two advantages and two disadvantages, linked to physics.

head: Advantages (heating is wanted)
Disadvantages (heating is unwanted)
rows: Heating water: kettles, showers, immersion heaters
Energy wasted in cables and wires
Filament lamps waste most energy as heat
Lower efficiency and higher energy bills
Easy to control, clean at point of use
Damage to electronics; need for cooling

callouts.p: 'Describe' needs facts with examples; 'explain' needs the reason (e.g. high resistance element, electron-ion collisions).

core.p: Mark schemes reward named examples and correct energy language.
bullets: Say energy is **transferred** or **dissipated**, never 'created' or 'lost' without saying where.
Name the store: **thermal energy store** (of the element, water or surroundings).
Distinguish **useful** and **wasted** energy clearly.
For evaluate questions, end with a judgement, e.g. 'the heating effect is an advantage in a kettle but a disadvantage in a computer'.

analogy.p: The heating effect is like friction on a playground slide. When you rub your hands together to warm them, the friction heating is exactly what you want. On a slide, friction just slows you and wastes energy as heat. Same effect, but whether it is good or bad depends on the job. Where it breaks down: electrical heating comes from electron-ion collisions inside a conductor, not two surfaces rubbing, and we can deliberately change it by choosing the wire's resistance.

terms.d: The energy transfer that heats a resistor when there is a current in it.
A high resistance wire or strip that heats up when a current passes, used in heating appliances.
Energy transferred to the store we want, for the purpose of the device.
Energy transferred to stores that are not wanted, usually dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings.
Spread out into the surroundings so it is less useful.
Energy an object has because of its temperature.
Useful energy output divided by total energy input.
A safety device with a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too large.
The current above which the fuse wire melts; chosen just above normal operating current.
Plastic covering on wires that does not conduct; can melt if the wire overheats.
A component or wire becoming dangerously hot, usually from too large a current.
A lamp that glows because a thin metal filament is heated by the current; wastes most energy as heat.
Light-emitting diode: produces light with much less wasted heating than a filament lamp.
A finned metal block that removes thermal energy from an electronic component.
Opposition to current; higher resistance means more heating for the same current.

mistakes.w: The heating effect is always a disadvantage because energy is lost.
mistakes.r: It is an advantage in heaters, kettles, toasters and fuses, where heating is the useful output.

mistakes.w: Electric heaters create heat.
mistakes.r: Electrical energy is transferred to the thermal store; energy is not created.

mistakes.w: Energy is lost / disappears.
mistakes.r: Energy is dissipated (transferred) to the thermal store of the surroundings.

mistakes.w: A fuse works because it stops electricity using a switch.
mistakes.r: The fuse wire heats up and melts when the current is too large, breaking the circuit.

mistakes.w: Heating elements have low resistance so they get hot.
mistakes.r: Heating elements have a high resistance (compared with connecting wires), so much energy is transferred where it is wanted.

mistakes.w: Disadvantage: it uses electricity.
mistakes.r: Give a specific disadvantage: energy wasted in wires, lower efficiency, overheating, melted insulation, fire risk.

mistakes.w: An electric heater is 100% efficient so it is the cheapest heating.
mistakes.r: It transfers nearly all energy to heating, but cost depends on electricity price and power station losses.

mistakes.w: Advantage: wires get warm.
mistakes.r: Warm wires are a disadvantage (wasted energy); name an appliance where heating is wanted.

exam.q: Give one advantage of the heating effect of an electric current.
model: It is used in heating appliances, e.g. kettle / toaster / electric heater / iron (or used in a fuse).
exam.tip: A named example is enough.

exam.q: Give one disadvantage of the heating effect of an electric current.
model: Energy is wasted (e.g. in wires or lamps) / wires can overheat and cause a fire.
exam.tip: Be specific about what goes wrong.

exam.q: Name an appliance in which the heating effect is the main useful output.
model: Kettle / toaster / electric heater / iron / hair dryer / electric shower.
exam.tip: Avoid 'TV' or 'computer'.

exam.q: Explain why the heating effect is a disadvantage in a laptop computer.
model: Energy is wasted / dissipated to the surroundings
it reduces efficiency (or may damage components, so a fan is needed).
exam.tip: Two linked points: what happens and why it is bad.

exam.q: Explain how a fuse uses the heating effect of a current to protect a circuit.
model: If the current is too large the fuse wire heats up (and melts)
this breaks the circuit so the current stops (preventing overheating/fire).
exam.tip: Mention both melting and breaking the circuit.

exam.q: A filament lamp transfers 60 J of electrical energy; 54 J is transferred by heating. Calculate its efficiency.
model: Useful energy = 60 - 54 = 6 J
efficiency = 6 / 60 = 0.1 (10%)
exam.tip: Useful energy is the light, not the heat.

exam.q: Explain why the heating element of a kettle has a much higher resistance than the cable connecting it to the plug.
model: Heating effect is greater where resistance is higher (for the same current)
so most energy is transferred in the element to heat the water (useful)
low resistance cable wastes little energy / does not overheat.
exam.tip: Same current in series: energy goes where resistance is.

exam.q: Explain why filament lamps have been replaced by LEDs in many homes.
model: Filament lamps transfer most of their energy by heating (wasted)
so they have low efficiency
LEDs waste less energy, so lower running costs (and longer life).
exam.tip: Classic disadvantage example.

exam.q: Describe what can happen if too many appliances are plugged into one socket extension.
model: Total current becomes large
the cables heat up a lot (heating effect)
insulation can melt / fire can start (unless the fuse melts first).
exam.tip: Link current size to heating.

exam.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the heating effect of an electric current. Refer to examples in your answer.
model: Heating effect: energy transferred by heating when current in a resistor
Advantage: heating appliances, e.g. kettles, heaters, toasters, irons, showers
Advantage: fuse melts to protect circuit; heating is easy to control and clean at point of use
Disadvantage: energy wasted in cables / transmission lines / devices such as computers, lowering efficiency
Disadvantage: filament lamps waste most energy; overheating can melt insulation and cause fires
Conclusion: useful where heating is the purpose, unwanted elsewhere; reduce waste with low resistance wires.
exam.tip: Balance both sides, use examples, and finish with a conclusion.

worked.q: An electric heater and a filament lamp each take 2000 J of electrical energy. The heater transfers all 2000 J to heating the room. The lamp transfers 200 J as light. Compare their efficiencies.
steps: Heater: useful output = 2000 J (heating is the purpose)
Lamp: useful output = 200 J of light; 1800 J wasted by heating
worked.ans: Heater 100%, lamp 10%: the same heating effect is useful in the heater but wasteful in the lamp.

worked.q: Model answer: give one advantage and one disadvantage of the heating effect for a household, with reasons.
steps: Advantage: an electric kettle uses the heating effect to boil water quickly; the element has high resistance so energy is transferred to the water.
Disadvantage: cables and appliances such as TVs also get warm, so some energy is dissipated to the surroundings as wasted energy, raising bills.
Safety point: if the current is too large, wires overheat; a fuse melts to break the circuit.
worked.ans: Useful in heating appliances (kettle); wasteful and potentially dangerous in wires and non-heating devices.

worked.q: A cable has resistance 0.5 ohms and carries 13 A. Use P = I squared x R to find the power wasted as heat, and say whether this is an advantage or a disadvantage.
steps: P = I squared x R = 13 squared x 0.5
This heating is in the cable, not the appliance, so it is wasted energy.
It is a disadvantage: lower efficiency and the cable could overheat; a thicker cable would reduce it.
worked.ans: About 85 W wasted: a disadvantage of the heating effect.

phy_edx.9.11.summary: When a current flows through a component, the charges transfer energy to it: the energy transferred is **E = I × V × t**. **Power** is the rate of energy transfer, **P = E / t**, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). Combining these gives **P = I × V**, and substituting V = I × R gives **P = I² × R**, which shows why the heating effect grows with the square of the current and why power is transmitted at low current.

core.p: A potential difference pushes charge round a circuit. Each coulomb of charge transfers V joules of energy to a component (E = Q × V), and the charge passing in time t is Q = I × t. Putting these together gives the energy transferred to a component.
bullets: **E = I × V × t** — energy transferred (J) = current (A) × potential difference (V) × time (s)
This equation must be **recalled** (it is not on the equation sheet)
Derivation: E = Q × V and Q = I × t, so E = (I × t) × V
Energy is transferred **electrically** (work is done by the current) from the source to the component
The bigger the current, the p.d. or the time, the more energy is transferred
Time must be in **seconds**: 1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 3600 s

callouts.p: E = I × V × t. Equivalent to E = Q × V with Q = I × t.

core.h: Why work is done in a component
core.p: As charges (electrons in a metal) move through a resistor they collide with the vibrating ions of the lattice. Work is done against resistance, and energy is transferred from the charges to the thermal store of the component. In a motor much of the energy instead ends up in the kinetic store.
bullets: **Work done = energy transferred** — both measured in joules
In a resistor or heater: energy goes to the **thermal energy store** of the resistor and then to the surroundings
In a motor: energy goes mainly to the **kinetic energy store** (some is wasted by heating)
The source (cell or mains) transfers energy to the charges; the components transfer it away
Energy is conserved: energy supplied by the source = total energy transferred by all components

core.h: Power: the rate of energy transfer
core.p: Power tells you how quickly energy is transferred, not how much. Two appliances can transfer the same total energy, but the one with the higher power does it in less time.
bullets: **P = E / t** — power (W) = energy transferred (J) ÷ time taken (s)
**1 watt = 1 joule per second**
1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W; 1 megawatt (MW) = 1 000 000 W
Rearranged: E = P × t and t = E / P
On an energy–time graph the **gradient is the power**
A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J every second

callouts.p: Power is the energy transferred per second (the rate of energy transfer).
Do not say a high-power device 'has more energy'. It transfers energy more quickly.

fig.cap: Energy transferred against time for two devices. Both lines go through the origin because energy transferred is proportional to time at constant power; the steeper line has the higher power, since gradient = energy ÷ time = power.

core.h: Power, current and potential difference: P = I × V
core.p: Dividing E = I × V × t by t gives P = I × V. The power transferred in any device depends on both the potential difference across it and the current through it.
bullets: **P = I × V** — power (W) = current (A) × potential difference (V)
Must be **recalled**
Why: V is the energy per coulomb and I is the coulombs per second, so I × V = joules per second
Doubling the current at the same p.d. doubles the power
Doubling the p.d. at the same current doubles the power
Rearranged: I = P / V (used to find the current an appliance draws) and V = P / I

callouts.p: Energy per coulomb (V) × coulombs per second (I) = energy per second (P).

fig.cap: Measuring the power transferred in a resistor: the ammeter (in series) measures the current I and the voltmeter (in parallel across the resistor) measures the potential difference V, so P = I × V.

core.h: Power and resistance: P = I² × R
core.p: Substituting V = I × R into P = I × V gives P = I × (I × R) = I² × R. This version is the best one to use when you know the current and the resistance, and it explains the heating effect of a current.
bullets: **P = I² × R** — power (W) = current squared (A²) × resistance (Ω)
Must be **recalled**
Power is proportional to the **square** of the current: doubling I makes P **four times** bigger (at constant R)
Halving the current cuts the power to one quarter
For a fixed current, a larger resistance means a larger power transfer
Square the current first, then multiply by R

callouts.p: I² × R means (I × I) × R, not (I × R)².

core.p: All three power equations describe the same quantity. Pick the one that uses the quantities given in the question so you do not need extra steps.
bullets: Given energy and time → **P = E / t**
Given current and p.d. → **P = I × V**
Given current and resistance → **P = I² × R**
Given current, p.d. and time and asked for energy → **E = I × V × t**
If you are given V and R, first find I = V / R, then use P = I × V
Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with a unit

fig.cap: Choosing a power equation: all three give power in watts, so choose the one that matches the two quantities the question gives you.

core.p: Many lost marks come from units. Convert to base units before substituting.
bullets: Current: mA → A by dividing by 1000 (250 mA = 0.25 A)
Power: kW → W by multiplying by 1000 (2.5 kW = 2500 W)
Energy: kJ → J by multiplying by 1000; MJ → J by multiplying by 1 000 000
Time: minutes × 60 = seconds; hours × 3600 = seconds
Resistance in ohms (Ω); kΩ × 1000 = Ω
Give the final unit: W for power, J for energy

callouts.p: Large energies are often best given in standard form, e.g. 7.2 × 10^6 J.

core.h: Power in series and parallel circuits
core.p: The equations apply to each component and to the whole circuit. The total power supplied by the source equals the sum of the powers transferred in all the components.
bullets: Series: same current I in every component, so the component with the **largest resistance** has the largest p.d. and the **largest power** (P = I² × R)
Parallel: same p.d. V across each branch, so the branch with the **smallest resistance** draws the largest current and has the **largest power** (P = V × I)
Total power from the supply = I(total) × V(supply)
Total power = sum of the powers in each component (energy is conserved)

core.h: Explaining the heating effect with P = I² × R
core.p: Because heating power depends on the square of the current, large currents cause a lot of heating. This is useful in heaters but wasteful in cables and devices where heating is unwanted.
bullets: Wires get hot when currents are large: power wasted = I² × R of the wire
Thick wires have lower resistance, so less power is wasted for the same current
Heating elements use high-resistance wire so that a lot of power is transferred to the thermal store
Reducing the current is the most effective way to reduce wasted power (halving I quarters the loss)

callouts.p: Wasted power in a cable ∝ I². This is why the National Grid uses very high p.d. and low current.

core.p: Power ratings let you compare how quickly appliances transfer energy and how much current they draw from a fixed supply.
bullets: Higher power rating → more energy transferred per second
On the same supply p.d., current I = P / V, so a higher power appliance draws a larger current
Energy used = power × time, so a low-power device left on for a long time can transfer more energy than a high-power device used briefly

core.p: Edexcel calculations usually award marks for substitution, rearrangement and evaluation. Show every step.
bullets: Step 1: write the equation in symbols
Step 2: convert units (mA → A, minutes → s, kW → W)
Step 3: substitute the numbers
Step 4: rearrange if needed (it is fine to rearrange before substituting)
Step 5: give the answer with a correct unit and sensible significant figures
For two-stage questions, find the missing quantity first (e.g. I from P = I × V, then E = I × V × t)

callouts.p: A correct substitution often earns a mark even if the final answer has an arithmetic slip.

analogy.p: Think of charges as delivery vans carrying energy parcels. The potential difference is the size of the parcel each van (each coulomb) drops off at a component; the current is how many vans pass per second. Power = parcel size × vans per second = energy delivered per second, which is P = I × V. Over a time t, the total delivered is I × V × t. Where it breaks down: real charges do not carry a parcel and run out; they transfer energy continuously as they move, the electrons drift slowly, and energy is transferred through the fields in the circuit, not physically carried by individual charges from the cell.

terms.d: The amount of work done by the current in a component, in joules; E = I × V × t.
The energy transferred per second (rate of energy transfer), in watts.
The unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second.
1000 watts.
The unit of energy and work done.
The rate of flow of charge, in amperes; I = Q / t.
The energy transferred per unit charge passed between two points, in volts; V = E / Q.
One joule per coulomb.
Opposition to current; R = V / I, measured in ohms (Ω).
Energy transferred when a force moves something or when a current flows through a component.
Measured in coulombs (C); Q = I × t.
Energy transferred to the thermal store of a conductor when a current flows through its resistance.
Meter connected in series to measure current.
Meter connected in parallel across a component to measure potential difference.

mistakes.w: Using time in minutes or hours in E = I × V × t.
mistakes.r: Convert time to seconds before substituting (e.g. 5 min = 300 s).

mistakes.w: Calculating I × R and then squaring for P = I² × R.
mistakes.r: Square the current only, then multiply by R: P = (I × I) × R.

mistakes.w: Power is the energy an appliance has.
mistakes.r: Power is the energy transferred per second (rate of energy transfer).

mistakes.w: Doubling the current doubles the heating in a resistor.
mistakes.r: P = I² × R, so doubling the current makes the power four times bigger.

mistakes.w: Leaving current in mA, e.g. P = 250 × 6.
mistakes.r: Convert to amperes first: 250 mA = 0.25 A, so P = 0.25 × 6 = 1.5 W.

mistakes.w: Writing the unit of power as J or the unit of energy as W.
mistakes.r: Power in watts (W); energy in joules (J).

mistakes.w: Rearranging P = I × V as I = P × V.
mistakes.r: I = P / V.

mistakes.w: Saying the resistor with the smallest resistance gets the most power in a series circuit.
mistakes.r: In series the current is the same, so P = I² × R is largest for the largest resistance.

exam.q: State the equation linking power, current and potential difference.
model: power = current × potential difference (P = I × V)
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols both earn the mark.

exam.q: State what is meant by power.
model: Energy transferred per second / rate of energy transfer
exam.tip: Include 'per second' or 'rate'.

exam.q: A lamp is connected to a 12 V supply and a current of 2.0 A flows for 60 s. Calculate the energy transferred.
exam.tip: Check time is in seconds.

exam.q: A heater has a power of 2.0 kW. Calculate the energy it transfers in 5 minutes.
model: Convert: 2.0 kW = 2000 W and 5 min = 300 s
exam.tip: Two conversions here; each is a common place to lose marks.

exam.q: A current of 3.0 A flows through a 4.0 Ω resistor. Calculate the power transferred.
model: P = 36 W

exam.q: A 230 V toaster has a power of 920 W. Calculate the current in the toaster.
model: P = I × V
exam.tip: Rearrangement mark is separate from the answer mark.

exam.q: The current in a resistor is doubled while its resistance stays the same. Describe and explain what happens to the power transferred.
model: Power becomes four times bigger
Because P = I² × R so power is proportional to current squared
exam.tip: Give the factor (four times), not just 'increases'.

exam.q: Explain why energy is transferred in a resistor when there is a current in it.
model: Electrons collide with ions in the lattice / work is done against resistance
Energy is transferred to the thermal store of the resistor (it heats up)
exam.tip: Mention both the cause (collisions) and the result (heating).

exam.q: Explain how the power transferred in a device is related to the potential difference across it and the current in it.
model: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge (per coulomb)
Current is charge flowing per second
So p.d. × current = energy transferred per second
Which is power, so P = I × V (power increases if either increases)
exam.tip: Linking 'per coulomb' and 'coulombs per second' is the key idea.

exam.q: Two resistors, 2 Ω and 6 Ω, are connected in series to a 12 V battery. Calculate the power transferred in the 6 Ω resistor and explain why it is greater than in the 2 Ω resistor.
model: Total resistance = 8 Ω so I = V / R = 12 / 8 = 1.5 A
Same current in series, so the larger resistance has the larger power (P = I² × R)
exam.tip: Find the current first; it is the same in both resistors.

exam.q: A student wants to find the power of a small motor. Describe how they could do this, including the measurements they would take and how they would calculate the power.
model: Connect the motor in series with a power supply/cell and an ammeter
Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the motor
Switch on and record the current I and potential difference V
Calculate power using P = I × V
Repeat readings and calculate a mean
Alternatively measure energy transferred with a joulemeter and time with a stopwatch and use P = E / t
Switch off between readings to avoid the wires heating up
exam.tip: Correct meter positions (ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel) are usually worth marks.

worked.q: A phone charger supplies 5.0 V and a current of 800 mA for 2 hours. Calculate the energy transferred.
A kettle transfers 540 000 J in 3 minutes from a 230 V supply. Calculate (a) its power and (b) the current.
A cable has a resistance of 0.50 Ω. Compare the power wasted in it when the current is 10 A and when it is 5 A.
steps: Halving the current quarters the power wasted because P ∝ I²
worked.ans: 50 W and 12.5 W; halving the current reduces the wasted power to one quarter.

phy_edx.9.12.summary: Domestic appliances are supplied with energy either by **batteries** (energy from a chemical store, direct current) or by the **a.c. mains** (energy from power stations). In both cases energy is **transferred electrically** by the current, and the appliance transfers it to a useful store: the **kinetic store** of a motor or the **thermal store** of a heating device, with some energy wasted, usually by heating the surroundings. You must be able to describe these transfers for named devices and judge how efficient they are.

core.h: Two sources of electrical energy at home
core.p: Every electrical appliance needs a source that does work on the charges. In homes this is either a battery or the mains supply.
bullets: **Batteries and cells**: energy comes from their **chemical energy store**; they supply **direct current (d.c.)**
**Mains supply**: energy comes from power stations via the National Grid; supplies **alternating current (a.c.)**
Either way, energy is **transferred electrically** (by the work done by the current) to the appliance
Battery devices are portable; mains devices can have much higher power
As a battery is used, its chemical store empties until it is 'flat' and must be recharged or replaced

callouts.p: Store → transferred electrically → useful store in the appliance (+ wasted energy to surroundings).

core.p: Edexcel uses the energy stores and pathways model. Describe where the energy starts, how it is transferred, and where it ends up.
bullets: Energy stores: chemical, kinetic, thermal, gravitational potential, elastic potential, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear
Transfer pathways: **electrically**, mechanically (by forces), by heating, by radiation (light, sound waves)
An electric current transfers energy **electrically**
Wasted energy usually ends up in the **thermal store of the surroundings**, which becomes spread out (dissipated)
Energy is always conserved: total energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy out

callouts.p: Avoid 'electrical energy turns into...'. Mark schemes reward 'energy is transferred electrically to the thermal store of ...'.

core.p: Heating devices contain a heating element: a wire with high resistance. When a current flows, electrons collide with ions in the wire, transferring energy to the thermal store of the element, which then heats its surroundings.
bullets: Examples: kettle, electric heater, toaster, iron, oven, immersion heater, hairdryer element
Useful transfer: electrically → **thermal store** of the element → thermal store of water, air or food
Some energy is wasted heating the kettle body and the surrounding air
Heating devices are very efficient at heating because heating is the intended output
Usually mains powered because heating needs high power (kilowatts)

fig.cap: Sankey diagram for a kettle: 2000 J is transferred electrically; 1600 J goes to the thermal store of the water (useful) and 400 J heats the kettle and surroundings (wasted). Efficiency = 1600 / 2000 = 0.8 (80%). Arrow widths are proportional to energy.

core.p: An electric motor transfers energy electrically to the kinetic store of its rotating parts. Motors are found in many appliances, both mains and battery powered.
bullets: Examples: fan, washing machine, food mixer, vacuum cleaner, electric drill, electric toothbrush, toy car
Useful transfer: electrically → **kinetic store** of the motor and what it drives
Wasted: thermal store of the motor and surroundings (friction and heating of the coils), and sound
Battery examples: toy car, cordless drill, electric toothbrush (chemical store → kinetic store)
Mains examples: washing machine drum, blender, vacuum cleaner

callouts.p: Always include the wasted energy: thermal (heating of the motor and surroundings) and sound.

fig.cap: A battery-powered fan: energy from the battery's chemical store is transferred electrically to the motor, then mechanically to the kinetic store of the blades. Some energy is wasted by heating the motor and its surroundings and as sound.

core.h: Appliances with more than one useful output
core.p: Some appliances contain both a heating element and a motor, so energy is usefully transferred to two stores.
bullets: Hairdryer: heating element → thermal store of the air; motor and fan → kinetic store of the air
Tumble dryer: heater warms the air; motor turns the drum
Washing machine: heater warms the water; motor spins the drum
Electric oven with fan: element heats, fan moves the hot air
Still some wasted energy: sound, heating the casing
