core.p: Batteries make devices portable but store only a limited amount of energy and supply low p.d., so battery devices tend to be low power.
bullets: Energy from the **chemical store** of the battery is transferred electrically
Torch: to the lamp, which radiates light (useful) and heats up (wasted)
Phone: to the speaker (sound), the screen (light) and the circuits (thermal, wasted)
Cordless drill: to the motor's kinetic store
Rechargeable batteries are recharged from the mains: energy is transferred electrically back into their chemical store

core.p: The mains supplies a.c. at about 230 V, so mains devices can draw large currents and have high power ratings.
bullets: Energy ultimately comes from power stations (fossil fuels, nuclear, renewables) via the National Grid
Mains supply transfers energy electrically to the appliance
High-power heating devices (kettles, ovens, heaters) are always mains powered
Mains devices can run continuously without running out, unlike batteries

core.p: No device transfers all the energy usefully except heaters, where all the energy eventually heats something. Wasted energy is dissipated, spreading out into the surroundings, so it becomes less useful.
bullets: **Useful energy**: transferred to the store you want
**Wasted energy**: transferred to stores you do not want, mainly the thermal store of the surroundings
Wasted energy is caused by resistance in wires (heating) and friction in moving parts
Dissipated energy cannot easily be used again
Reduce waste in motors with lubrication; reduce heating losses with insulation

core.p: Efficiency tells you what fraction of the energy supplied is transferred usefully.
bullets: **efficiency = useful energy transferred ÷ total energy supplied**
Can be given as a decimal (0.8) or a percentage (80%)
Can also use power: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input
Efficiency is always less than 1 (100%) for real devices that have wasted outputs
Energy wasted = total energy supplied − useful energy

callouts.p: Efficiency = (useful energy transferred by the device) / (total energy supplied to the device).

core.p: How much energy an appliance transfers depends on its power and on how long it is used.
bullets: E = P × t: energy (J) = power (W) × time (s)
A higher power appliance transfers energy to its useful store faster
A 3 kW kettle heats water faster than a 2 kW kettle (more energy per second to the thermal store)
A battery with a bigger chemical store lasts longer for the same power

core.p: For 'describe the energy transfers' questions, give a full chain.
bullets: 1. Name the starting store (chemical store of battery, or energy from the mains)
2. Say it is **transferred electrically** by the current
3. Name the useful store (kinetic store of motor, thermal store of the heating element/water)
4. Name the wasted energy and where it goes (thermal store of the surroundings, sound)
5. Mention conservation: total in = useful + wasted

callouts.p: 'Thermal store of the water' scores better than just 'heat'.

analogy.p: Think of the battery or mains as a pump and the current as water flowing through pipes. The water turns a water wheel (a motor, kinetic store) or flows through a narrow, rough pipe where it rubs and warms the pipe (a heating element, thermal store). Some energy is always lost to friction and splashing, like the wasted heat and sound. Where it breaks down: in a circuit the charges are not used up or stored in the appliance, and a battery's energy is in a chemical store, not a reservoir of charge; mains a.c. also reverses direction, unlike a steady pump.

terms.d: A way energy is held, e.g. chemical, kinetic, thermal, gravitational potential.
Energy stored in chemical bonds, e.g. in a battery or fuel.
Energy a moving object has because of its motion.
Energy an object has because of its temperature (the motion of its particles).
Energy transfer by an electric current doing work.
The a.c. electricity supply to homes, about 230 V at 50 Hz in the UK.
Two or more cells; a source of d.c. that transfers energy from a chemical store.
A high-resistance wire that heats up when a current flows through it.
A device that transfers energy electrically to a kinetic store (rotation).
Energy transferred to the store that the device is designed to fill.
Energy transferred to unwanted stores, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
Spreading out of energy into the surroundings so it is less useful.
Useful energy transferred divided by total energy supplied.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.

mistakes.w: Electrical energy is turned into heat energy.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred electrically to the thermal store of the heating element/water.

mistakes.w: The battery stores electricity/charge.
mistakes.r: The battery has a chemical energy store; energy is transferred electrically when current flows.

mistakes.w: A motor transfers all the energy to kinetic energy.
mistakes.r: Some energy is wasted, heating the motor and surroundings and as sound.

mistakes.w: Energy is used up in the appliance.
mistakes.r: Energy is conserved; it is transferred to other stores, ending up dissipated in the surroundings.

mistakes.w: A kettle wastes energy as kinetic energy.
mistakes.r: A kettle's wasted energy mainly heats the kettle body and the surrounding air (thermal store of surroundings).

mistakes.w: Efficiency = wasted energy ÷ useful energy.
mistakes.r: Efficiency = useful energy transferred ÷ total energy supplied.

mistakes.w: Batteries supply alternating current like the mains.
mistakes.r: Batteries and cells supply direct current; the mains supplies alternating current.

mistakes.w: Only listing 'sound' and 'heat' as outputs without saying which are useful.
mistakes.r: State the useful store clearly and identify the wasted outputs separately.

exam.q: Name the energy store of a battery.
model: Chemical (energy store)
exam.tip: One word answer, but must be 'chemical'.

exam.q: State the useful energy store that a heating element transfers energy to.
model: Thermal (energy store) of the element / of the surroundings being heated
exam.tip: 'Heat' alone may not score.

exam.q: Describe the energy transfers when a battery-powered toy car is moving.
model: Energy from the chemical store of the battery
Transferred electrically to the motor
To the kinetic store of the car (wheels), with some wasted to the thermal store of the surroundings/sound
exam.tip: Start store, pathway, end store.

exam.q: Describe the energy transfers in an electric kettle.
model: Energy is transferred electrically from the mains to the heating element
to the thermal store of the water (and some to the thermal store of the kettle/surroundings)
exam.tip: Mention both useful and wasted.

exam.q: A food mixer is supplied with 500 J of energy and transfers 350 J to the kinetic store of the blades. Calculate the efficiency.
model: efficiency = useful / total = 350 / 500
exam.tip: No unit for efficiency.

exam.q: For the food mixer above, calculate the wasted energy and state where it goes.
model: Thermal store of the motor/surroundings and sound
exam.tip: Use conservation of energy.

exam.q: Explain why heating appliances such as ovens are usually mains powered rather than battery powered.
model: Heating requires a high power / large energy transfer per second
Batteries have a limited chemical store/low p.d. so cannot supply that power for long (mains can)
exam.tip: Link power to the supply.

exam.q: A hairdryer contains a heating element and a motor. Describe the useful energy transfers.
model: Heating element: energy transferred electrically to the thermal store of the air
Motor and fan: energy transferred to the kinetic store of the air
exam.tip: Two separate useful transfers.

exam.q: Explain why some of the energy transferred to an electric motor is wasted.
model: Current in the coils/wires heats them because of resistance
Friction between moving parts transfers energy to thermal stores
Energy is dissipated to the surroundings (and as sound)
exam.tip: Two causes: resistance and friction.

exam.q: Compare the energy transfers in a battery-powered electric toothbrush and a mains-powered electric heater.
model: Toothbrush energy source: chemical store of the battery (d.c.)
Heater energy source: mains supply from power station (a.c.)
Both transfer energy electrically
Toothbrush: useful energy to the kinetic store of the moving brush head via a motor
Heater: useful energy to the thermal store of the element and then the air in the room
Toothbrush wastes energy as heating of motor and sound
Heater is (nearly) 100% efficient at heating; toothbrush is less efficient
Heater has a much higher power
exam.tip: A 6-mark compare needs points about both devices, linked with 'whereas'.

worked.q: A 1200 W microwave runs for 2 minutes. 115 200 J ends up in the thermal store of the food. Calculate the efficiency.
steps: Total energy supplied E = P × t = 1200 × 120 = 144 000 J
worked.ans: 0.8 (80%); the other 28 800 J is wasted heating the oven and surroundings.

worked.q: Describe fully the energy transfers when a cordless drill is used to drill a hole.
steps: Starting store: chemical energy store of the battery
Pathway: energy transferred electrically by the current to the motor
Useful store: kinetic store of the motor and drill bit
Wasted: thermal store of the motor, the drill bit, the wood and the surroundings (friction) and sound
Conservation: chemical energy decrease = kinetic + thermal + sound
worked.ans: Chemical store of battery → electrically → kinetic store of drill (useful); thermal and sound to surroundings (wasted).

phy_edx.9.13.summary: **Direct current (d.c.)** is a movement of charge in **one direction only**; cells and batteries supply d.c. because their potential difference (a **direct voltage**) always has the same direction. In **alternating current (a.c.)** the movement of charge **repeatedly changes direction**, because the **alternating voltage** keeps reversing. The UK domestic (mains) supply is a.c. at a **frequency of 50 Hz** and a voltage of **about 230 V**.

core.p: The type of current depends on the voltage (potential difference) driving it. A direct voltage always pushes charge the same way; an alternating voltage keeps reversing, so the charge keeps reversing too.
bullets: **Direct voltage**: the potential difference always acts in the **same direction**; one terminal is always positive
**Alternating voltage**: the potential difference **repeatedly reverses direction**; each terminal swaps between positive and negative
A direct voltage from a cell is usually constant in size
An alternating voltage changes size continuously as well as changing direction
Direct voltage produces direct current; alternating voltage produces alternating current

callouts.p: Direct voltage: fixed direction. Alternating voltage: direction keeps reversing.

core.p: In a d.c. circuit the charges (electrons in metal wires) drift steadily around the circuit in one direction, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal; conventional current is taken as flowing from positive to negative.
bullets: **Direct current is movement of charge in one direction only**
**Cells and batteries supply direct current**
Examples: torches, phones, laptops (from their batteries), remote controls, cars' 12 V systems
Solar cells also produce d.c.
The current-time graph is a horizontal line (above the axis) for a steady d.c.

callouts.p: Direct current (d.c.) is the movement of charge in one direction only.

fig.cap: Voltage–time graph for a 12 V battery: a horizontal line that stays on one side of the time axis, showing a direct voltage that is constant and never changes direction.

core.p: In an a.c. circuit the charges do not travel round the circuit; they vibrate back and forth about the same positions, reversing direction many times a second. Energy is still transferred to the appliance, because work is done on the charges whichever way they move.
bullets: **In alternating current the movement of charge changes direction** repeatedly
Charges oscillate (move back and forth) rather than drifting round the circuit
The mains supply is a.c.; it is produced by generators in power stations
A.C. is used for the mains because its voltage can easily be changed with transformers
Energy is transferred even though there is no net movement of charge round the circuit

callouts.p: Alternating current (a.c.) is a current in which the movement of charge changes direction (back and forth) repeatedly.

fig.cap: In d.c. the charges drift in one direction only; in a.c. they move back and forth, reversing direction twice in every cycle. At 50 Hz there are 50 cycles each second, so the direction reverses 100 times per second.

core.p: You must recall the three facts about the UK domestic supply: it is a.c., at 50 Hz, about 230 V.
bullets: **Alternating current (a.c.)**
Frequency **50 Hz** (50 complete cycles every second)
Voltage **about 230 V**
Compare: a typical cell is 1.5 V d.c.; a car battery is 12 V d.c.
The mains is dangerous: 230 V can drive a fatal current through the body

callouts.p: UK domestic supply: a.c., 50 Hz, about 230 V.

core.p: Frequency is the number of complete cycles of the alternating voltage each second. The time for one cycle is the period.
bullets: Frequency measured in **hertz (Hz)**; 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second
50 Hz means 50 complete back-and-forth cycles every second
In each cycle the current changes direction twice, so at 50 Hz it reverses 100 times a second
A higher frequency would show more cycles in the same time on a graph

fig.cap: Voltage–time graph for an alternating voltage: the line goes above and below the time axis, showing the direction reversing. One full cycle takes 0.02 s for the 50 Hz UK mains.

core.p: Exam questions often show an oscilloscope trace or a graph and ask you to identify a.c. or d.c.
bullets: D.C.: line stays on **one side** of the time axis (usually a flat horizontal line)
A.C.: line crosses the time axis, going **positive then negative**
The height above the axis shows the size of the voltage; the side shows the direction
Count the cycles in a time interval to find frequency: f = number of cycles ÷ time
Measure the time for one cycle to find the period, then f = 1 / T

callouts.p: If the graph goes below zero, the direction has reversed: it is a.c.

core.p: Power stations use generators, which naturally produce an alternating voltage as coils rotate in magnetic fields. A.C. also allows transformers to step the voltage up and down for efficient transmission.
bullets: Generators produce a.c.
Transformers only work with a.c.
The National Grid steps voltage up (low current) to reduce energy wasted heating the cables, then down to about 230 V for homes
D.C. cannot be stepped up or down with a transformer

core.h: Devices that need d.c. from the mains
core.p: Many electronic devices need low-voltage d.c. so they use a charger or adapter that converts the mains a.c.
bullets: Phone and laptop chargers convert 230 V a.c. to low-voltage d.c.
Batteries can only be recharged with d.c.
Heaters and filament lamps work with either a.c. or d.c. because the heating effect does not depend on the direction of the current
Diodes only let current through in one direction, so they can be used to turn a.c. into d.c.

core.p: Even though charges in a.c. only shuffle back and forth, energy is still transferred to appliances. Each time the charges move, work is done in the components.
bullets: The heating effect occurs whichever direction the charges move
So a 230 V a.c. supply can heat a kettle just as a d.c. supply could
The 'about 230 V' value is an effective value: the alternating voltage actually varies, rising above and falling below it during each cycle
Energy comes from the generator, not from the charges themselves

callouts.p: In a.c. the electrons do not travel from the power station to your home. Energy is transferred, not charge.

core.p: The mains voltage is high enough to be dangerous, which is why mains plugs and wiring have safety features (covered in the mains wiring point).
bullets: 230 V can drive a current through the human body large enough to kill
Battery voltages (1.5 V to 12 V) are generally safe to touch
Never compare a battery and the mains as equally safe

core.h: Comparing a.c. and d.c. in exam answers
core.p: Use clear comparative language.
bullets: 'In d.c. charge flows in one direction only, whereas in a.c. the direction of flow of charge keeps changing'
'A direct voltage has a constant direction, whereas an alternating voltage keeps reversing'
'Cells and batteries supply d.c.; the UK mains supplies a.c. at 50 Hz and about 230 V'
Mention both sides of the comparison to gain full marks

analogy.p: Direct current is like traffic on a one-way street: everything moves steadily in the same direction. Alternating current is like the teeth of a saw cutting wood: the saw moves back and forth, going nowhere overall, yet it still does work (cutting and heating the wood) on every stroke. 50 Hz is like 50 complete back-and-forth strokes per second. Where it breaks down: a saw's blade moves as one solid object, whereas charges in a wire each oscillate only a tiny distance, and energy in a circuit is transferred by the electric field, not pushed along by the charges like a solid rod.

terms.d: Movement of charge in one direction only.
Current in which the movement of charge repeatedly changes direction.
A potential difference that always acts in the same direction.
A potential difference that repeatedly reverses direction.
The UK domestic supply: a.c., 50 Hz, about 230 V.
The number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Unit of frequency; one cycle per second.
The time for one complete cycle; T = 1 / f (0.02 s for 50 Hz).
One complete back-and-forth variation of an alternating voltage or current.
A single source of d.c. that transfers energy from a chemical store.
Two or more cells connected together; supplies d.c.
Device in power stations that produces an alternating voltage.
Instrument that displays a voltage–time trace, used to show a.c. and d.c.
Energy transferred per unit charge between two points, in volts.

mistakes.w: The UK mains is 240 V.
mistakes.r: About 230 V.

mistakes.w: The UK mains frequency is 60 Hz.
mistakes.r: 50 Hz (60 Hz is used in some other countries, e.g. the USA).

mistakes.w: Batteries supply alternating current.
mistakes.r: Cells and batteries supply direct current.

mistakes.w: In a.c. the current goes round and round in a circle faster.
mistakes.r: In a.c. the movement of charge changes direction repeatedly (back and forth).

mistakes.w: Direct current is current that goes directly to the appliance.
mistakes.r: Direct current is movement of charge in one direction only.

mistakes.w: In a.c. the electrons travel from the power station to the house.
mistakes.r: The charges oscillate back and forth; energy, not charge, is transferred.

mistakes.w: A voltage–time graph that varies in size but stays positive is a.c.
mistakes.r: It is only a.c. if the direction reverses (graph goes below the axis).

mistakes.w: 50 Hz means the current changes direction 50 times a second.
mistakes.r: 50 complete cycles per second; the direction reverses twice per cycle (100 times a second).

exam.q: State the frequency of the UK mains supply.
model: 50 Hz
exam.tip: Include the unit.

exam.q: State the voltage of the UK domestic supply.
model: About 230 V
exam.tip: Not 240 V.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by direct current.
model: Movement of charge in one direction only
exam.tip: 'One direction' is the key phrase.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by alternating current.
model: Movement of charge that (repeatedly) changes direction
exam.tip: Say 'changes direction', not just 'changes'.

exam.q: Name one source of direct current.
model: Cell / battery (or solar cell)
exam.tip: Cells and batteries are the spec examples.

exam.q: Describe the difference between a direct voltage and an alternating voltage.
model: Direct voltage always acts in the same direction / one terminal is always positive
Alternating voltage keeps reversing direction
exam.tip: Give one point about each.

exam.q: Calculate the time for one cycle of the UK mains supply.
exam.tip: Period is the reciprocal of frequency.

exam.q: An oscilloscope trace shows 5 complete cycles in 0.10 s. Calculate the frequency and state whether this could be the UK mains.
model: f = cycles / time = 5 / 0.10
f = 50 Hz
Yes, the UK mains frequency is 50 Hz
exam.tip: Number of cycles divided by time.

exam.q: Two voltage–time graphs are shown: graph A is a horizontal line above the axis; graph B is a wave above and below the axis. Identify which shows a.c. and explain your answer.
model: Graph B is a.c.
Because the voltage goes positive and negative / reverses direction
exam.tip: Refer to the axis crossing.

exam.q: Compare the electricity supplied by a battery with the UK mains supply.
model: Battery supplies d.c.; mains supplies a.c.
In d.c. charge moves in one direction only; in a.c. charge changes direction
Mains frequency is 50 Hz; d.c. has no frequency
Mains is about 230 V; a battery's p.d. is much smaller (e.g. 1.5 V to 12 V)
exam.tip: Each mark needs both sides of the comparison.

exam.q: Explain how energy can be transferred to a heater by alternating current even though the charges do not travel around the circuit.
model: The charges move back and forth through the heater
Work is done / energy transferred whichever direction they move (collisions with ions)
So energy is transferred to the thermal store of the heater; energy, not charge, is delivered
exam.tip: Separate the ideas of charge and energy.

worked.q: Calculate the period of the UK mains supply in milliseconds and the number of times the current reverses in one minute.
steps: Current reverses twice per cycle, so 2 × 50 = 100 reversals per second
worked.ans: 20 ms; 6000 reversals per minute.

worked.q: An oscilloscope shows an alternating voltage where one cycle covers 4 squares and each square represents 5 ms. Find the frequency.
worked.ans: 50 Hz, the same as the UK mains.

phy_edx.9.14.summary: UK mains electricity reaches appliances through three wires: the **live wire** (brown, at a potential of about 230 V), the **neutral wire** (blue, at or close to 0 V) and the **earth wire** (green and yellow, at 0 V, only carrying current if there is a fault). Because your body is at about 0 V, touching the live wire puts a large potential difference across you and can drive a dangerous current through you, even when the appliance switch is open. Fuses, circuit breakers and the earth wire work together to cut off the supply when a fault happens, and switches and fuses are always placed in the live wire so that switching off or a blown fuse disconnects the appliance from the high potential.

core.p: In the UK the domestic mains supply is **alternating current (a.c.)** at a frequency of **50 Hz** and a voltage of about **230 V**. The mains is connected to appliances through cables that usually contain three wires, each with a different job and a different potential.
bullets: Alternating means the potential of the live wire keeps changing between positive and negative, so the current changes direction 50 times each way every second.
The **potential difference between the live and neutral wires** is what pushes charge through an appliance.
The **earth wire** is a safety wire. In normal use it carries **no current**.
A **cable** is several insulated wires inside an outer plastic sheath; the insulation stops the wires touching each other or you.

callouts.p: UK mains: a.c., 50 Hz, about 230 V.

core.h: The three wires and their colours
core.p: Each wire has a standard colour so electricians can never confuse them. You must know the colour, the potential and the job of each one.
bullets: **Live wire (brown)**: carries the alternating potential of about 230 V from the supply to the appliance.
**Neutral wire (blue)**: completes the circuit back to the supply; it is at or close to 0 V.
**Earth wire (green and yellow stripes)**: a safety wire connected to the metal case of an appliance and to the ground; at 0 V.
Current flows into the appliance through the live wire and back through the neutral wire (and the direction keeps reversing because it is a.c.).
The earth wire only carries a current if there is a **fault**.

rows: Carries the supply potential to the appliance
Completes the circuit back to the supply

callouts.p: Brown = live (brown like a burn), blue = neutral (cool and calm), green/yellow = earth.

core.h: Difference in potential between the wires
core.p: The live wire is at a high potential (about 230 V) while the neutral and earth wires are at or close to 0 V, which is the potential of the ground. A current only flows when there is a **potential difference** and a complete path, so current flows between live and neutral through the appliance.
bullets: **Live to neutral**: potential difference about 230 V, so current flows through the appliance and energy is transferred.
**Live to earth**: potential difference about 230 V, so if anything connects live to earth a current will flow along that path.
**Neutral to earth**: potential difference about 0 V, so no current flows between them normally.
The ground, and a person standing on it, is at about **0 V (earth potential)**.
The neutral wire is connected to earth at the local substation, which is why it is close to 0 V.

callouts.p: The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit; current flows only where there is a potential difference and a complete conducting path.

core.p: A UK three-pin plug connects the three wires of the cable to the socket. The fuse is built into the plug and is connected to the live pin, so the live current must pass through the fuse.
bullets: The **earth pin** is the longest and goes in first, so the appliance is earthed before it is connected to the live supply.
The **fuse** sits next to the live pin and is connected in series with the live wire.
The **cable grip** clamps the outer sheath so the wires cannot be pulled out of their terminals.
Pins are made of **brass**: a good conductor that is hard and does not corrode easily.
The plug case is made of **plastic or rubber**, which are electrical insulators.
Wires must be connected firmly with no bare copper showing outside the terminals.

callouts.p: Looking at the back of an open plug with the cable at the bottom: earth at the top, live on the right (with the fuse), neutral on the left.

core.h: Why touching the live wire is dangerous
core.p: Your body is a conductor and you are normally at about 0 V because you are in contact with the ground. If you touch the live wire, there is a potential difference of about 230 V across your body, so a current flows through you to earth. This is an **electric shock**, which can stop the heart, cause burns and can kill.
bullets: Danger comes from the **large potential difference** between the live wire (about 230 V) and you (about 0 V).
The p.d. drives a **current through your body** to earth; it is the current that causes injury.
Even a small current through the heart (tens of milliamps) can be fatal.
Touching the **neutral wire** is normally much less dangerous because it is close to 0 V, so there is very little p.d. across you.
Touching the **earth wire** is safe in normal use because it is at 0 V, the same as you.
Wet skin has lower resistance, so the same p.d. drives a larger current: water and electricity are a deadly combination.

callouts.p: Live wire at about 230 V, body at 0 V, so large p.d. across body, so current flows through body to earth, so electric shock.

core.h: A live wire can be dangerous even when the switch is open
core.p: Opening a switch breaks the circuit so no current flows through the appliance, but the **live wire on the supply side of the switch is still at about 230 V**. Anything that provides a connection between that live wire and earth, such as a person, a damp surface or a metal tool, completes a new path and a current will flow through it.
bullets: A switch only stops current flowing in **that circuit**; it does not remove the potential of the live wire before the switch.
If you touch the live wire while standing on the ground, **you complete a circuit between live and earth**, so current flows through you.
If a switch were wrongly placed in the **neutral wire**, opening it would leave the whole appliance connected to the live wire at 230 V, so touching parts inside it could give a shock.
This is why you must **switch off at the mains and unplug** before opening or repairing an appliance, not just turn off its own switch.
Any connection between live and earth (for example a frayed cable touching a metal pipe) can also cause a large current, overheating and **fire**.

callouts.t: Open switch does not mean safe
callouts.p: An open switch means no current in the appliance circuit, but the live wire can still be at 230 V relative to earth.

core.h: Why switches and fuses go in the live wire
core.p: Switches and fuses must be connected in the **live wire** so that, when the switch is opened or the fuse melts, the appliance is **disconnected from the high potential** of the live wire. If they were in the neutral wire, the appliance would stop working but would still be at 230 V, so it could still give a shock.
bullets: Switch in live wire: opening it isolates the appliance from 230 V, so the appliance and its wiring are at about 0 V.
Fuse in live wire: when it melts, the live supply is cut off from the appliance, so a faulty metal case is no longer live.
Switch or fuse in neutral wire: current stops, but the appliance remains connected to the live wire, so it is **still live** and dangerous to touch.
This is why the fuse in a plug sits beside the **live pin**.

callouts.p: Say the switch or fuse in the live wire disconnects the appliance from the live wire, so the appliance is no longer at a high potential (it is at 0 V).

core.h: The earth wire: how it protects you
core.p: The earth wire connects the **metal case** of an appliance to the ground. If a fault makes the live wire touch the metal case, the case would become live at 230 V. The earth wire gives a **very low resistance path** from the case to earth, so a very large current flows through the earth wire instead of through a person.
bullets: Normal use: earth wire carries **no current**.
Fault: live wire touches the metal case, e.g. a loose or frayed wire.
The earth wire has **very low resistance**, so a **very large current** flows from live, through the case and earth wire, to earth.
This large current is bigger than the fuse rating, so the **fuse melts** (or the circuit breaker trips) and the live supply is disconnected.
The case can then no longer become live, so anyone touching it later is safe.
The earth wire keeps the case at about 0 V, so there is **no large p.d. between the case and a person**.

callouts.t: Earth wire and fuse work together
callouts.p: Earth wire gives a low resistance path, so a large current flows, so the fuse melts, so the live wire is disconnected.

core.p: A **fuse** is a thin piece of wire inside a glass or ceramic cartridge, connected in series in the live wire. If the current gets too large, the **heating effect** of the current makes the fuse wire **melt**, which breaks the circuit and disconnects the live supply.
bullets: The fuse wire is thin so it heats up quickly when the current exceeds its rating.
Common UK plug fuse ratings: **3 A, 5 A and 13 A**.
Choose a fuse with a rating **just above the normal working current** of the appliance.
Too low a rating: the fuse melts in normal use. Too high: the fuse may not melt during a fault, so the cable can overheat and cause a fire.
Find the normal current using **I = P / V** (from P = I x V), with V = 230 V.
A fuse protects the **wiring and appliance** from overheating and fire, and with the earth wire it protects the user from shock.
Once melted, a fuse must be **replaced**, and the fault should be found first.

callouts.p: A safety device in the live wire containing a thin wire that melts when the current is too large, breaking the circuit and disconnecting the live supply.
Do not say a fuse stops you getting a shock on its own. It melts because of a large current; it protects the circuit, and protects people only when used with the earth wire.

core.p: A **circuit breaker** does the same job as a fuse: it disconnects the live supply when the current is too large. Instead of melting, it uses an **automatic switch** (often operated by an electromagnet) that opens when the current goes above a set value.
bullets: Circuit breakers are found in the consumer unit (fuse box) of a house and protect whole circuits.
They **switch off faster** than a fuse melts.
They can be **reset** by flicking a switch, instead of being replaced.
They are **more expensive** than fuses.
A **residual current device (RCD)** compares the current in the live and neutral wires; if they differ (current is leaking to earth, e.g. through a person), it switches off very quickly.
Like fuses, circuit breakers are connected in the **live** wire.

core.p: Some appliances, such as hairdryers and phone chargers, have a casing made entirely of **plastic (an insulator)** with no metal parts that could be touched. These are **double insulated** and do not need an earth wire, because the case can never become live.
bullets: They use a **two-core cable** (live and neutral only).
They still have a fuse in the live wire to protect against too large a current.
They are marked with a symbol of a square inside a square.
Metal-cased appliances (kettles, toasters, washing machines) **must be earthed**.

core.p: In a 6 mark question you are usually asked to explain how a set of features keeps people safe. Build a clear chain of cause and effect for each feature.
bullets: **Insulation** on wires and plastic casings: stops people touching conductors at high potential.
**Switch in live wire**: switching off disconnects the appliance from 230 V.
**Fuse in live wire**: melts if current is too large, disconnecting the live supply and preventing overheating and fire.
**Earth wire**: low resistance path from metal case to earth, so a fault causes a large current which melts the fuse.
**Circuit breaker**: opens automatically and quickly if the current is too large, can be reset.
**Cable grip**: stops wires being pulled out and touching each other or the case.
**Earth pin longest**: the appliance is earthed before it is connected to live.

callouts.p: For each feature: what it is, what happens in a fault, and why that makes it safe. Use the words potential, current, resistance, melts and disconnects.

analogy.t: A high water tank and a drain
analogy.p: Think of the live wire as a pipe connected to a water tank high on a hill (high potential, 230 V) and the neutral and earth as drains at ground level (0 V). Water only flows when there is a height difference and a path. The appliance is a water wheel between the tank pipe and the drain. A tap (switch) in the tank pipe stops water reaching the wheel, but the pipe before the tap is still full and under pressure, so a leak to the ground (you touching the live wire) still lets water gush out. The earth wire is a wide overflow drain that carries a gush away so fast that it triggers a valve (the fuse) to shut. Where it breaks down: mains is alternating, so the live potential swings positive and negative rather than staying high, and charge in wires is not used up like water is drained away.

terms.d: Brown wire that carries the alternating potential of about 230 V from the supply to an appliance.
Blue wire that completes the circuit back to the supply; at or close to 0 V.
Green and yellow safety wire connecting the metal case of an appliance to the ground; at 0 V and carries current only when there is a fault.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points; about 230 V between live and neutral or between live and earth.
The potential of the ground, taken as 0 V; a person standing on the ground is at about this potential.
Injury caused when a current passes through the body because of a potential difference across it.
Thin wire in the live wire that melts when the current is too large, breaking the circuit.
The current above which a fuse melts; chosen just above the normal working current of the appliance.
Automatic switch in the live wire that opens when the current is too large; can be reset.
Device that switches off the supply when the currents in the live and neutral wires are different.
An unintended connection, for example the live wire touching a metal case.
A route through which a large current can flow easily; the earth wire provides one from the case to earth.
Appliance design with a plastic casing and no touchable metal parts, so no earth wire is needed.
Cable containing live, neutral and earth wires, each with its own insulation, inside an outer sheath.
Clamp in a plug that holds the cable sheath so the wires cannot be pulled out of their terminals.
Current that repeatedly changes direction; UK mains is a.c. at 50 Hz.

mistakes.w: The earth wire carries current all the time.
mistakes.r: The earth wire carries no current in normal use; it only carries current if there is a fault.

mistakes.w: The neutral wire is at 230 V.
mistakes.r: The live wire is at about 230 V; the neutral wire is at or close to 0 V.

mistakes.w: If the switch is off, the wire is safe to touch.
mistakes.r: The live wire can still be at 230 V; touching it connects live to earth through your body, so a current flows through you.

mistakes.w: The fuse stops current flowing through you.
mistakes.r: The large fault current through the low resistance earth wire melts the fuse, which disconnects the live supply so the case is not live.

mistakes.w: The earth wire has a high resistance to stop the current.
mistakes.r: The earth wire has a very low resistance so a large current flows through it (and not through a person).

mistakes.w: Electricity flows through you because you are a conductor.
mistakes.r: There is a large potential difference between the live wire and you (at 0 V), so a current flows through your body to earth.

mistakes.w: Put the fuse in the neutral wire, it still breaks the circuit.
mistakes.r: Fuses and switches go in the live wire so the appliance is disconnected from the high potential; in the neutral the appliance would still be live.

mistakes.w: Choose a 13 A fuse for everything to be safe.
mistakes.r: Choose the rating just above the normal current; too high a rating may not melt in a fault, so wires can overheat and cause a fire.

mistakes.w: A fuse breaks when the voltage is too high.
mistakes.r: A fuse melts when the current is too large, because of the heating effect of the current.

exam.q: State the colour of the live wire in a UK mains cable.
model: Brown
exam.tip: Brown live, blue neutral, green and yellow earth.

exam.q: State the potential of the neutral wire.
model: 0 V or close to 0 V
exam.tip: Accept about 0 V; never 230 V.

exam.q: Explain the difference in potential between the live wire and the neutral wire.
model: The live wire is at a high potential of about 230 V (alternating)
The neutral wire is at (or close to) 0 V, so there is a p.d. of about 230 V between them
exam.tip: Give values for both wires.

exam.q: Explain why a person touching the live wire can get an electric shock.
model: The live wire is at about 230 V and the person is at about 0 V / earth potential
So there is a large potential difference across the person
So a current flows through the person to earth
exam.tip: The p.d. causes a current through the body; mention both.

exam.q: A lamp is switched off. Explain why the live wire in the lamp circuit can still be dangerous.
model: The live wire (on the supply side of the switch) is still at about 230 V
Touching it provides a connection between live and earth, so current flows through the person
exam.tip: An open switch stops current in the circuit but does not remove the potential.

exam.q: Explain why switches must be connected in the live wire and not the neutral wire.
model: Opening the switch in the live wire disconnects the appliance from the high potential / 230 V
If it were in the neutral wire the appliance would still be connected to the live wire so would still be live and could give a shock
exam.tip: Compare both positions.

exam.q: Give two advantages of a circuit breaker compared with a fuse.
model: Acts / switches off faster
Can be reset (does not need replacing)
exam.tip: Disadvantage if asked: more expensive.

exam.q: A heater has a power of 2000 W and runs on the 230 V mains. Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Calculate the normal current and choose the correct fuse.
model: 13 A fuse because it is the lowest rating above 8.7 A
exam.tip: Rearrange P = IV and justify the fuse choice.

exam.q: Explain why a fuse with too high a rating should not be used.
model: The fuse may not melt when a fault causes a larger than normal current
So the cable / appliance could overheat and cause a fire (or the case could stay live)
exam.tip: Link rating to the current needed to melt the fuse.

exam.q: A toaster has a metal case. Explain how the earth wire and the fuse work together to protect the user if the live wire touches the case.
model: The earth wire connects the metal case to earth and has a low resistance
A large current flows from the live wire through the case and earth wire to earth
The large current is above the fuse rating so the fuse melts
This disconnects the live supply so the case is no longer live / the user cannot get a shock
exam.tip: Use a step by step chain: low resistance, large current, fuse melts, live disconnected.

exam.q: Explain how the design of mains wiring and appliances keeps people safe. Refer to the live, neutral and earth wires, switches, fuses and circuit breakers.
model: Live wire is at about 230 V, neutral about 0 V, so the p.d. drives current through the appliance
Wires are insulated / casings are plastic so people cannot touch conductors at high potential
Switches are in the live wire so switching off disconnects the appliance from 230 V
Fuse in the live wire melts if the current is too large, disconnecting the live supply and preventing overheating / fire
Earth wire connects the metal case to earth with low resistance so a fault causes a large current that melts the fuse
Circuit breakers switch off automatically, faster than a fuse, and can be reset
exam.tip: Level 3 answers link each feature to what happens in a fault and why that prevents a shock or fire.

worked.q: A kettle is rated 2300 W, 230 V. Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Which should be fitted?
steps: Use P = I x V, so I = P / V
The fuse must be just above the normal current, so 3 A and 5 A would melt in normal use
The 13 A fuse is the lowest rating above 10 A
worked.ans: Normal current 10 A, so fit a 13 A fuse.

worked.q: A lamp is rated 60 W, 230 V. Which fuse should be fitted?
steps: The smallest rating above 0.26 A is 3 A
worked.ans: Fit a 3 A fuse (normal current 0.26 A).

worked.q: Model answer: an electrician wires a switch into the neutral wire of a light fitting by mistake. Explain why this is dangerous.
steps: When the switch is opened, current stops so the lamp goes off
But the lamp holder is still connected to the live wire, so it is at about 230 V
A person changing the bulb is at about 0 V, so there is a p.d. of about 230 V across them
Touching the holder connects live to earth through their body, so a current flows through them: an electric shock
worked.ans: The lamp looks off but is still live, so anyone touching it could get an electric shock.

phy_edx.9.15.summary: The **power rating** of a domestic appliance tells you how much energy it transfers every second when it is working normally, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). When an appliance is in use, electrical work done by the mains supply changes the energy in stores, such as the thermal store of water in a kettle or the kinetic store of a fan. The higher the power rating, the faster the energy in those stores changes, and the total energy transferred depends on both the power and the time it is used for: E = P x t.

core.p: Every mains appliance is labelled with a **power rating**, for example 2000 W for a kettle or 10 W for an LED lamp. This is the **rate of energy transfer** when the appliance runs normally on the 230 V mains. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 joules of energy every second.
bullets: Power is measured in **watts (W)**; 1 W = 1 joule per second (1 J/s).
1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W.
The rating tells you the energy transferred **per second**, not the total energy.
Ratings are often printed on a label with the voltage, for example 230 V, 2.4 kW.
A higher power rating means the appliance transfers energy **more quickly**.

callouts.p: Power is the rate of energy transfer, or the energy transferred per second.
One watt is a rate of energy transfer of one joule per second.

core.h: The equation linking power, energy and time
core.p: The energy an appliance transfers depends on its power and on how long it is used. The equation is **power = energy transferred / time taken**, which rearranges to **energy transferred = power x time**.
bullets: P = E / t, so E = P x t and t = E / P.
E in **joules (J)**, P in **watts (W)**, t in **seconds (s)**.
Always convert minutes and hours to seconds: 1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 3600 s.
Convert kW to W by multiplying by 1000.
Doubling the power at the same time doubles the energy transferred.
Doubling the time at the same power also doubles the energy transferred.

callouts.p: power (W) = energy transferred (J) / time taken (s), P = E / t

core.h: Power ratings and changes in stored energy
core.p: When an appliance is switched on, the mains supply does **electrical work** on it and energy is transferred to one or more **energy stores**. The power rating tells you **how quickly the energy in those stores changes**. A higher power appliance makes the same change in a store in less time.
bullets: **Kettle / immersion heater / electric heater**: energy transferred to the **thermal store** of the water or the room.
**Fan, food mixer, washing machine drum, drill**: energy transferred by a motor to the **kinetic store** of the moving parts.
**Phone or laptop charger**: energy transferred to the **chemical store** of the battery.
**Lift or crane motor**: energy transferred to the **gravitational potential store** of the load (and kinetic store while it moves).
**Hairdryer**: energy to the thermal store of the air (heater) and the kinetic store of the air and fan (motor).
In every case some energy is **dissipated** to the thermal store of the surroundings, usually by heating.

callouts.p: Higher power rating means more energy is transferred to the stores every second, so the energy in the stores changes faster.

core.p: Appliances that **heat** things usually have the highest power ratings, because large amounts of energy are needed to raise the temperature of water or air quickly. Appliances that mainly produce light or run electronics have much lower ratings.
bullets: Heating appliances (kettles, heaters, ovens, showers) are typically **1 kW to several kW**.
Motors (vacuum cleaners, washing machines) are often hundreds of watts to around 2 kW.
Electronics (TVs, laptops) are typically tens to a few hundred watts.
LED lamps are only a few watts because they waste much less energy by heating than filament lamps.
These are typical values; always use the value given in the question.

core.h: Comparing two appliances: faster change in the store
core.p: If two kettles hold the same mass of water and heat it through the same temperature rise, the same energy must be added to the thermal store of the water. The kettle with the **higher power rating** transfers this energy **in less time**.
bullets: Same energy needed: t = E / P, so a larger P gives a smaller t.
A 3000 W kettle boils the same water in about two thirds of the time taken by a 2000 W kettle (ignoring losses).
In the same time, a higher power appliance transfers **more** energy: E = P x t.
A high power appliance used for a short time can transfer **less** total energy than a low power appliance left on for a long time.
So the total energy (and the cost) depends on **power and time**, not power alone.

callouts.p: Do not say a 2000 W appliance uses 2000 J. It transfers 2000 J every second; the total depends on how long it is on.

core.p: You may be asked to describe the energy transfers when an appliance is in use. Start with the **mains supply doing electrical work**, then name the store or stores that increase, and the energy that is **wasted**.
bullets: Energy is transferred **electrically** (electrical work) from the mains to the appliance.
It is then transferred **by heating**, **mechanically** (by forces doing work) or **by radiation** (light, infrared).
Useful energy goes to the store you want to increase; wasted energy is dissipated to the **thermal store of the surroundings**.
Total energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy out (conservation of energy).
Energy is never used up; it is transferred and spreads out (dissipates).

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward 'thermal energy store of the water' or 'kinetic energy store of the motor', not vague words like 'heat energy' or 'movement energy'.

core.p: All UK mains appliances run on about 230 V, so a higher power rating means a **larger current**. This links power ratings to the choice of fuse and the thickness of cable needed.
bullets: P = I x V, so I = P / V.
A 2300 W kettle on 230 V draws 10 A; a 23 W lamp draws only 0.1 A.
High power appliances need **thicker cables** (lower resistance, less heating) and higher rated fuses.
Energy can also be found from E = I x V x t, which is the same as E = P x t because P = IV.

core.p: The power rating is the **total (input) power**. Only part of it ends up in the useful store. The rest is wasted, usually by heating the surroundings.
bullets: efficiency = useful power output / total power input.
Example: a 1000 W microwave that transfers 650 J/s to the food has efficiency 650 / 1000 = 0.65 (65%).
Two appliances with the same rating can make different useful changes if their efficiencies differ.
A more efficient appliance needs a **lower power rating** to make the same useful change, so it transfers less energy in total and costs less to run.
This is why LED lamps (about 10 W) can replace filament lamps (about 60 W) for similar light output.

callouts.p: efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy supplied (or useful power / total power).

core.p: Energy companies measure the energy transferred by appliances in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)** because joules are very small units. This is useful for comparing appliances in real homes.
bullets: 1 kWh is the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour.
Energy (kWh) = power (kW) x time (h).
Cost = number of kWh x price per kWh.
In exam calculations using E = P x t, use joules, watts and seconds unless kWh is asked for.

core.p: Because energy transferred depends on power and time, households can reduce energy use (and cost) in two ways.
bullets: Use **lower power** appliances for the same job (e.g. LED instead of filament lamps).
Use appliances for **less time** (switch off when not needed, avoid standby).
Only heat the water you need in a kettle: less mass means less energy needed for the same temperature rise.
Choose **more efficient** appliances so less energy is wasted to the surroundings.

core.p: Power calculations are common in Paper 2. Show every step so you can earn method marks even if you make an arithmetic slip.
bullets: Write the equation first: E = P x t.
Convert units: kW to W, minutes or hours to s.
Substitute values with units.
Give the answer with the correct unit (J, kJ or MJ) and sensible significant figures.
When comparing appliances, calculate the energy for each and state which is larger and by how much.

callouts.p: Forgetting to change 3 minutes into 180 s gives an answer 60 times too small.

analogy.p: An appliance is like a tap filling a bath, where the water in the bath is the energy in a store. The power rating is how fast the tap runs: litres per second is like joules per second. A fast tap (high power) fills the bath in less time, but a slow tap left on all day can still put more water in the bath than a fast tap opened for a minute: total water = flow rate x time, just like E = P x t. Some water splashes onto the floor and is wasted, like energy dissipated to the surroundings. Where it breaks down: energy can go into several different stores at once (thermal, kinetic), and energy is not a substance that flows through a pipe.

terms.d: The rate of energy transfer; energy transferred per second.
The power of an appliance when it operates normally on its rated voltage, e.g. 2000 W at 230 V.
Unit of power; 1 W = 1 J/s.
1000 watts.
Unit of energy.
The energy moved between stores; E = P x t.
A way energy is held, such as thermal, kinetic, chemical or gravitational potential.
Energy held by an object because of its temperature; increased by a kettle or heater.
Energy held by a moving object; increased by a motor in a fan or drill.
Energy held in chemical bonds, e.g. in a battery being charged.
Energy transferred when a current flows due to a potential difference.
Energy spread out to the surroundings, usually by heating, so it is less useful.
useful energy (or power) output divided by total energy (or power) input.
Energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour; equal to 3.6 MJ.

mistakes.w: A 2000 W kettle uses 2000 J of energy.
mistakes.r: It transfers 2000 J every second; total energy = power x time.

mistakes.w: Power is the amount of energy an appliance uses.
mistakes.r: Power is the rate of energy transfer, the energy transferred per second.

mistakes.w: E = 2000 x 3 = 6000 J for a 2000 W kettle on for 3 minutes.
mistakes.r: Convert time to seconds: E = 2000 x 180 = 360 000 J.

mistakes.w: A higher power appliance always transfers more energy.
mistakes.r: Only in the same time; a low power appliance on for longer can transfer more energy.

mistakes.w: The kettle turns electricity into heat energy.
mistakes.r: Electrical work increases the thermal energy store of the water; some energy is dissipated to the surroundings.

mistakes.w: Using 2 kW in E = P x t gives E = 2 x 60 = 120 J for one minute.
mistakes.r: Convert kW to W first: E = 2000 x 60 = 120 000 J.

mistakes.w: The energy gets used up.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred to stores or dissipated to the surroundings; it is conserved.

mistakes.w: The unit of power is J.
mistakes.r: Power is in watts (W), which is joules per second (J/s).

exam.q: State what is meant by a power rating of 1500 W.
model: 1500 J of energy is transferred every second (when operating normally)
exam.tip: Always say per second.

exam.q: State the equation linking power, energy transferred and time.
model: power = energy transferred / time (P = E / t)
exam.tip: Word equations are accepted.

exam.q: Name the energy store that increases when an electric fan is switched on.
model: Kinetic energy store (of the fan blades / motor)
exam.tip: Name the object as well as the store.

exam.q: A 2.5 kW kettle is used for 2 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
model: Convert: P = 2500 W and t = 120 s
exam.tip: Two conversions: kW to W and minutes to seconds.

exam.q: A heater transfers 540 000 J in 5 minutes. Calculate its power.
exam.tip: Show the conversion as a separate line.

exam.q: Two kettles each heat 1 kg of water from 20 C to 100 C. Kettle A is 2000 W, kettle B is 3000 W. Explain which kettle boils the water first.
model: Both need the same energy transferred to the thermal store of the water
Kettle B has a higher power so transfers energy faster / more energy per second, so boils it first
exam.tip: Link power to rate of energy transfer.

exam.q: A 2000 W hairdryer is used for 5 minutes. A 100 W television is used for 2 hours. Show which transfers more energy.
model: Hairdryer: E = 2000 x 300 = 600 000 J
Television: t = 2 x 3600 = 7200 s
The television transfers more energy (120 000 J more)
exam.tip: Calculate both and compare explicitly.

exam.q: A 1000 W microwave transfers 700 J of energy to the food each second. Calculate its efficiency.
model: efficiency = useful power / total power = 700 / 1000
exam.tip: Efficiency has no unit.

exam.q: A charger has a power rating of 20 W. Calculate how long it takes to transfer 36 000 J to the chemical store of a battery.
model: t = E / P
t = 1800 s (30 minutes)
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: Describe, with examples, the relationship between the power ratings of domestic appliances and the changes in stored energy when they are in use.
model: Power rating is the energy transferred per second / rate of energy transfer
Energy transferred = power x time, so energy depends on power and time
A kettle / heater increases the thermal store of water or air
A fan / drill / washing machine motor increases the kinetic store of moving parts
A higher power rating means the store changes faster / more energy per second, e.g. a higher power kettle boils water in less time
Some energy is wasted / dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings, so not all of the power rating ends up in the useful store
exam.tip: Give at least two named appliances with their stores and link power to rate of change.

worked.q: A 2.4 kW kettle takes 3 minutes to boil some water. Calculate the energy transferred.
A 50 W fan runs for 2 hours. A 2000 W heater runs for 3 minutes. Which transfers more energy?
worked.ans: They transfer the same energy, 360 000 J, even though the heater's power is 40 times higher, because the fan runs 40 times longer.

worked.q: An electric shower must transfer 1 800 000 J to the thermal store of the water. How long does a 9 kW shower take, compared with a 7.5 kW shower?
worked.ans: The 9 kW shower takes 200 s, 40 s less than the 7.5 kW shower, because it transfers energy at a higher rate.

phy_edx.9.2.summary: Potential difference (p.d. or voltage) tells you how much energy is transferred by each coulomb of charge as it moves between two points in a circuit. Because it is energy per unit charge, one volt is one joule per coulomb, and the total energy transferred is found from **E = Q x V**. A cell or battery gives energy to the charge; components such as lamps and resistors transfer that energy to their surroundings, and the p.d. across each one measures the energy transferred per coulomb.

core.p: Charge flowing round a circuit carries energy from the power supply to the components. The **potential difference** between two points is the **energy transferred per unit charge** that passes between those points. It is a measure of how much energy each coulomb gives up (in a component) or gains (in a cell).
bullets: Potential difference is often called **voltage**; both words mean the same thing at GCSE.
It is always measured **between two points**, so we talk about the p.d. **across** a component, never the p.d. through it.
A large p.d. across a component means **each coulomb transfers a lot of energy** in it.
A p.d. across a cell or power supply tells you the energy **given to** each coulomb; across a lamp, resistor or motor it tells you the energy **transferred by** each coulomb.
P.d. does not say how many charges flow or how fast; that is the job of current.

callouts.p: Potential difference (voltage) is the energy transferred per unit charge passed between two points in a circuit.

fig.cap: In a simple circuit each coulomb leaving the 6 V cell carries 6 J of energy. As it passes through the lamp it transfers all 6 J, so it returns to the cell having transferred 6 J, and the cell then gives it another 6 J.

core.h: The volt is a joule per coulomb
core.p: Since p.d. = energy / charge, its unit must be the unit of energy divided by the unit of charge. So **1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C)**. This is exactly what the spec asks you to explain.
bullets: Energy is measured in **joules (J)**.
Charge is measured in **coulombs (C)**.
So p.d. = J / C, which is given the special name the **volt (V)**.
A 9 V battery transfers **9 J of energy to every coulomb** of charge that passes through it.
A lamp with 3 V across it has **3 J transferred from each coulomb** passing through it, mostly as light and heat to the surroundings.

callouts.p: 1 volt is 1 joule per coulomb. If asked to explain why, say p.d. is energy transferred per unit charge, so its unit is joules divided by coulombs.

core.h: The equation E = Q x V
core.p: Rearranging the definition gives the equation you must **recall and use**: **energy transferred (joule, J) = charge moved (coulomb, C) x potential difference (volt, V)**, or E = Q x V. More charge, or more energy per coulomb, means more energy transferred in total.
bullets: E = Q x V (energy in J, charge in C, p.d. in V).
Rearranged: **Q = E / V** and **V = E / Q**.
This equation is **not given** on the Edexcel equation sheet, so learn it.
Doubling the charge that flows doubles the energy transferred (at the same p.d.).
Doubling the p.d. doubles the energy transferred by the same charge.

callouts.p: V is used both for the quantity (p.d.) and its unit (volt). Write 'V = 6 V' carefully, and never confuse Q (charge) with q for heat or anything else.

fig.cap: Equation triangle for E = Q x V. Cover the quantity you want: E is Q times V, Q is E divided by V, and V is E divided by Q.

core.h: Where energy is gained and transferred
core.p: Energy is **conserved** around a circuit. The cell transfers energy from its **chemical energy store** to the charges, and the components transfer that energy away, for example by heating or as light. So the energy gained per coulomb in the cell equals the energy transferred per coulomb in all the components on any one loop.
bullets: In a cell, energy is transferred from the **chemical store** to the charge (work is done on the charge).
In a resistor, energy is transferred **by electrical working** to the **thermal store** of the resistor and surroundings.
In a lamp, energy is transferred to the thermal store and carried away by **light** (radiation).
In a motor, energy is transferred mainly to a **kinetic store**.
Charge is not used up: the same charge keeps circulating. Only its energy is transferred.

callouts.p: Students often write that the lamp 'uses up the current' or 'uses up charge'. The mark scheme wants: the charge transfers energy to the lamp; current is the same before and after the lamp.

core.p: In a series circuit there is only one path, so every coulomb passes through every component. The energy each coulomb gains from the supply must be shared between the components, so the **p.d.s across the components add up to the supply p.d.**
bullets: Supply p.d. = sum of p.d.s across the components in series.
A component with **more resistance** has a **bigger share** of the p.d., because each coulomb transfers more energy in it.
This is a direct result of **conservation of energy** applied per coulomb.
Two identical lamps in series on a 6 V supply each have 3 V across them: 3 J per coulomb in each.

callouts.p: For a grade 9 answer link the rule to energy: each coulomb gains 12 J from a 12 V supply and must transfer all 12 J in the components, so the p.d.s add to 12 V.

fig.cap: Two resistors in series with a 12 V supply. Each coulomb gains 12 J in the cell, transfers 8 J in R1 and 4 J in R2, so the voltmeter readings add up to the supply p.d.

core.p: In a parallel circuit each coulomb goes through only **one** branch. It still has to transfer all the energy it gained from the supply, so the **p.d. across each branch is the same** and equals the supply p.d.
bullets: Each branch has the **full supply p.d.** across it.
A coulomb in branch A transfers all its energy in branch A, and one in branch B transfers all its energy in branch B.
This is why lamps in parallel are brighter than the same lamps in series: each has the full p.d., so each coulomb transfers more energy in each lamp.
Household appliances are connected in parallel so each gets the full mains p.d.

core.p: P.d. is measured with a **voltmeter** connected **in parallel** (across) the component. The voltmeter compares the energy per coulomb at the two points it is connected to.
bullets: Voltmeter goes **across** (in parallel with) the component, never in series.
An ideal voltmeter has a **very high resistance**, so almost no current flows through it and it does not change the circuit.
Readings are in **volts (V)**; small p.d.s may be shown in millivolts (1 mV = 0.001 V).
To find the energy transferred you also need the charge, for example from Q = I x t (covered in the current notes).

callouts.p: When asked to add a voltmeter to a circuit diagram, draw its two leads joining the wire on either side of the component. A voltmeter drawn in the main loop loses the mark.

core.h: Using E = Q x V in calculations
core.p: Exam questions usually give two of the three quantities and ask for the third. Always write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with a unit. Watch for prefixes and for questions that make you find the charge first.
bullets: Step 1: write the equation, E = Q x V.
Step 2: convert units: kJ to J (x 1000), mC to C (divide by 1000), kV to V (x 1000).
Step 3: rearrange if needed, then substitute.
Step 4: give the answer with the correct unit and sensible significant figures.
If you are given current and time instead of charge, first use **Q = I x t**, then E = Q x V. Combining them gives **E = I x V x t**, which links to the energy and power notes.

callouts.p: A missing or wrong unit commonly costs the final mark. The unit of energy is J, not V or C.

core.h: Why p.d. is energy per charge, not energy per second
core.p: Students often confuse p.d. with power. P.d. is **energy per coulomb**; power is **energy per second**. They are linked through current, which is **charge per second**.
bullets: p.d. (V) = energy / charge, unit J/C.
current (A) = charge / time, unit C/s.
power (W) = energy / time, unit J/s.
Multiplying: (J/C) x (C/s) = J/s, which is why **P = I x V**.
So a high p.d. does not by itself mean high power; it also depends on how much charge flows each second.

callouts.p: Energy per coulomb times coulombs per second gives energy per second. This chain of units helps you check any electricity equation.

core.h: Applying the idea to real cells and supplies
core.p: The number written on a cell or battery is its p.d. It tells you how much energy the battery gives each coulomb of charge that it pushes round the circuit.
bullets: A 1.5 V cell gives **1.5 J to each coulomb**.
Cells in series (all the same way round) add their p.d.s: four 1.5 V cells give 6 V, so 6 J per coulomb.
A cell connected the wrong way round in series subtracts its p.d.
The UK mains supply is about 230 V, so each coulomb transfers about 230 J in an appliance. This is why mains electricity is much more dangerous than a torch battery.
The total energy a battery can supply depends on its p.d. and on the total charge it can move before it goes flat (E = Q x V).

analogy.t: Delivery vans on a loop road
analogy.p: Imagine coulombs of charge as delivery vans driving round a one-way loop. At the depot (the cell) each van is loaded with parcels of energy; a 6 V cell loads 6 J onto every van. At each shop (a component) the vans unload parcels; the p.d. across a shop is the number of joules each van drops off there. In series the vans visit every shop and must share their load between them, so the drop-offs add up to the load. In parallel each van visits only one shop and unloads everything there. The vans themselves are never used up, they just go back to be reloaded. The analogy breaks down because real electrons do not carry energy as separate parcels, the energy is actually transferred by the electric field in the wires almost instantly, and electrons drift very slowly rather than racing round the loop.

terms.d: The energy transferred per unit charge passed between two points in a circuit; measured in volts.
Another name for potential difference.
The unit of potential difference; one volt is one joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C).
The unit of energy.
The unit of electric charge.
A property of particles such as electrons; the amount of charge moved is measured in coulombs.
The energy moved from one store to another, in joules; for charge in a circuit E = Q x V.
One coulomb of charge.
A meter connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference across it.
A source of p.d. that transfers energy from a chemical store to the charge passing through it.
Two or more cells connected together; their p.d.s add if connected in series the same way round.
A circuit with one path; the p.d.s across the components add up to the supply p.d.
A circuit with more than one branch; the p.d. across each branch is the same.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred; so energy gained per coulomb in the supply equals energy transferred per coulomb in the components of a loop.

mistakes.w: Voltage is the amount of current flowing.
mistakes.r: Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge (per coulomb) between two points.

mistakes.w: The p.d. through the lamp is 3 V.
mistakes.r: The p.d. across the lamp is 3 V; p.d. is between two points.

mistakes.w: A volt is a joule per second.
mistakes.r: A volt is a joule per coulomb; a joule per second is a watt.

mistakes.w: E = V / Q or V = Q x E.
mistakes.r: E = Q x V, so V = E / Q and Q = E / V.

mistakes.w: Energy = 0.2 kJ x 12 = 2.4 (no conversion, no unit).
mistakes.r: Convert to base units first and always give the unit, for example 2.4 J or 2400 J as appropriate.

mistakes.w: The lamp uses up the charge so less comes out.
mistakes.r: Charge is not used up; the charge transfers energy to the lamp and the current is the same either side.

mistakes.w: In parallel the p.d. is shared between the branches.
mistakes.r: Each parallel branch has the same p.d. as the supply; it is the current that is shared.

mistakes.w: Connect the voltmeter in series with the lamp.
mistakes.r: The voltmeter must be connected in parallel (across) the component.

exam.q: State what is meant by the potential difference across a component.
model: Energy transferred per unit charge (per coulomb) passing through the component.
exam.tip: Use the words energy and per unit charge; 'push of the current' scores nothing.

exam.q: Which of these is equal to one volt? A: one joule per second B: one coulomb per second C: one joule per coulomb D: one coulomb per joule
model: C: one joule per coulomb.
exam.tip: J/s is a watt and C/s is an ampere; learn all three.

exam.q: State the equation linking energy transferred, charge moved and potential difference.
model: Energy transferred = charge moved x potential difference (E = Q x V).
exam.tip: Words or symbols both score, but if you use symbols they must be the standard ones.

exam.q: Explain why the volt is the same as a joule per coulomb.
model: Potential difference is energy transferred divided by charge (V = E / Q).
Energy is in joules and charge in coulombs, so the unit is J/C.
exam.tip: Two marks means two linked steps: the definition, then the units.

exam.q: A charge of 15 C passes through a lamp. The potential difference across the lamp is 4.0 V. Calculate the energy transferred by the lamp.
model: E = Q x V = 15 x 4.0
E = 60 J
exam.tip: Show the substitution; you can still get a mark if the arithmetic slips.

exam.q: A battery transfers 3600 J of energy to 400 C of charge. Calculate the potential difference of the battery.
model: V = E / Q
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting and give the unit volts.

exam.q: A heater has a potential difference of 230 V across it and transfers 46 kJ of energy. Calculate the charge that flows through the heater.
exam.tip: The kilo prefix is the trap here; convert first.

exam.q: A current of 0.50 A flows through a motor for 2 minutes. The p.d. across the motor is 6.0 V. Calculate the energy transferred to the motor.
model: E = Q x V = 60 x 6.0
exam.tip: Two-step questions: find Q first from Q = I x t, and convert minutes to seconds.

exam.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series to a 12 V battery. Explain, in terms of energy and charge, why the p.d. across each lamp is 6 V.
model: Each coulomb gains 12 J from the battery.
In a series circuit each coulomb passes through both lamps and must transfer all 12 J.
Lamps are identical so each coulomb transfers the same energy (6 J) in each lamp, so 6 J per coulomb is 6 V.
exam.tip: Use 'per coulomb' throughout and refer to conservation of energy.

exam.q: Explain how energy is transferred from a battery to a lamp in a circuit and why the battery eventually goes flat even though charge is not used up. Use ideas about potential difference and charge.
model: The battery has a p.d., so it transfers energy from its chemical store to each coulomb of charge passing through it.
The p.d. of the battery equals the energy given to each coulomb (J per C).
The charge flows round the circuit to the lamp; the p.d. across the lamp is the energy transferred per coulomb in the lamp.
In the lamp energy is transferred to the thermal store of the filament and the surroundings, and by light.
The charge is not used up; the same charge returns to the battery and the current is the same all round the loop.
Total energy transferred E = Q x V; the battery's chemical store is finite, so once it has transferred its energy it can no longer give energy to the charge (goes flat).
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical chain: source of energy, energy per coulomb, transfer in the lamp, charge conserved, energy store depleted.

worked.q: A 1.5 V cell drives 300 C of charge round a circuit. How much energy does the cell transfer to the charge?
steps: Write the equation: E = Q x V.

worked.q: A kettle connected to the 230 V mains transfers 690 kJ of energy while boiling water. Calculate the charge that flows through the kettle.
steps: Rearrange E = Q x V to give Q = E / V.

worked.q: A current of 2.0 A flows through a resistor for 30 s. The resistor transfers 180 J of energy. Calculate the p.d. across the resistor.
steps: Find the charge first: Q = I x t = 2.0 x 30 = 60 C.
Rearrange E = Q x V to give V = E / Q.

phy_edx.9.3.summary: An electric current is the **rate of flow of charge**, and in metals that charge is carried by **free electrons** drifting through the metal. The amount of charge that passes a point is found from **Q = I x t**, with charge in coulombs, current in amperes and time in seconds. Current is measured with an **ammeter in series**; it is the **same at every point in a single closed loop**, and at a junction it is **conserved**, so the total current in equals the total current out. The size of the current depends on both the potential difference and the resistance.

core.h: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge
core.p: A current flows when charge moves around a complete circuit. The **current** is the amount of charge passing a point **each second**. A bigger current means more coulombs pass every second, not that the charges are 'stronger'.
bullets: Current = charge / time, so it is a **rate**: like litres per second for water in a pipe.
Current is measured in **amperes (amps, A)**.
**1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C/s)**.
A current needs **a complete (closed) circuit** and **a source of potential difference** such as a cell.
Small currents are often given in **milliamps**: 1 mA = 0.001 A.

callouts.p: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge.

core.h: Current in metals is a flow of electrons
core.p: Metals contain **free (delocalised) electrons** that are not tied to any one atom. The metal is a lattice of positive ions with these electrons moving between them. When a p.d. is applied, the free electrons drift through the metal, and this flow of negative charge is the current.
bullets: The charge carriers in a metal wire are **electrons**, which are **negatively charged**.
Electrons flow from the **negative terminal** of the cell, round the circuit, to the **positive terminal**.
**Conventional current** is drawn from **positive to negative**; this convention was chosen before electrons were discovered.
Both descriptions give the same circuit results; circuit diagrams and arrows use conventional current.
The positive ions in the lattice **do not move along** the wire; they only vibrate.
In other materials (such as solutions) the charge carriers can be ions, but the spec point concerns metals.

callouts.p: If a question asks which way the electrons move, answer negative to positive. If it asks for the conventional current direction, answer positive to negative.

fig.cap: Inside a metal wire. Free electrons (small blue) drift between fixed positive metal ions (large yellow). Electrons move towards the positive terminal; conventional current is shown in the opposite direction.

core.h: The equation Q = I x t
core.p: Because current is the rate of flow of charge, the total charge that passes a point is the current multiplied by the time. You must **recall and use**: **charge (coulomb, C) = current (ampere, A) x time (second, s)**, Q = I x t.
bullets: Q = I x t; rearranged **I = Q / t** and **t = Q / I**.
This equation is **not on the equation sheet**, so learn it.
Time **must be in seconds**: minutes x 60, hours x 3600.
Current must be in **amps**: mA divided by 1000.
Doubling the current or doubling the time doubles the charge that flows.

callouts.p: The most common lost mark on Q = I x t is leaving time in minutes or hours. Convert first.

core.p: An **ammeter** measures current in **amps**. It must be placed **in series** with the component, so that all the charge flowing through the component also flows through the ammeter.
bullets: Connect the ammeter **in series**: break the circuit and put the ammeter in the gap.
An ideal ammeter has **very low (almost zero) resistance**, so it does not reduce the current it is measuring.
Never connect an ammeter in parallel across a component: its tiny resistance would let a large current flow and could damage it.
Choose a suitable range (A or mA) for an accurate reading.
Its circuit symbol is a circle containing the letter A.

callouts.p: Ammeter: in series, measures current in A, very low resistance. Voltmeter: in parallel, measures p.d. in V, very high resistance.

core.h: Current is the same everywhere in a single loop
core.p: In a **series circuit** (a single closed loop) there is only one path. Charge cannot pile up anywhere or disappear, so the same number of coulombs per second must pass every point. So **the current is the same at any point in a single closed loop**.
bullets: Ammeters placed anywhere in a series loop give **the same reading**.
The current is the same **before and after** a lamp or resistor: components do not use up current.
What the components do is **transfer energy** from the charge, which shows up as a drop in p.d., not current.
Adding more components in series increases the total resistance, so the current everywhere in the loop gets smaller, but it is still the same at every point.

callouts.p: Charge is conserved: it is not used up by components. So current is the same at all points in a series circuit.

fig.cap: A series circuit with three ammeters. Because there is only one path for the charge, all three ammeters read the same current, 0.4 A, including the one after the lamp.
