core.h: Current is conserved at a junction
core.p: A **junction** is a point where the circuit splits into branches or where branches rejoin. Charge is conserved, so the charge arriving at a junction each second must equal the charge leaving each second. Therefore **the total current into a junction equals the total current out of it**.
bullets: Total current in = total current out (sum of branch currents = main current).
In a parallel circuit the main current **splits** between the branches and **recombines** afterwards.
The branch currents **add up to the current from the supply**.
The branch with the **lower resistance** carries the **larger share** of the current.
Identical branches carry equal currents.

callouts.p: The sum of the currents entering a junction is equal to the sum of the currents leaving the junction, because charge is conserved.

fig.cap: Current at a junction. 5.0 A flows in and splits into 3.0 A and 2.0 A. No charge is lost or created, so 3.0 A + 2.0 A = 5.0 A.

core.h: Series and parallel compared for current
core.p: Putting the two rules together lets you predict every ammeter reading in a simple circuit.
bullets: Series: one path, **same current everywhere**.
Parallel: several paths, **current splits** at junctions and the branch currents add up to the total.
Adding another branch in parallel gives the charge an extra path, so the **total current from the supply increases**.
The current in the existing branches stays the same if the supply p.d. is unchanged, because each branch still has the full supply p.d.

head: Feature
Series circuit
Parallel circuit
rows: splits at junctions; branch currents add to total

core.p: The size of the current depends on **both the potential difference and the resistance**. The p.d. provides the energy that drives charge round; the resistance opposes the flow.
bullets: Increasing the **p.d.** (at fixed resistance) **increases** the current.
Increasing the **resistance** (at fixed p.d.) **decreases** the current.
Current is measured in **amps (A)**, p.d. in **volts (V)** and resistance in **ohms (ohm symbol)**.
A **variable resistor** in series can be adjusted to change the resistance and so control the current, for example in a dimmer switch.
The exact relationship, V = I x R, is covered in the resistance notes.

callouts.p: Explain changes: 'the resistance increases, so the current decreases because the same p.d. pushes less charge per second through the circuit'.

core.h: Using Q = I x t in calculations
core.p: Follow the same method every time and show your working, as method marks are awarded even if the final answer is wrong.
bullets: Write the equation: Q = I x t.
Convert units: minutes to seconds, mA to A, kC to C.
Rearrange if needed, then substitute values with units.
Give the answer with the unit (C, A or s).
Combine with other equations: for example, find Q from Q = I x t, then energy from E = Q x V.

core.h: Why charge flow explains these rules
core.p: All the current rules come from one idea: **charge is conserved**. Electrons are not created or destroyed in a wire, and they cannot build up at a point in a steady circuit. Grade 9 answers make this link explicit.
bullets: Same current in a loop: electrons cannot pile up or vanish, so the flow rate is the same everywhere.
Junction rule: charge per second in must equal charge per second out.
Charges in a wire all start moving almost at once when the circuit is closed, which is why a lamp lights immediately even though electrons drift slowly.
Components transfer **energy**, not charge, so current does not drop across them.

callouts.p: Charge is conserved; energy is transferred. Current rules come from charge conservation, p.d. rules from energy conservation.

analogy.t: Water in a closed loop of pipes
analogy.p: Think of a circuit as a sealed loop of pipes completely full of water, driven by a pump. The current is like the flow rate: litres passing a point per second, just as amps are coulombs per second. Because the pipes are full and sealed, the flow rate is the same everywhere in a single loop, and where a pipe splits the flows in the two branches add up to the flow in the main pipe. A water meter must be fitted into the pipe (in series) so all the water goes through it, like an ammeter. A narrow pipe (high resistance) reduces the flow, and a stronger pump (higher p.d.) increases it. The analogy breaks down because water flows when a pipe is cut but charge stops flowing in an open circuit, electrons drift very slowly while the energy is transferred almost instantly by the electric field, and electrons actually move opposite to conventional current.

terms.d: The rate of flow of charge; measured in amperes.
The unit of current; 1 A is a flow of 1 coulomb per second.
The quantity of electricity carried by particles such as electrons; measured in coulombs.
The unit of charge; the charge passing a point when 1 A flows for 1 s.
Electrons in a metal that are not bound to one atom and can move through the metal lattice, carrying the current.
Current direction shown from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to the electron flow.
The actual movement of electrons in a metal, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
A meter placed in series with a component to measure the current through it, in amps.
Connected one after another in a single path so the same current passes through each.
A complete circuit path with no gaps, needed for a current to flow.
A point in a circuit where the current splits into branches or branches join.
Charge cannot be created or destroyed, so current is the same around a loop and is conserved at junctions.
One of two or more separate paths between the same two points; the branch currents add to the total current.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed, used to control the current in a circuit.
One thousandth of an amp; 1 mA = 0.001 A.

mistakes.w: Current is the speed of the electrons.
mistakes.r: Current is the rate of flow of charge: the charge passing a point per second.

mistakes.w: Current in metals is a flow of protons or positive ions.
mistakes.r: Current in metals is a flow of (free) electrons; the positive ions do not move along the wire.

mistakes.w: Current is used up by the lamp, so it is smaller after the lamp.
mistakes.r: Current is the same at all points in a single closed loop; the lamp transfers energy, not charge.

mistakes.w: Put the ammeter in parallel with the resistor.
mistakes.r: The ammeter is placed in series with the component.

mistakes.w: Q = 0.5 x 3 = 1.5 C when 0.5 A flows for 3 minutes.
mistakes.r: Convert 3 minutes to 180 s, so Q = 0.5 x 180 = 90 C.

mistakes.w: At a junction the current is the same in every branch.
mistakes.r: Total current into a junction equals total current out; branch currents add up to the main current and are only equal if the branches are identical.

mistakes.w: Electrons flow from positive to negative.
mistakes.r: Electrons flow from negative to positive; conventional current is from positive to negative.

mistakes.w: Increasing resistance increases current.
mistakes.r: For a fixed p.d., increasing resistance decreases current; current depends on both p.d. and resistance.

exam.q: State what is meant by electric current.
model: The rate of flow of charge.
exam.tip: 'Flow of electrons' alone may not score for current in general; 'rate of flow of charge' always does.

exam.q: Name the particles that carry the current in a metal wire.
model: (Free / delocalised) electrons.
exam.tip: Do not write 'charges' or 'ions'; be specific.

exam.q: State the equation linking charge, current and time.
model: Charge = current x time (Q = I x t).
exam.tip: This must be recalled; it is not on the equation sheet.

exam.q: Describe how an ammeter should be connected to measure the current in a lamp.
model: In series with the lamp.
exam.tip: On a diagram, draw it in the same loop as the lamp, not across it.

exam.q: A current of 0.25 A flows through a lamp for 40 s. Calculate the charge that flows through the lamp.
model: Q = 10 C
exam.tip: Give the unit coulombs (C).

exam.q: A charge of 1800 C flows through a heater in 5 minutes. Calculate the current in the heater.
exam.tip: The time conversion is usually worth a mark on its own.

exam.q: A current of 2.0 A flows into a junction. The current splits into two branches. One branch carries 0.8 A. Calculate the current in the other branch and explain your answer.
model: Current is conserved at a junction / total current in equals total current out (charge is conserved).
exam.tip: Name the rule as well as doing the subtraction.

exam.q: A student says 'the ammeter after the lamp will show a smaller reading than the ammeter before it because the lamp uses up some current.' Explain why the student is wrong.
model: Current is the same at all points in a series circuit / single loop.
Charge is not used up (conserved); the lamp transfers energy from the charge, not the charge itself.
exam.tip: Correct the misconception explicitly using charge and energy.

exam.q: A mobile phone battery delivers a current of 150 mA for 2.0 hours. Calculate the charge that flows.
exam.tip: Two conversions here: mA to A and hours to seconds.

exam.q: Explain what an electric current in a metal wire is, and why the current is the same at every point in a series circuit but splits at a junction in a parallel circuit.
model: Current is the rate of flow of charge.
In a metal the charge is carried by free electrons that drift through the lattice of positive ions when a p.d. is applied.
Charge is conserved: it is not created, destroyed or used up by components.
In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same charge passes every point each second; current is the same everywhere.
At a junction the charge has more than one path, so the charge per second divides between the branches.
The total current into the junction equals the total current out, so branch currents add up to the supply current.
exam.tip: Build from definition to particles to conservation of charge, then apply it to each circuit.

worked.q: A current of 3.0 A flows through a toaster for 2.5 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows.
steps: Write the equation: Q = I x t.

worked.q: How long does it take for 96 C of charge to pass through a resistor carrying a current of 0.40 A?
steps: Rearrange Q = I x t to t = Q / I.

worked.q: In a parallel circuit the supply current is 1.5 A. Branch 1 contains an ammeter reading 0.6 A and branch 2 an ammeter reading 0.4 A. There is a third branch. Find the current in the third branch.
steps: Current is conserved at the junction: total in = total out.

phy_edx.9.4.summary: **Resistance** is a measure of how much a component opposes the flow of current. Potential difference, current and resistance are linked by **V = I x R**, with p.d. in volts, current in amps and resistance in ohms. For a fixed p.d., a larger resistance means a smaller current, and resistance can be found by measuring V with a voltmeter and I with an ammeter and calculating R = V / I. In metals, resistance arises because free electrons collide with the vibrating ions of the metal lattice.

core.p: Every component **opposes** the flow of charge through it to some extent. This opposition is its **resistance**. The higher the resistance, the more p.d. is needed to drive each amp of current through it.
bullets: Resistance is measured in **ohms** (symbol: the Greek letter omega).
**1 ohm** is the resistance of a component that has a p.d. of **1 V** across it when a current of **1 A** flows: 1 ohm = 1 V/A.
Connecting wires have a very low resistance; resistors, lamps and heating elements have larger resistances.
Large resistances are given in kilohms (k ohm = 1000 ohms) and megohms (M ohm = 1 000 000 ohms).
Resistance is a property of the component; current and p.d. are what happen in the circuit.

callouts.p: Resistance is the opposition to the flow of current (charge) in a component; R = V / I, measured in ohms.

core.p: A metal is a lattice of **positive ions** with **free electrons** moving between them. As the electrons drift through the metal they **collide with the ions**, which slows their flow. These collisions are the cause of resistance.
bullets: Collisions transfer energy from the electrons to the ions, making the ions **vibrate more**.
So the metal's **thermal energy store increases**: it heats up. This is the heating effect of a current.
Hotter metal ions vibrate more, so electrons collide more often and the **resistance increases with temperature**.
A **longer** wire means more ions to collide with, so more resistance.
A **thinner** wire gives the electrons less room to flow, so more resistance.

callouts.p: More collisions per second between electrons and ions means higher resistance and more energy transferred to the thermal store.

core.h: The equation V = I x R
core.p: You must **recall and use**: **potential difference (volt, V) = current (ampere, A) x resistance (ohm)**, V = I x R. It tells you the p.d. needed to push a given current through a given resistance.
bullets: V = I x R; rearranged **I = V / R** and **R = V / I**.
This equation must be **learned**; it is not on the equation sheet.
For a fixed resistance, **doubling the p.d. doubles the current**.
For a fixed p.d., **doubling the resistance halves the current**.
The equation applies at any instant to any component, even if its resistance changes.

callouts.t: Do not write I = R / V
callouts.p: A common error is inverting the equation. Check with numbers: 6 V across 2 ohms must give 3 A, so I = V / R.

fig.cap: Equation triangle for V = I x R. Cover the quantity you want: V is I times R, I is V divided by R, and R is V divided by I.

core.p: The current in a circuit depends on **both** the p.d. and the resistance. The p.d. drives the charge; the resistance opposes it. Because I = V / R, the current is directly proportional to the p.d. and inversely proportional to the resistance (for a fixed resistance and a fixed p.d. respectively).
bullets: Increase R, same V: **current decreases**.
Decrease R, same V: **current increases**.
Increase V, same R: **current increases**.
A very small resistance (for example a short circuit) gives a very large current, which can overheat wires.
Ammeters have very low resistance so they barely change the current; voltmeters have very high resistance so almost no current flows through them.

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions say what changes, in which direction, and why: 'the resistance increases so the current decreases, because I = V / R and V is constant'.

core.h: Changing resistance with a variable resistor
core.p: A **variable resistor** (rheostat) has a resistance that can be changed, usually with a slider or a knob. Placed in series with a component, it lets you **control the current** in the circuit.
bullets: Increasing the resistance of the variable resistor **decreases the current** in the series circuit.
It also changes how the supply p.d. is shared: more resistance in the variable resistor means it takes **more of the p.d.** and less is left for the other component.
Uses: dimmer switches, volume controls, speed controls for motors.
In investigations it is used to take **a range of readings** of current and p.d. for a component.

core.p: Resistance cannot be read directly from a simple meter at GCSE, so it is **calculated** from measurements of p.d. and current using **R = V / I**.
bullets: Connect an **ammeter in series** with the component to measure the current I in amps.
Connect a **voltmeter in parallel** (across) the component to measure the p.d. V in volts.
Use a **variable resistor** to change the current and take several pairs of readings.
Calculate R = V / I for each pair and find a mean, or plot a graph.
Switch off between readings so the component does not heat up, because heating changes its resistance.

callouts.p: Typical marks: ammeter in series, voltmeter across the component only, correct symbols, complete circuit with a power supply.

core.p: If you plot p.d. (y axis) against current (x axis) for a resistor at constant temperature, you get a **straight line through the origin**. The **gradient** of this graph equals the resistance, because R = V / I.
bullets: Steeper line on a V against I graph: **higher resistance**.
A straight line through the origin shows **V is directly proportional to I**, so R is constant.
If the graph is plotted the other way round (I on the y axis against V), the gradient is 1 / R, so a steeper line means **lower** resistance.
Always check which quantity is on which axis before reading resistance from a graph.
You can also read one point off the line and calculate R = V / I.

callouts.p: On an I against V graph (the usual I-V characteristic), a steeper line means a smaller resistance. Read the axis labels.

core.h: Using V = I x R in calculations
core.p: Follow a clear method and always convert to volts, amps and ohms first.
bullets: Write the equation V = I x R.
Convert: mA divided by 1000 to A; k ohm x 1000 to ohms; kV x 1000 to V.
Rearrange, then substitute values.
Give the answer with the correct unit: V, A or ohms.
Linked problems: use Q = I x t or E = Q x V alongside V = I x R, for example find I from V = I x R, then Q from Q = I x t.

callouts.p: With mA and k ohm together, 20 mA x 4.7 k ohm = 0.020 A x 4700 ohm = 94 V, not 94 000 V.

core.h: Resistance and the shares of p.d.
core.p: Because V = I x R and the current is the same in every part of a series circuit, the component with the **larger resistance** has the **larger p.d.** across it. Each coulomb transfers more energy in a component with more resistance.
bullets: Series: same I, so V is proportional to R for each component.
A 4 ohm and a 2 ohm resistor in series share the supply p.d. in the ratio 2 : 1.
Detailed series and parallel combination rules are covered in the series and parallel notes.

core.p: The resistance of a metal conductor is not always fixed. Knowing what changes it helps you explain experimental results.
bullets: **Temperature**: for a metal, higher temperature means more ion vibration and **higher resistance**. This is why a filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats up.
**Length**: longer wire, more resistance (more collisions along the path).
**Cross-sectional area**: thicker wire, less resistance (more paths for electrons).
**Material**: different metals have different numbers of free electrons and lattice structures, so different resistances.
A **fixed resistor** kept at constant temperature has a constant resistance.

head: Change
Effect on resistance
Reason
rows: more room for electrons to flow

analogy.p: Picture electrons as students hurrying along a school corridor between lessons, and the metal ions as pillars spaced along it. The p.d. is how strongly the bell urges students to move; the current is how many students pass a door each second. The pillars get in the way: students bump into them and slow down, and that obstruction is the resistance. A longer corridor has more pillars (more resistance), a wider corridor lets more students through (less resistance), and if the pillars start shaking about (a hotter metal) students bump into them more often (more resistance). The analogy breaks down because real electrons are not 'pushed' by a bell but by an electric field, their collisions transfer energy to the ions as heat in a way students do not, and electrons are identical, tiny and drift extremely slowly.

terms.d: The opposition of a component to the flow of current; R = V / I, measured in ohms.
The unit of resistance, symbol omega; 1 ohm = 1 volt per amp.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points; measured in volts.
The rate of flow of charge; measured in amps.
Potential difference (V) = current (A) x resistance (ohms).
A component designed to have a particular resistance, used to control current and p.d.
A resistor whose resistance is constant at constant temperature.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed to control the current in a circuit.
Meter connected in series to measure current; has very low resistance.
Meter connected in parallel to measure p.d.; has very high resistance.
Electrons in a metal that can move through the lattice and carry the current.
The positive metal ions fixed in a regular arrangement; electrons collide with them, causing resistance.
When one quantity doubles the other doubles; shown by a straight-line graph through the origin.
The slope of a graph; for V against I it equals the resistance.
A path of very low resistance, giving a very large current.

mistakes.w: Resistance is how much current a component lets through.
mistakes.r: Resistance is the opposition to current; R = V / I.

mistakes.w: I = R / V or R = I x V.
mistakes.r: V = I x R, so I = V / R and R = V / I.

mistakes.w: Increasing the resistance increases the current.
mistakes.r: At a fixed p.d., increasing resistance decreases the current.

mistakes.w: Resistance is measured in volts per second or in amps.
mistakes.r: Resistance is measured in ohms (1 ohm = 1 V/A).

mistakes.w: 20 mA through 50 ohms gives V = 20 x 50 = 1000 V.
mistakes.r: Convert 20 mA to 0.020 A, so V = 0.020 x 50 = 1.0 V.

mistakes.w: Resistance is caused by electrons colliding with each other.
mistakes.r: Resistance in metals is caused by free electrons colliding with the (positive) ions of the metal lattice.

mistakes.w: On an I against V graph the steeper line has the greater resistance.
mistakes.r: On an I against V graph the steeper line has the smaller resistance; on a V against I graph steeper means greater resistance.

mistakes.w: Put the voltmeter in series and the ammeter in parallel to find R.
mistakes.r: Ammeter in series with the component, voltmeter in parallel across it; then R = V / I.

exam.q: State the unit of resistance.
model: Ohm (omega).
exam.tip: Spell it correctly or draw the omega symbol.

exam.q: State the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance.
model: Potential difference = current x resistance (V = I x R).
exam.tip: Recall equation: learn it in words and symbols.

exam.q: A current of 0.30 A flows through a resistor of 20 ohms. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.
exam.tip: Show the substitution for the method mark.

exam.q: The potential difference across a lamp is 12 V and the current through it is 0.50 A. Calculate the resistance of the lamp.
model: R = V / I
R = 24 ohms
exam.tip: The unit is part of the answer mark.

exam.q: A 9.0 V battery is connected to a 1.5 k ohm resistor. Calculate the current in milliamps.
model: R = 1500 ohms
I = 6.0 mA
exam.tip: Watch both the k prefix on resistance and the mA requested in the answer.

exam.q: Explain what happens to the current in a circuit when the resistance of a variable resistor in it is increased. The supply p.d. stays the same.
model: The current decreases.
Because I = V / R, and V is constant, so a larger R gives a smaller I.
exam.tip: State the change and give the reason.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of electrons and ions, why a metal wire has resistance.
model: Free electrons moving through the metal collide with the (positive) ions in the lattice.
These collisions oppose / reduce the flow of electrons (and transfer energy to the ions).
exam.tip: Name both particles and the word collide.

exam.q: Draw a circuit diagram that could be used to find the resistance of a resistor. Include a variable resistor.
model: Ammeter in series with the resistor.
Voltmeter in parallel with the resistor only.
Variable resistor in series with a power supply, complete circuit with correct symbols.
exam.tip: Use standard symbols and make sure the voltmeter leads join on either side of the resistor.

exam.q: A current of 0.20 A flows through a 30 ohm resistor for 50 s. Calculate the energy transferred by the resistor.
model: E = Q x V = 10 x 6.0
E = 60 J
exam.tip: Chain the equations: V = IR, Q = It, E = QV.

exam.q: A student measures the current through a resistor for several values of p.d. Describe how they could use the results to find the resistance, and explain why the resistor should not be allowed to get hot.
model: Use an ammeter in series to measure current and a voltmeter in parallel to measure p.d.
Use a variable resistor to change the p.d. / current and record several pairs of readings.
Calculate R = V / I for each pair and find a mean, or plot V against I.
The gradient of the V against I straight line through the origin gives R.
If the resistor gets hot the ions vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often.
So the resistance increases and the results would not be for a constant resistance; switch off between readings / use small currents.
exam.tip: Cover method, calculation and the physics of heating in a logical order.

worked.q: A heater has a resistance of 46 ohms and is connected to the 230 V mains. Calculate the current in the heater.
steps: Write the equation: V = I x R, so I = V / R.

worked.q: The current through a component is 40 mA when the p.d. across it is 2.0 V. Calculate its resistance.
worked.ans: 50 ohms

worked.q: A resistor of 12 ohms has a current of 0.75 A. The resistance is then doubled with the same p.d. Find the p.d. and the new current.
steps: Doubling the resistance at the same p.d. halves the current.
worked.ans: p.d. = 9.0 V; new current = 0.375 A (about 0.38 A)

phy_edx.9.5.summary: Resistors can be joined end to end in **series** or side by side in **parallel**. Adding a resistor in series **increases** the total resistance because charge has to pass through every resistor, while adding one in parallel **decreases** the total resistance because charge has extra paths to flow through. In a series circuit the **current is the same everywhere**, the supply p.d. is **shared** between components in proportion to their resistance, and the total resistance is the **sum** R = R1 + R2, so you can calculate any current, p.d. or resistance using V = I x R.

core.h: Series and parallel: what the words mean
core.p: Before any calculation you must be able to recognise how components are connected. In a **series** circuit there is only **one path** for the charge, so it flows through each component in turn. In a **parallel** circuit the circuit splits at a **junction** into two or more **branches**, and each charge goes through only one branch before the branches join again.
bullets: Series: components connected **end to end** in a single loop.
Parallel: each component is connected **directly across the supply** in its own branch.
If one component in a series circuit breaks, the circuit is broken and **everything stops** working.
If one branch of a parallel circuit breaks, the **other branches keep working** (this is why house lights are wired in parallel).
Ammeters are always connected **in series**; voltmeters are always connected **in parallel** across the component.

head: Quantity
Series circuit
Parallel circuit
rows: Splits between branches; branch currents add up to the total
Shared between components; adds up to supply p.d.
Same across every branch (equal to supply p.d.)
Sum of the resistances: R = R1 + R2
Less than the smallest single resistance
Total resistance goes up, current goes down
Total resistance goes down, total current goes up

callouts.p: Series: current is the same, p.d. is shared. Parallel: p.d. is the same, current is shared.

core.h: Why two resistors in series have a bigger total resistance
core.p: The spec asks you to **explain** this, not just state it. In series, every charge must flow through **both** resistors one after the other. Each resistor opposes the flow of charge, so the oppositions add together. For the same supply p.d., this means a **smaller current** flows, and since R = V / I, a smaller current for the same p.d. means a **larger resistance**.
bullets: Charge must pass through **each resistor in turn**, so it meets more opposition.
The supply p.d. is **shared**, so each resistor has less p.d. across it than the supply.
With less p.d. across each resistor, the **current through it is smaller**.
Same p.d. from the supply + smaller current = **bigger total resistance**.
Think of it as making one long resistor: the electrons collide with more ions on their journey.

callouts.p: Link three ideas: charge passes through both resistors, so the current is less for the same p.d., so the total resistance (V / I) is greater.

core.h: Why two resistors in parallel have a smaller total resistance
core.p: In parallel, each resistor gets the **full supply p.d.** across it and provides its own **separate path** for charge. Adding a second branch adds a second current on top of the first. The total current from the supply therefore **increases** while the p.d. stays the same, so the total resistance R = V / I **decreases**.
bullets: Each branch has the **same p.d.** as the supply.
Adding a branch gives charge **an extra path** to flow through.
The current in the new branch **adds** to the current already flowing, so the **total current increases**.
Same p.d. + bigger total current = **smaller total resistance**.
The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is always **less than the smaller** of the two resistances.
Two identical resistors in parallel have **half** the resistance of one of them.

callouts.p: Adding a resistor in parallel does NOT add more opposition. It adds another route, so the total resistance falls even though you have added more resistors.

core.h: Total resistance in series: R = R1 + R2
core.p: For resistors in series, the total (net) resistance is simply the **sum** of the individual resistances. This works for any number of resistors: R total = R1 + R2 + R3 + ... The total resistance is always **bigger than the biggest** single resistor.
bullets: Equation: **R total = R1 + R2** (resistance in ohms, Ω).
Example: 4 Ω + 8 Ω = 12 Ω.
Five 10 Ω resistors in series = 50 Ω.
Once you know the total resistance you can find the circuit current using **I = V / R total**.
Resistances in kΩ must be converted: 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω.

callouts.p: R total = R1 + R2 + ... and the same current flows through every resistor.

fig.cap: A series circuit with a 12 V supply. Total resistance = 4 Ω + 8 Ω = 12 Ω, so I = 12 / 12 = 1 A everywhere. The 12 V is shared: V1 = 1 x 4 = 4 V and V2 = 1 x 8 = 8 V, and 4 V + 8 V = 12 V.

core.p: Charge cannot be stored or lost anywhere in a wire, so in a single loop the **rate of flow of charge is the same at every point**. An ammeter placed anywhere in a series circuit gives the same reading. The size of that current is set by the supply p.d. and the **total** resistance.
bullets: **I = V supply / R total**.
The current through R1 is the **same** as the current through R2.
Adding another resistor in series makes the total resistance bigger, so the current everywhere **falls**.
Current is **not used up** by components; energy is transferred, but charge carries on round the circuit.
Ammeter readings before and after a resistor are **identical**.

callouts.p: Students often say the current is smaller after a resistor. It is the same: it is energy, not charge, that is transferred in the resistor.

core.h: Potential difference in a series circuit
core.p: The supply p.d. is **shared** between the components in a series circuit, and the p.d.s across the components **add up to the supply p.d.** This happens because the energy given to each coulomb of charge by the supply is all transferred in the components as it goes round the loop.
bullets: **V supply = V1 + V2**.
p.d. across each resistor: **V1 = I x R1** and **V2 = I x R2**.
Because the current is the same, the **bigger resistor gets the bigger share** of the p.d.
The p.d.s are in the **same ratio** as the resistances: V1 / V2 = R1 / R2.
Example: 4 Ω and 8 Ω share 12 V in the ratio 1 : 2, giving 4 V and 8 V.
If you know the supply p.d. and one component p.d., subtract to find the other: V2 = V supply - V1.

callouts.p: After any series calculation, add your component p.d.s together. If they do not equal the supply p.d. you have made an error.

core.p: Most exam questions on this point are multi-step. Write down what you know, find the total resistance, then the current, then the individual p.d.s. Always write the equation first, substitute with units, and give the answer with the correct unit.
bullets: Step 1: list the known values with units (convert kΩ to Ω, mA to A).
Step 2: find **R total = R1 + R2**.
Step 3: find the current: **I = V / R total**.
Step 4: find each p.d.: **V1 = I x R1**, V2 = I x R2.
Step 5: check V1 + V2 = V supply.
To find an unknown resistor: find the current from a resistor you know, then R unknown = V unknown / I.
Rearranging V = I x R: I = V / R and R = V / I.

callouts.p: potential difference (volt, V) = current (ampere, A) x resistance (ohm, Ω), V = I x R

core.h: Current and p.d. in parallel circuits
core.p: In a parallel circuit, each branch is connected **directly across the supply**, so the p.d. across every branch is the **same as the supply p.d.** The current from the supply **splits** at the junction and the branch currents **add up** to the total current (charge is conserved at a junction). The branch with the **smaller resistance takes the larger current**.
bullets: **V branch = V supply** for every branch.
**I total = I1 + I2**.
Current in each branch: I1 = V / R1, I2 = V / R2.
A smaller resistance in a branch means **more current** through that branch.
Adding another branch **increases** the total current drawn from the supply.
Calculations of total parallel resistance from a formula are not required at GCSE, but you must explain why it is **less than either resistor**.

callouts.p: Every branch of a parallel circuit has the full supply p.d. across it.

fig.cap: A parallel circuit with a 6 V supply. Each resistor has the full 6 V across it, so the 10 Ω branch takes 6 / 10 = 0.6 A and the 20 Ω branch takes 6 / 20 = 0.3 A. The supply current is the sum, 0.9 A, so the total resistance is 6 / 0.9 = 6.7 Ω, less than either resistor.

core.p: A good way to remember the rules is to compare what happens when you take one resistor and add a second identical one in series or in parallel. In series the resistance **doubles**; in parallel it **halves**.
bullets: One 10 Ω resistor: 10 Ω.
Two 10 Ω in series: 10 + 10 = **20 Ω** (bigger than either).
Two 10 Ω in parallel: **5 Ω** (smaller than either).
Adding resistors in series **always increases** the total resistance.
Adding resistors in parallel **always decreases** the total resistance.
The more resistors in parallel, the lower the total resistance and the higher the current from the supply.

core.h: Effect of adding components on current and p.d.
core.p: Exam questions often describe a change to a circuit and ask what happens to the ammeter and voltmeter readings. Always reason from the **total resistance**, to the **current**, to the **p.d.**
bullets: Add a resistor in series: R total up, so **current down**; the p.d. across the original resistor goes **down** because V = I x R and I has fallen.
Add a resistor in parallel: R total down, so **total current up**; p.d. across each branch stays equal to the supply.
Replace a resistor in series with a bigger one: current falls, and the bigger resistor takes a **bigger share** of the p.d.
Lamps in series are **dimmer** than one lamp alone, because the current is smaller and the p.d. is shared.
Lamps in parallel each get the full p.d., so each is as bright as a single lamp on its own.

callouts.p: Resistance changes, so current changes (I = V / R), so p.d. across each component changes (V = I x R). Mark schemes reward each link.

core.p: Cells connected in series in the same direction **add their p.d.s together**, giving a bigger supply p.d. and therefore a bigger current through a given resistance.
bullets: Two 1.5 V cells in series in the same direction give **3.0 V**.
If one cell is reversed, the p.d.s **cancel**: 1.5 V - 1.5 V = 0 V.
Doubling the supply p.d. across a fixed total resistance **doubles the current**.
The supply p.d. is always shared among the series components, however many cells there are.

core.p: Calculation marks are lost through unit errors and missing working far more than through difficult physics. Show each stage clearly so that method marks can be given even if the final answer is wrong.
bullets: Write the **equation** you are using before substituting.
Convert **mA to A** (divide by 1000) and **kΩ to Ω** (multiply by 1000).
Give the **unit** with every answer: V, A or Ω.
Round only at the end; use the number of significant figures given in the question (usually 2 or 3).
If an ammeter reading is given in series, use it for **every** component in that loop.
Use the ratio idea (V1 / V2 = R1 / R2) as a quick check, or as a short cut in 1 or 2 mark questions.

callouts.t: Do not divide by the wrong resistance
callouts.p: To find the series current, divide the SUPPLY p.d. by the TOTAL resistance, or a component p.d. by THAT component's resistance. Never mix them.

analogy.p: Imagine people (charge) leaving a stadium. Two turnstiles one after another (series) slow everyone down more than one, because every person has to get through both, so fewer people per second get out: more resistance. Opening a second exit side by side (parallel) lets more people per second leave in total, even though each exit is just as narrow, so the overall resistance falls. The push from the crowd behind is like the p.d. The analogy breaks down because people get tired and can be stopped or stored, whereas charge is never used up or stored in a wire, and the current in a series circuit is exactly the same everywhere.

terms.d: A circuit with only one path for the current, with components connected end to end.
A circuit in which the current splits into two or more branches, each connected across the supply.
A point where the circuit splits into branches or where branches rejoin; current in equals current out.
One of the separate paths in a parallel circuit.
The opposition to the flow of current in a component, measured in ohms (Ω); R = V / I.
The single resistance that would draw the same current from the supply as the whole combination of resistors.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit, measured in volts (V).
The rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A).
The unit of resistance; 1 Ω is the resistance when a p.d. of 1 V drives a current of 1 A.
Potential difference (V) = current (A) x resistance (Ω).
The total resistance of two resistors connected in series.
Meter that measures current; connected in series with the component.
Meter that measures potential difference; connected in parallel across the component.
In series, the supply p.d. is divided between components in proportion to their resistances, and the component p.d.s add up to the supply p.d.

mistakes.w: Adding a resistor in parallel increases the total resistance because there are more resistors.
mistakes.r: Adding a resistor in parallel **decreases** the total resistance because there are more paths for the charge, so the total current increases for the same p.d.

mistakes.w: The current is smaller after it has gone through a resistor.
mistakes.r: The current is the **same at all points** in a series circuit; charge is not used up.

mistakes.w: Each resistor in series has the full supply p.d. across it.
mistakes.r: The supply p.d. is **shared** between resistors in series; V supply = V1 + V2.

mistakes.w: The p.d. across each branch of a parallel circuit is shared.
mistakes.r: Each branch of a parallel circuit has the **same p.d. as the supply**.

mistakes.w: I = 12 / 4 = 3 A (using one resistor instead of the total).
mistakes.r: Use the **total resistance**: I = 12 / (4 + 8) = 1 A.

mistakes.w: The smaller resistor in series has the bigger p.d. across it.
mistakes.r: The **larger** resistor has the larger p.d., because V = I x R and the current is the same.

mistakes.w: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel have a resistance of 12 Ω.
mistakes.r: 12 Ω is the series value; in parallel the total is **less than 6 Ω** (it is 3 Ω).

mistakes.w: Answer given as 2000 with no unit after not converting kΩ.
mistakes.r: Convert units first (2 kΩ = 2000 Ω) and **always give the unit**.

mistakes.w: Voltmeter connected in series to measure the p.d. across a resistor.
mistakes.r: Voltmeters are connected **in parallel** across the component.

exam.q: State the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance.
model: potential difference = current x resistance (V = I x R)
exam.tip: Write it in words or standard symbols; both are accepted.

exam.q: A 3 Ω resistor and a 9 Ω resistor are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance.
exam.tip: Include the unit Ω.

exam.q: Two resistors are connected in series to a 6.0 V battery. The p.d. across one resistor is 2.5 V. State the p.d. across the other resistor and explain your answer.
model: the p.d.s across components in series add up to the supply p.d. / the p.d. is shared
exam.tip: Subtract from the supply p.d.; explain using the sharing rule.

exam.q: Explain why the total resistance of two resistors in series is greater than the resistance of either resistor.
model: charge has to flow through both resistors / the p.d. is shared between them
so the current is smaller for the same supply p.d. (so R = V / I is larger)
exam.tip: Link the arrangement to the current, then to resistance.

exam.q: Explain why adding a second resistor in parallel with the first decreases the total resistance of the circuit.
model: each resistor has the full supply p.d. across it
the second resistor provides an extra path for charge / extra current
so the total current increases for the same p.d., so total resistance (V / I) decreases
exam.tip: Mention the extra path and the larger total current.

exam.q: A 4.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in series with a 5.0 V supply. Calculate the current in the circuit.
exam.tip: Find the total resistance first.

exam.q: Using the circuit in the previous question, calculate the p.d. across the 6.0 Ω resistor.
exam.tip: Use the same current for both resistors in series.

exam.q: A resistor R is connected in series with a 20 Ω resistor and a 9.0 V battery. The current is 0.30 A. Calculate the resistance of R.
model: p.d. across 20 Ω = 0.30 x 20 = 6.0 V
p.d. across R = 9.0 - 6.0 = 3.0 V
R = 10 Ω
exam.tip: Alternative method: R total = 9.0 / 0.30 = 30 Ω, so R = 30 - 20 = 10 Ω. Either earns full marks.

exam.q: A lamp is connected to a battery. A second identical lamp is added in series. State and explain what happens to the current from the battery.
model: the current decreases
the total resistance increases
the battery p.d. is unchanged so I = V / R is smaller
exam.tip: State the change before explaining it.

exam.q: A student has two 10 Ω resistors and a 6 V battery. Compare the currents from the battery and the p.d.s across the resistors when the resistors are connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel. Use calculations in your answer.
model: series: total resistance = 10 + 10 = 20 Ω
series: current = 6 / 20 = 0.3 A, the same through both resistors
series: p.d. is shared, 3 V across each resistor
parallel: each resistor has the full 6 V across it
parallel: current in each resistor = 6 / 10 = 0.6 A, so battery current = 1.2 A
parallel total resistance (6 / 1.2 = 5 Ω) is less than series (20 Ω), so the battery supplies four times the current in parallel
exam.tip: For 6 markers, structure your answer: series first, then parallel, then a clear comparison.

worked.q: A 2.0 kΩ resistor and a 3.0 kΩ resistor are connected in series to a 10 V supply. Calculate (a) the current and (b) the p.d. across each resistor.
steps: Check: 4.0 V + 6.0 V = 10 V, equal to the supply
worked.ans: Current = 0.002 A (2 mA); p.d.s are 4.0 V across the 2.0 kΩ resistor and 6.0 V across the 3.0 kΩ resistor.

worked.q: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 15 Ω resistor and an unknown resistor X. A voltmeter across the 15 Ω resistor reads 4.5 V. Find the resistance of X.
steps: Current through 15 Ω resistor: I = V / R = 4.5 / 15 = 0.30 A
Same current flows through X because they are in series
worked.ans: X = 25 Ω

worked.q: A 6.0 V supply is connected across a 10 Ω resistor and a 20 Ω resistor in parallel. Find the current in each branch, the supply current and the total resistance.
steps: Each branch has the full 6.0 V across it
6.7 Ω is less than 10 Ω, the smaller resistor, as expected for parallel
worked.ans: 0.60 A and 0.30 A in the branches, 0.90 A from the supply, total resistance about 6.7 Ω.

phy_edx.9.6.summary: In this core practical you build circuits to measure how the **current** through a component changes with the **potential difference** across it, for a **fixed resistor** and a **filament lamp**, and you test **series and parallel** circuits made from resistors and lamps. An **ammeter in series** measures current, a **voltmeter in parallel** measures p.d., and a **variable resistor** (or variable power supply) changes the p.d. so a range of readings can be taken. You use **R = V / I** to calculate resistance at each reading and plot an I-V graph: a straight line through the origin for the resistor, and a curve for the lamp because its resistance rises as it gets hotter.

core.p: Edexcel's core practical has two parts. First, **investigate the relationship between potential difference, current and resistance** for a resistor and a filament lamp. Second, **test series and parallel circuits** using resistors and filament lamps. Both parts depend on connecting meters correctly and using V = I x R.
bullets: Part 1: measure I for a range of V for a **fixed resistor**, then repeat for a **filament lamp**.
Calculate **R = V / I** for each pair of readings.
Plot a graph of **current (y axis) against potential difference (x axis)**.
Part 2: build series and parallel circuits and measure the **current at different points** and the **p.d. across each component**.
Use the results to confirm the series and parallel rules for current and p.d.

callouts.p: potential difference (V) = current (A) x resistance (Ω), V = I x R, so R = V / I.

core.p: You need to know what each piece of apparatus does and why it is there, because questions often ask you to name or justify equipment.
bullets: **Power supply** (low voltage d.c. supply or battery) to provide the p.d.
**Variable resistor** (rheostat) to change the current and p.d. across the component.
**Ammeter** to measure current in amperes (A).
**Voltmeter** to measure p.d. in volts (V).
**Fixed resistor** and **filament lamp** as the components being tested.
**Switch** so the circuit can be turned off between readings.
Connecting leads (and crocodile clips).

head: Apparatus
How connected
Purpose
rows: Measures the current through the component
Measures the p.d. across the component
Changes the current, so the p.d. across the component can be varied
Provides the p.d. that drives the current

core.p: You must be able to draw this circuit using correct symbols. The ammeter, variable resistor and component are all in **one series loop**, while the voltmeter is connected **across the component only**, not across the variable resistor or the supply.
bullets: Ammeter: circle with A, in series.
Voltmeter: circle with V, connected in parallel across the component.
Variable resistor: rectangle with a diagonal arrow through it.
Filament lamp: circle with a cross inside.
The same circuit is used for both components: simply swap the resistor for the lamp.

callouts.p: A voltmeter placed across the supply or the variable resistor does not measure the p.d. across the component. Put it directly across the component being tested.

core.p: The method must produce a **range** of paired readings of p.d. and current. A good method also includes repeats and a way of avoiding heating effects.
bullets: Set up the circuit as in the diagram with the resistor in place.
Set the variable resistor so the current is small, close the switch and **record the voltmeter and ammeter readings**.
Adjust the variable resistor to increase the p.d. and record the new pair of readings.
Take **at least 5 to 8** pairs of readings over the full range.
**Switch off between readings** so the resistor does not heat up.
**Reverse the connections** to the power supply (or component) to obtain negative values of p.d. and current.
**Repeat** the whole set of readings and calculate mean values.
Calculate R = V / I for each pair and plot I against V.

callouts.p: Name the apparatus, describe how meters are connected, say how the p.d. is changed, state what is recorded, mention repeats and range, and say how results are processed (R = V / I and graph).

core.p: The method is the same as for the resistor, but the lamp behaves very differently because it gets **hot**. You do not switch off to keep it cool, because its heating is the very effect being investigated, but you must still keep within the lamp's rated p.d.
bullets: Replace the fixed resistor with the filament lamp.
Start at a low p.d. and increase it in steps, recording V and I each time.
Include **more readings at low p.d.**, where the graph changes shape quickly.
Do not exceed the lamp's **rated voltage**, or the filament may blow.
Reverse the supply connections to obtain negative readings.
Calculate R = V / I at each reading: R **increases** as the p.d. and current increase.

core.p: Identifying variables is a common 1 or 2 mark question. In each investigation, you change one variable and measure another, keeping everything else the same.
bullets: **Independent variable**: potential difference across the component (changed using the variable resistor).
**Dependent variable**: current through the component (read from the ammeter).
**Control variables**: the same component, the same temperature (for the resistor), the same meters and leads.
For the fixed resistor, temperature must stay constant or the resistance will change.
Resistance is a **calculated** quantity, not measured directly.

callouts.p: The variable that the experimenter deliberately changes.

core.p: Record results in a table with columns for p.d. (V), current (A), and resistance (Ω), with units in the headings. Plot **current on the y axis** and **p.d. on the x axis** with a smooth line or curve of best fit.
bullets: Fixed resistor: **straight line through the origin**; current is **directly proportional** to p.d. at constant temperature.
Fixed resistor: R = V / I is the **same** for every reading.
Filament lamp: a **curve** whose gradient gets **less steep** as the p.d. increases.
Filament lamp: R = V / I **increases** as the current increases.
With reversed connections, both graphs are the same shape in the negative quadrant (rotational symmetry about the origin).
Use a line of best fit; do not join the dots.

fig.cap: Typical results: the fixed resistor gives a straight line through the origin (constant resistance), while the filament lamp gives a curve that flattens because its resistance increases as the filament heats up.

core.p: As the current through the filament increases, more energy is transferred to the filament and its **temperature rises**. The metal ions in the filament **vibrate more**, so the electrons collide with them more often. This makes it harder for charge to flow, so the **resistance increases** and the current rises less for each extra volt.
bullets: Higher current means **greater heating effect** in the filament.
Hotter filament means **ions vibrate more**.
More **collisions** between electrons and ions.
So **resistance increases** and the I-V graph curves and becomes less steep.
A fixed resistor kept at constant temperature does not show this effect.

callouts.p: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases.

core.p: In the second part of the practical, you connect two resistors or two lamps first in series and then in parallel, and use ammeters and voltmeters to test the rules for current and p.d.
bullets: **Series**: place the ammeter at different points; the readings are **the same everywhere**.
**Series**: put a voltmeter across each component; the p.d.s **add up to the supply p.d.**
**Parallel**: put a voltmeter across each branch; each shows the **same p.d. as the supply**.
**Parallel**: the currents in the branches **add up** to the current from the supply.
Calculate the total resistance from R = V supply / I supply: it is **higher** in series and **lower** in parallel.
Lamps in series are **dimmer** than in parallel with the same supply, because the p.d. is shared and the current is smaller.

core.h: Errors and how to reduce them
core.p: Questions often ask how to improve accuracy or why results differ from expected values. Know the main sources of error and the fix for each.
bullets: **Heating of the resistor** increases its resistance: switch off between readings and use small currents.
**Zero error** on meters: check they read zero before starting, or subtract the zero reading.
**Fluctuating readings**: wait for the reading to settle, take repeats and calculate a mean.
Resistance of **connecting wires** adds to the measured value: keep leads short.
Use meters with a suitable **resolution** (for example, an ammeter reading to 0.01 A).
**Anomalous results** should be identified, retaken if possible, and ignored when finding the mean.

callouts.p: Mark schemes want a specific source of error, such as the resistor heating up or a zero error on the ammeter, with a specific improvement.

core.p: The currents are low, so the main hazard is **heating** rather than electric shock. A good risk assessment names the hazard and the precaution.
bullets: Resistors and lamps can become **hot**: do not touch them, and switch off between readings.
Keep the p.d. **low** and do not exceed the lamp's rated voltage.
Avoid **short circuits**: check the circuit before switching on.
Turn off the supply before changing any connections.

core.p: Higher-level marks come from interpreting the graph and linking it to resistance. Remember that for an I-V graph, resistance at a point is **V / I** at that point (use the coordinates, not the gradient of a curve).
bullets: For the resistor, the constant ratio V / I shows **constant resistance**.
For the lamp, read pairs of values from the curve and calculate R = V / I to show it **increases**.
A straight line through the origin means current is **directly proportional** to p.d.
Readings in both directions show that the resistor and the lamp behave the same either way round.
To improve the reliability, repeat the readings and check they agree (are repeatable).

callouts.p: Pick a point, read off V and I, then calculate R = V / I. For a straight line through the origin, every point gives the same R.

analogy.t: A tap and a flow meter
analogy.p: Testing a component is like testing a hose pipe. The variable resistor is a tap that lets you control how hard the water is pushed (p.d.), and the flow meter in the pipe measures how much water per second goes through (current). A new garden hose (the fixed resistor) lets through twice the flow for twice the push. A hose that gets narrower when lots of water rushes through (the filament lamp, whose resistance rises as it heats) gives less extra flow for each extra push. The analogy breaks down because a voltmeter has to be connected across the component, comparing the two ends, rather than in the pipe, and electrical resistance rises because hot ions vibrate, not because anything gets narrower.

terms.d: An experiment named in the Edexcel specification that can be examined in written papers.
Meter that measures current in amperes; connected in series with the component.
Meter that measures potential difference in volts; connected in parallel across the component.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed, used to control the current and p.d. in a circuit.
A resistor whose resistance stays constant at constant temperature.
A lamp containing a thin metal wire that glows when hot; its resistance increases as its temperature increases.
A graph of current (y axis) against potential difference (x axis) for a component.
Opposition to current, calculated using R = V / I, measured in ohms (Ω).
When one quantity doubles the other doubles; shown by a straight line through the origin.
The variable deliberately changed: here, the potential difference.
The variable measured: here, the current.
A variable kept the same so the test is fair, such as the temperature of the resistor.
When a meter does not read zero with nothing connected, so every reading is out by the same amount.
Results are repeatable if the same experimenter gets similar results when repeating the method.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others.

mistakes.w: Connect the voltmeter in series with the resistor.
mistakes.r: The voltmeter is connected **in parallel across** the component.

mistakes.w: Connect the ammeter in parallel with the lamp.
mistakes.r: The ammeter is connected **in series** with the component.

mistakes.w: The variable resistor measures the current.
mistakes.r: The variable resistor **changes** the current and p.d.; the ammeter measures current.

mistakes.w: The lamp's graph curves because the lamp runs out of energy.
mistakes.r: The filament **gets hotter**, its ions vibrate more, so its **resistance increases**.

mistakes.w: Resistance of the lamp = gradient of the I-V graph.
mistakes.r: Resistance at a point = **V / I** using the coordinates of that point.

mistakes.w: The fixed resistor's graph is a straight line.
mistakes.r: It is a **straight line through the origin**, showing current is directly proportional to p.d.

mistakes.w: Take readings with the resistor switched on all the time to save time.
mistakes.r: **Switch off between readings** so the resistor does not heat up and change its resistance.

mistakes.w: Independent variable is the current.
mistakes.r: Independent variable is the **potential difference**; current is the dependent variable.

mistakes.w: Improve accuracy by avoiding human error.
mistakes.r: Name a specific improvement, such as **checking meters for zero error** or **repeating and taking a mean**.

exam.q: Name the instrument used to measure the current through the resistor.
model: ammeter
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for name questions.

exam.q: State how the voltmeter should be connected in the circuit.
model: in parallel across the component (resistor or lamp)
exam.tip: Say across the component, not just 'in parallel'.

exam.q: Give the purpose of the variable resistor in the circuit.
model: to change / control the current (and so the p.d. across the component)
exam.tip: Use the word change or vary.

exam.q: State the independent and dependent variables in this investigation.
model: independent: potential difference (across the component)
dependent: current (through the component)
exam.tip: Independent is what you change.

exam.q: Draw a circuit diagram for the investigation of a filament lamp.
model: lamp, supply and ammeter in series
voltmeter in parallel across the lamp
variable resistor in series (correct symbols throughout)
exam.tip: Use a ruler, correct symbols, and no gaps in the wires.

exam.q: A student measures a p.d. of 3.0 V and a current of 0.25 A for a lamp. Calculate the resistance of the lamp.
model: R = 12 Ω
exam.tip: Rearrange V = I x R before substituting.

exam.q: Explain why the student should switch the circuit off between readings when testing the fixed resistor.
model: the current heats the resistor
so its resistance would increase / change, so the temperature must be kept constant
exam.tip: Link heating to change in resistance.

exam.q: Explain why the I-V graph for a filament lamp is a curve.
model: as current increases, the filament gets hotter
the ions in the filament vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more
so the resistance increases (current increases less for each volt)
exam.tip: Temperature, ions, collisions, resistance: in that order.

exam.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series with a cell, then in parallel with the same cell. Describe how the student could use meters to show the parallel rules for current and p.d., and state the results expected.
model: voltmeter across each lamp in turn (and across the cell)
each lamp has the same p.d. as the cell
ammeters in each branch and in the main circuit
branch currents add up to the main current
exam.tip: Give both the method and the expected result for each meter.

exam.q: Describe a method to investigate how the current in a fixed resistor varies with the potential difference across it. Your answer should include how you would use your results.
model: connect resistor in series with ammeter, variable resistor and power supply
connect voltmeter in parallel across the resistor
adjust variable resistor to change the p.d.; record p.d. and current
take at least 5 readings over a wide range; reverse connections for negative values
switch off between readings to stop the resistor heating; repeat and take means
calculate R = V / I for each reading and plot a graph of current against p.d.; a straight line through the origin shows constant resistance
exam.tip: Write a logical sequence: set up, change, measure, repeat, process.

worked.q: A student records these readings for a component: 1.0 V, 0.20 A; 2.0 V, 0.33 A; 4.0 V, 0.50 A. Calculate the resistance at each p.d. and state whether the component is a fixed resistor or a filament lamp.
steps: R = V / I for each reading
The resistance increases as the p.d. and current increase
This matches a filament lamp heating up
worked.ans: 5.0 Ω, 6.1 Ω and 8.0 Ω: resistance increases with current, so it is a filament lamp.

worked.q: In a series test, two resistors are connected to a 6.0 V supply. An ammeter reads 0.20 A and the voltmeter across the first resistor reads 2.0 V. Predict the reading on a voltmeter across the second resistor and calculate both resistances.
steps: In series the p.d.s add up to the supply p.d.
Check: total R = 30 Ω and 6.0 / 30 = 0.20 A
worked.ans: Second voltmeter reads 4.0 V; R1 = 10 Ω and R2 = 20 Ω.

worked.q: Model answer: evaluate a student's plan that connects the voltmeter across the power supply instead of across the lamp.
steps: The voltmeter would measure the supply p.d., not the lamp p.d.
Part of the supply p.d. is across the variable resistor and the ammeter
So the recorded p.d. would be too large and would not change in the same way as the lamp p.d.
Calculated resistances (V / I) would be wrong
Improvement: connect the voltmeter directly across the lamp
worked.ans: The plan is invalid because the voltmeter is not across the lamp; move it to be in parallel with the lamp.

phy_edx.9.7.summary: An **I-V characteristic** is a graph of current against potential difference that shows how a component behaves. A **fixed resistor** at constant temperature gives a **straight line through the origin**, so current is directly proportional to p.d. and its resistance is constant. A **filament lamp** gives an S-shaped curve because its **resistance increases as the filament gets hotter**, while a **diode** only lets current flow in **one direction** (the forward direction), having a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

core.p: An I-V characteristic is a graph with **current (I) on the y axis** and **potential difference (V) on the x axis**. The p.d. is varied, including in the reverse direction (negative values), and the current is measured each time. The **shape** of the graph tells you how the resistance of the component changes.
bullets: Current on the **y axis**, p.d. on the **x axis**.
Negative values mean the p.d. and current are in the **reverse direction**.
Resistance at any point = **V / I** (from the coordinates of that point).
A straight line through the origin means **constant resistance**.
A curve means the resistance is **changing**.
Steeper line (more current per volt) means **lower resistance**.

callouts.p: R = V / I: potential difference (V) divided by current (A), in ohms (Ω).

core.h: Fixed resistor: shape of the graph
core.p: For a fixed resistor at **constant temperature**, the graph is a **straight line through the origin**. This means the **current is directly proportional to the potential difference**: double the p.d. and the current doubles. The graph is the same in both directions, so it does not matter which way round the resistor is connected.
bullets: **Straight line through the origin** in both quadrants.
Current is **directly proportional** to p.d.
The ratio V / I is the same at every point, so the **resistance is constant**.
A component like this is called **ohmic** (it obeys Ohm's law at constant temperature).
Works the same in **both directions**.

callouts.p: A fixed resistor only has constant resistance if its temperature stays constant.

fig.cap: I-V characteristic of a fixed resistor at constant temperature: a straight line through the origin, showing current is directly proportional to p.d. and the resistance is constant.

core.p: You can compare resistors from the steepness of their lines. Since R = V / I, a line that rises more steeply has more current for each volt, which means a **smaller resistance**.
bullets: **Steeper** line = **lower** resistance.
**Shallower** line = **higher** resistance.
For a straight line through the origin, R = 1 / gradient of the I-V graph.
Example: a line through (4.0 V, 0.20 A) gives R = 4.0 / 0.20 = 20 Ω.

callouts.p: On an I-V graph, the gradient is I / V, which is 1 / R. Always calculate R = V / I using a point on the line.

core.h: Filament lamp: shape of the graph
core.p: A filament lamp gives a **curve** through the origin. At low p.d. it is nearly straight, but as the p.d. increases the curve **gets less steep**, so each extra volt produces a smaller increase in current. The curve has the same shape in the reverse direction, giving an S shape.
bullets: Curve through the origin, **flattening** at higher p.d.
**Same shape in both directions** (symmetrical about the origin).
Current is **not** directly proportional to p.d.
V / I gets bigger as V increases, so the **resistance increases**.
The lamp is a **non-ohmic** component.

fig.cap: I-V characteristic of a filament lamp: an S-shaped curve. The gradient decreases at higher p.d. because the filament gets hotter and its resistance increases. The shape is the same in both directions.

core.h: Filament lamp: why the resistance increases
core.p: This is the most commonly examined explanation on this point. The current in the filament causes a **heating effect**. As the current increases, the filament gets **hotter**. The metal ions in the filament **vibrate more**, so the electrons flowing through it **collide with the ions more often**. This opposes the flow of charge more, so the **resistance increases**.
bullets: Bigger p.d. leads to bigger current.
Bigger current leads to more energy transferred to the filament: **temperature rises**.
Hotter metal means **ions vibrate more** (with greater amplitude).
Electrons have **more collisions** with the ions.
So the **resistance increases** and the current rises less steeply.
The filament can become hot enough to glow (white hot), which is how the lamp emits light.

callouts.p: Current up, temperature up, ions vibrate more, more collisions with electrons, resistance up.

core.p: A diode allows current to flow in **one direction only**. In the **reverse** direction, the current is zero (or almost zero) because the resistance is **very high**. In the **forward** direction, almost no current flows until the p.d. reaches about **0.6 V**; above this the current **rises very steeply** because the resistance becomes **very low**.
bullets: **Reverse direction**: current is about zero, **very high resistance**.
**Forward direction**: very little current below about 0.6 V.
Above about 0.6 V the current **increases rapidly**, so the resistance is **low**.
The graph is **not symmetrical**: the diode behaves differently in each direction.
The diode is a **non-ohmic** component.

callouts.p: A component that allows current to flow in one direction only.

fig.cap: I-V characteristic of a diode: almost no current flows in the reverse direction (very high resistance). In the forward direction, current starts to flow at about 0.6 V and then rises steeply (low resistance).

core.p: Because it only conducts one way, a diode is used to control the direction of current. This links to the circuit symbol, where the triangle points in the direction of conventional current flow.
bullets: Protects circuits from damage if a battery is connected the **wrong way round**.
Used to convert **alternating current to direct current** (rectification), for example in chargers.
**Light-emitting diodes (LEDs)** also conduct in one direction and give out light when current flows.
The diode symbol is a triangle pointing towards a bar; current flows in the direction of the triangle.

core.p: Exam questions often show several I-V graphs and ask you to identify the component or compare their resistance. Learn the three shapes and what each one says about resistance.
bullets: Straight line through origin: **fixed resistor** (constant resistance).
S-shaped curve, symmetrical: **filament lamp** (resistance increases with current).
Zero in reverse, steep rise after about 0.6 V: **diode** (one direction only).
Only the fixed resistor has current directly proportional to p.d.
Lamp and diode are both **non-ohmic**.
