core.h: Calculating resistance from an I-V graph
core.p: To find resistance at a point on any I-V graph, read the p.d. and current at that point and use **R = V / I**. For the lamp and diode the answer depends on which point you choose, because their resistance is not constant.
bullets: Choose a point on the line or curve and read off V (x axis) and I (y axis).
Convert mA to A before calculating.
**R = V / I**, answer in ohms (Ω).
For a lamp, compare R at a low and a high p.d. to show that it **increases**.
For a diode in reverse, I is close to zero, so R is **extremely large**.

callouts.p: Check the axis scales and units (mA or A) before reading values. Many lost marks come from misreading the scale.

core.p: These graphs are produced with the circuit from the core practical: the component in series with an ammeter and a variable resistor, with a voltmeter across the component. The supply connections are **reversed** to obtain the negative half of the graph.
bullets: Ammeter **in series**, voltmeter **in parallel** across the component.
Variable resistor (or variable supply) changes the p.d.
Take readings in **both directions** by reversing the connections.
For a diode, a **protective resistor** in series stops the current getting too big in the forward direction.
For a fixed resistor, switch off between readings to keep the temperature constant.

core.h: Linking to temperature and other components
core.p: The key idea is that resistance depends on what happens inside the component. In metals, temperature increases resistance because of increased ion vibration. This is why a fixed resistor must be kept at constant temperature for a straight-line graph, and why a lamp does not give one.
bullets: A fixed resistor that **heats up** would start to curve like a lamp.
Wire and filament resistance **increases with temperature**.
The lamp's graph shows the effect of heating clearly because the filament becomes extremely hot.
The diode's behaviour comes from its construction, not from heating.

callouts.p: The lamp's resistance increases because of heating. The diode's high reverse resistance is because it only conducts one way, not because of temperature.

core.p: Questions on this point include sketching graphs, identifying components from graphs, explaining the lamp's curve, and calculating resistance from data. Use precise language.
bullets: When sketching, always include **labelled axes** (current, p.d.) and show both quadrants if asked.
Make the lamp curve pass through the **origin** and flatten at both ends.
Draw the diode graph along the axis in reverse and rising steeply at about 0.6 V forward.
Describe a graph using **'directly proportional'** only for a straight line through the origin.
Explain using **cause and effect** words: 'so', 'because', 'therefore'.

callouts.p: Describe: 'as the p.d. increases, the current increases but by smaller amounts'. Explain: 'because the resistance increases as the filament gets hotter'.

analogy.p: Picture electrons as pupils walking along a corridor lined with people standing still (the metal ions). In a fixed resistor at constant temperature, the people stand still and twice the push moves twice as many pupils per second: a straight line. In a filament lamp, the more pupils rush through, the hotter it gets and the more the standing people start jostling about, so pupils bump into them more and the flow cannot keep up with the push: resistance rises. A diode is a one-way turnstile that only turns once you push hard enough (about 0.6 V) and will not turn backwards at all. The analogy breaks down because electrons are not slowed by tiredness, the 'jostling' is vibration of ions caused by thermal energy, and a real diode's threshold is a property of its semiconductor material, not a mechanical lock.

terms.d: A graph showing how the current through a component varies with the potential difference across it.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts (V).
The rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A).
The opposition to current; R = V / I, measured in ohms (Ω).
A resistor with constant resistance at constant temperature.
A lamp with a thin metal filament whose resistance increases as its temperature increases.
A component that allows current to flow in one direction only.
The direction in which a diode conducts once the p.d. exceeds about 0.6 V.
The direction in which a diode has a very high resistance and almost no current flows.
Two quantities that increase in the same ratio, shown as a straight line through the origin.
A component in which current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature.
A component whose resistance changes, so its I-V graph is not a straight line through the origin.
Movement of the metal ions about fixed positions; it increases as temperature increases, causing more collisions with electrons.
The p.d. (about 0.6 V for a silicon diode) above which a diode starts to conduct significantly.

mistakes.w: The lamp's resistance decreases as it gets brighter.
mistakes.r: The lamp's resistance **increases** as the filament gets hotter.

mistakes.w: The lamp's resistance increases because the electrons slow down when hot.
mistakes.r: The **ions vibrate more**, so there are **more collisions** between electrons and ions.

mistakes.w: A fixed resistor's graph shows current proportional to p.d. at all temperatures.
mistakes.r: Only **at constant temperature**.

mistakes.w: The diode lets current flow in both directions but less in one.
mistakes.r: A diode lets current flow in **one direction only**; very high resistance in reverse.

mistakes.w: The diode conducts as soon as any forward p.d. is applied.
mistakes.r: It needs about **0.6 V** before significant current flows.

mistakes.w: The steeper line has the higher resistance.
mistakes.r: On an I-V graph the **steeper line has the lower resistance** (more current per volt).

mistakes.w: Any straight line graph means current is directly proportional to p.d.
mistakes.r: It must be a straight line **through the origin**.

mistakes.w: Resistance = gradient of the I-V graph.
mistakes.r: Resistance = **V / I** at a point (gradient is 1 / R for a straight line through the origin).

mistakes.w: Sketch of lamp graph drawn only in one quadrant when both were asked for.
mistakes.r: The lamp curve is **symmetrical**: draw it in both positive and negative quadrants.

exam.q: State what is meant by a diode.
model: a component that allows current to flow in one direction only
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'one direction only'.

exam.q: Name the component whose I-V graph is a straight line through the origin.
model: fixed resistor (at constant temperature)
exam.tip: Adding 'at constant temperature' shows understanding.

exam.q: Describe the relationship between current and p.d. for a fixed resistor at constant temperature.
model: current is directly proportional to p.d.
shown by a straight line through the origin / resistance is constant
exam.tip: 'Directly proportional' is the key phrase.

exam.q: Sketch the I-V characteristic of a filament lamp. Label the axes.
model: axes labelled current and potential difference
curve passing through the origin
curve becomes less steep at higher p.d. in both directions (S shape)
exam.tip: Show both quadrants unless the axes given show only one.

exam.q: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current through it increases.
model: the filament gets hotter / temperature increases
the ions vibrate more
so electrons collide with ions more often, increasing resistance
exam.tip: Three separate linked steps for three marks.

exam.q: Describe the I-V characteristic of a diode.
model: in the reverse direction, current is (almost) zero / very high resistance
in the forward direction, little current flows until about 0.6 V
then current increases rapidly / resistance is low
exam.tip: Cover the reverse direction and both parts of the forward direction.

exam.q: A filament lamp has a current of 0.10 A at 1.0 V and 0.25 A at 6.0 V. Calculate its resistance at each p.d. and state what this shows.
model: the resistance increases as p.d. / current increases
because the filament gets hotter
exam.tip: Show the equation and both substitutions.

exam.q: A diode is connected in a circuit with a lamp. When the battery is reversed, the lamp goes out. Explain why.
model: diode only lets current flow in one direction
in reverse it has a very high resistance, so (almost) no current flows through the lamp
exam.tip: Link the diode's resistance to the current in the lamp.

exam.q: Two straight-line I-V graphs A and B pass through the origin. A is steeper than B. State and explain which resistor has the greater resistance.
model: B has the greater resistance
B has less current for the same p.d., so V / I is larger
exam.tip: Pick one p.d. and compare the currents.

exam.q: Compare the I-V characteristics of a fixed resistor, a filament lamp and a diode. Explain how the resistance of each component changes as the potential difference changes.
model: fixed resistor: straight line through origin, current directly proportional to p.d.
fixed resistor: constant resistance (at constant temperature), same in both directions
lamp: curve through origin, less steep at higher p.d., symmetrical in both directions
lamp: resistance increases because filament heats up, ions vibrate more, more collisions with electrons
diode: (almost) no current in reverse, very high resistance
diode: forward current flows above about 0.6 V then rises steeply, low resistance; current in one direction only
exam.tip: Cover the shape and the resistance for each of the three components.

worked.q: A fixed resistor's I-V graph passes through the point (5.0 V, 0.25 A). Calculate its resistance and predict the current at 8.0 V.
steps: Resistance is constant for a fixed resistor at constant temperature
worked.ans: R = 20 Ω; at 8.0 V the current is 0.40 A.

worked.q: Readings for a filament lamp: 2.0 V, 0.20 A and 12 V, 0.50 A. Calculate the resistance at each p.d. and explain the difference.
steps: Higher current makes the filament hotter
Ions vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often
So the resistance is greater at higher p.d.
worked.ans: 10 Ω at 2.0 V and 24 Ω at 12 V: resistance increases because the filament gets hotter.

worked.q: A diode has a current of 20 mA when the forward p.d. is 0.70 V. Calculate its resistance. Explain why its resistance in the reverse direction at -0.70 V is much larger.
steps: In reverse, the diode allows (almost) no current to flow
With I almost zero, R = V / I is extremely large
worked.ans: Forward resistance = 35 Ω; reverse resistance is very high because almost no current flows.

phy_edx.9.8.summary: Thermistors and light-dependent resistors (LDRs) are resistors whose resistance is not fixed: a thermistor's resistance **decreases as temperature increases** and an LDR's resistance **decreases as light intensity increases**. You must be able to explain how a circuit with an ammeter, voltmeter and variable resistor (or variable supply) is designed and used to explore how resistance changes for filament lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs, and describe how thermistors are used in thermostats and LDRs in lights that switch on when it gets dark.

core.p: This point has three parts. 10.19: explain how the **design and use of circuits** can be used to explore the variation of resistance in filament lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs. 10.20: recall how the resistance of a thermistor and an LDR changes. 10.21: describe uses of thermistors (e.g. thermostats) and LDRs (e.g. switching lights on when it gets dark).
bullets: Both are **input sensors**: a change in the surroundings (temperature or light) causes a change in **resistance**.
A change in resistance changes the **current** in the circuit (for a fixed p.d.) and the **p.d. shared** across components in series.
The resistance is always found from **R = V / I** using meter readings.
Filament lamps and diodes are included in 10.19 because their resistance also varies, but with **current/p.d.** rather than surroundings.

callouts.p: Thermistor: as **temperature increases, resistance decreases**. LDR: as **light intensity increases, resistance decreases**.

core.p: You need to recognise and draw both symbols. Each is a resistor box with an extra feature showing what controls it.
bullets: **Thermistor**: a resistor rectangle with a diagonal line through it that has a short horizontal 'foot' at the bottom.
**LDR**: a resistor rectangle inside a circle, with **two arrows pointing in** towards it (light falling on it).
Do not confuse the LDR arrows (pointing **in**) with an LED, whose arrows point **out** (light given out).
A **variable resistor** has a plain diagonal arrow through it; this is a component you adjust by hand, not a sensor.

callouts.p: LDR arrows point towards the component; LED arrows point away. Examiners use this to test recognition.

core.h: Thermistors: how resistance changes with temperature
core.p: The thermistors used at GCSE are **NTC (negative temperature coefficient)** thermistors. They are made of a semiconductor. When the temperature rises, more charge carriers are freed in the material, so charge flows more easily and the **resistance falls**.
bullets: Cold: **high resistance**, so a small current for a given p.d.
Hot: **low resistance**, so a larger current for a given p.d.
The graph of resistance against temperature is a **curve that falls steeply at first then levels off**; it is **not** a straight line and it never reaches zero.
On an I-V graph at a fixed temperature a thermistor behaves like an ohmic resistor; if it heats up, the gradient increases.
Exam answers should state the direction of both quantities: 'as temperature increases the resistance decreases'.

callouts.p: A resistor whose resistance **decreases as temperature increases**.

fig.cap: Resistance of an NTC thermistor against temperature: a falling curve, steep at low temperature and flatter at high temperature. Resistance never reaches zero.

core.h: LDRs: how resistance changes with light intensity
core.p: An LDR is also made from a semiconductor. Light energy frees charge carriers, so in **bright light the resistance is low** and in **darkness the resistance is very high**.
bullets: Dark: **very high resistance** (can be millions of ohms), tiny current.
Bright: **low resistance** (a few hundred ohms), larger current.
Graph of resistance against light intensity: a **falling curve** that levels off, not a straight line.
Light intensity can be varied by moving a lamp closer or further away, or by covering the LDR.
Light intensity can be measured with a **light meter** (lux).

callouts.p: A resistor whose resistance **decreases as light intensity increases**.

fig.cap: Resistance of an LDR against light intensity: high in the dark, falling as light intensity increases and levelling off in bright light.

core.h: Designing a circuit to explore resistance
core.p: The same basic circuit is used for all four components. You need to measure the **current through** the component and the **p.d. across** it, then calculate R = V / I. A way of **changing** the current or p.d. lets you take a range of readings.
bullets: **Ammeter in series** with the component, to measure current through it (in amperes, A).
**Voltmeter in parallel** with the component, to measure p.d. across it (in volts, V).
**Variable resistor** (or a variable power supply) in series to change the current and p.d.
Calculate resistance for each pair of readings: **R = V / I**, in ohms.
For a thermistor or LDR, keep the p.d. **small** so the current does not heat the component and change its resistance by itself.
Alternatively an **ohmmeter** can measure resistance directly, but exam answers usually expect the ammeter and voltmeter method.

callouts.p: Mark schemes give separate marks for ammeter **in series** and voltmeter **in parallel across the component** (not across the battery).

fig.cap: Circuit to explore the resistance of a thermistor: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the thermistor, variable resistor to adjust the current. The thermistor sits in a water bath so its temperature can be changed and measured.

core.p: To find how resistance depends on temperature, the independent variable is **temperature**, the dependent variable is **resistance** (found from V and I) and the p.d. should be kept the same each time.
bullets: Place the thermistor in a **beaker of water** (in a sealed tube or with waterproofed leads) with a **thermometer**.
Heat the water (or add hot water / ice) to change the temperature in steps, e.g. every 10 °C.
**Stir** and wait for the reading to settle so the thermistor is at the same temperature as the thermometer.
At each temperature record V and I, then calculate R = V / I.
Plot **resistance (y-axis) against temperature (x-axis)** and draw a smooth curve of best fit.
Repeat and average to improve reliability; take readings both while heating and cooling.

callouts.p: A large current heats the thermistor itself and lowers its resistance, so the thermometer reading would no longer match the thermistor's temperature. Keep the current small.

core.p: For an LDR the independent variable is **light intensity**. The rest of the method is the same: measure V and I and calculate R.
bullets: Vary light intensity by placing a lamp at different **distances** from the LDR (closer = brighter).
Do it in a **darkened room** so background light does not affect results.
Keep the lamp the same (same power) and pointing straight at the LDR.
Measure light intensity with a light meter, or use distance as the independent variable.
Plot resistance against light intensity (or against distance; resistance then **increases** with distance).
Avoid a hot lamp very close to the LDR for a long time, so heating does not affect results.

callouts.p: If the graph uses distance from the lamp, resistance goes **up** as distance goes up, because the light gets dimmer. Read axes carefully.

core.h: Using the circuit: filament lamps and diodes
core.p: Spec 10.19 also lists filament lamps and diodes. Here the circuit is used to vary the **p.d. and current** and see how resistance changes with them (linked to the I-V graphs in 10.18).
bullets: **Filament lamp**: as current increases the filament gets **hotter**, metal ions vibrate more, so **resistance increases**; the I-V graph curves and flattens.
**Diode**: current flows in **one direction only** (forward). Resistance is **very high in the reverse direction** and becomes low once the forward p.d. exceeds a small threshold.
To test a diode in both directions, **reverse the connections** (or the supply) and record negative values.
Use the variable resistor to take a wide range of readings, including small values near zero.

head: Component
What varies its resistance
How resistance changes
rows: Very high in reverse, low in forward direction

core.h: Effect on current and p.d. in a circuit
core.p: Because a thermistor or LDR changes resistance, it changes what happens in the rest of the circuit. This is how they act as sensors.
bullets: With a fixed supply p.d., **lower resistance means a larger current** (I = V / R).
In a series circuit with a fixed resistor, the component with the **larger resistance takes the larger share of the p.d.**
So when an LDR gets darker, its resistance rises and the **p.d. across the LDR rises** while the p.d. across the fixed resistor falls.
When a thermistor gets hotter, its resistance falls and the **p.d. across the thermistor falls**.
The total p.d. shared between series components always equals the supply p.d.

callouts.p: Change in surroundings -> change in resistance -> change in current and p.d. share -> something switches on or off.

core.p: A **thermostat** keeps a room, oven, fridge or water heater at a set temperature. The thermistor senses temperature and the circuit switches the heater (or cooler) on or off.
bullets: Room gets **colder** -> thermistor resistance **increases** -> circuit detects the change and **switches the heater on**.
Room gets **warmer** -> resistance **decreases** -> heater switched **off**.
Other uses: **fire alarms** and overheating alarms, car engine temperature sensors, electronic thermometers, fridge and freezer controls.
Thermistors respond quickly and are small and cheap.

callouts.p: For full marks name the use, say what changes (temperature), and say how the resistance changes and what the circuit then does.

core.h: Uses of LDRs: lights that switch on in the dark
core.p: LDRs are used in **automatic night lights** and **street lights** that switch on when it gets dark.
bullets: It gets **dark** -> LDR resistance **increases** -> the p.d. across the LDR increases -> this switches the lamp **on**.
It gets **light** -> LDR resistance **decreases** -> lamp switches **off**.
This saves energy because lights are only on when needed.
Other uses: security lights, burglar alarms (beam broken), camera light meters, automatic brightness on phone screens.

callouts.p: Darkness makes the LDR's resistance go **up**, not down. Many students reverse this.

core.p: These two components are a favourite source of short recall questions and longer describe or explain questions linking resistance to a practical use.
bullets: Both are semiconductor devices whose resistance **decreases** as their input (heat or light) **increases**.
Both curves are **non-linear** and level off.
Both are used as **sensors** to control circuits automatically.
Both resistances are found experimentally with **R = V / I**.

head: Feature
Thermistor
LDR
rows: How to vary input in practical

analogy.p: Think of charge moving through the material like people walking down a corridor where only a few people are free to move. Heat (for a thermistor) or light (for an LDR) is like a bell that releases more people from classrooms to join the flow: more movers means a bigger flow for the same push, which is like lower resistance. Where it breaks down: in real metals heating makes resistance go up (the filament lamp), so this analogy only fits semiconductor devices, and 'more people' is a simplification of more free charge carriers.

terms.d: A resistor whose resistance decreases as temperature increases.
Negative temperature coefficient thermistor: resistance goes down as temperature goes up.
Light-dependent resistor: a resistor whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases.
How bright the light falling on a surface is; can be measured with a light meter.
How much a component opposes the current; R = V / I, measured in ohms.
The unit of resistance; 1 ohm is the resistance when 1 V drives a current of 1 A.
Meter connected in series to measure current in amperes.
Meter connected in parallel across a component to measure the potential difference across it, in volts.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed by hand, used to vary the current in a circuit.
An input component whose property (here resistance) changes in response to a change in the surroundings.
A device that keeps temperature at a set value by switching heating or cooling on and off.
A component that lets current flow in one direction only; very high resistance in the reverse direction.
A lamp whose resistance increases as the current increases because the filament gets hotter.
The variable you change in an investigation, e.g. temperature or light intensity.
A material whose ability to conduct changes greatly with conditions such as temperature or light.

mistakes.w: The resistance of a thermistor increases when it gets hotter.
mistakes.r: For an (NTC) thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature increases.

mistakes.w: In the dark an LDR has low resistance.
mistakes.r: In the dark an LDR has high resistance; resistance decreases as light intensity increases.

mistakes.w: The resistance is directly proportional to temperature / the graph is a straight line.
mistakes.r: Resistance decreases non-linearly: a curve that falls steeply then levels off.

mistakes.w: Voltmeter placed in series or across the battery.
mistakes.r: Voltmeter in parallel across the thermistor/LDR; ammeter in series.

mistakes.w: The LDR detects light because more light 'gives it more energy so resistance goes up'.
mistakes.r: More light means lower resistance and a larger current.

mistakes.w: Thermistor used in a street light.
mistakes.r: Street lights use an LDR; thermostats and fire alarms use a thermistor.

mistakes.w: Measure the temperature of the water and use it straight away.
mistakes.r: Stir and wait so the thermistor reaches the same temperature as the water before taking readings.

mistakes.w: Use a large current to get bigger readings.
mistakes.r: Keep current small so the component does not heat itself and change its resistance.

mistakes.w: Resistance = current / p.d.
mistakes.r: Resistance = potential difference / current, R = V / I.

exam.q: State how the resistance of a thermistor changes as its temperature increases.
model: Resistance decreases.
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for 1 mark, but 'decreases' must be clear.

exam.q: State how the resistance of an LDR changes when the light intensity falling on it decreases.
model: Resistance increases.
exam.tip: Watch the direction: this question asks about light decreasing.

exam.q: Draw the circuit symbol for an LDR.
model: Resistor rectangle in a circle with two arrows pointing towards it.
exam.tip: Arrows must point in, not out.

exam.q: A student measures a p.d. of 6.0 V across a thermistor and a current of 0.012 A. Calculate its resistance.
model: = 500 ohms
exam.tip: Always show the equation and substitution for the first mark.

exam.q: Describe how a thermistor could be used in a thermostat to control a room heater.
model: When the room cools, the thermistor's resistance increases
the change in resistance (current/p.d.) is used to switch the heater on (and off when warm).
exam.tip: Link the resistance change to the action of the circuit.

exam.q: Explain why a street light uses an LDR.
model: When it gets dark the LDR resistance increases
this change (in current/p.d.) switches the lamp on automatically.
exam.tip: Mention darkness and the resistance change.

exam.q: Explain why the student should use a small current when investigating how the resistance of a thermistor varies with temperature.
model: A large current would heat the thermistor
so its temperature (and resistance) would change / not match the thermometer reading.
exam.tip: This links 10.19 with the heating effect of current.

exam.q: Sketch a graph to show how the resistance of an LDR varies with light intensity.
model: Curve showing resistance decreasing as light intensity increases
Curve gets less steep / levels off (not straight, not reaching zero).
exam.tip: Label both axes.

exam.q: A thermistor and a fixed resistor are connected in series to a 12 V battery. Explain what happens to the p.d. across the thermistor when its temperature increases.
model: Thermistor resistance decreases
the thermistor now has a smaller share of the total resistance
so the p.d. across the thermistor decreases (p.d. across the fixed resistor increases; total still 12 V).
exam.tip: In series, the bigger resistance gets the bigger share of the p.d.

exam.q: Describe how you would investigate how the resistance of a thermistor changes with temperature. You may include a circuit diagram.
model: Circuit: thermistor with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel across it, connected to a power supply
Place thermistor in a beaker of water with a thermometer
Heat the water / add hot water to change temperature in steps (e.g. 10 °C)
Stir and wait for temperature to become steady before reading
Record V and I at each temperature and calculate R = V / I
Keep the p.d. constant/small to avoid self-heating; repeat readings and plot R against temperature.
exam.tip: Six-mark method: equipment, what you change, what you measure, how you calculate, control variables, and how you present results.

exam.q: Describe how the circuit could be used to show that a diode has a very high resistance in one direction.
model: Use the variable resistor to change the p.d. and record current
reverse the diode (or supply) and repeat
current is (almost) zero in reverse so R = V / I is very large.
exam.tip: Remember 10.19 includes diodes and filament lamps as well.

worked.q: An LDR in a circuit has a p.d. of 4.5 V across it. In daylight the current is 0.015 A; at night the current is 0.000 45 A. Calculate its resistance in each case and comment.
steps: Resistance at night is about 33 times greater.
This fits the rule: resistance decreases as light intensity increases.
worked.ans: 300 ohms in daylight, 10 000 ohms at night: much higher resistance in the dark.

worked.q: A thermistor (resistance 2000 ohms at 10 °C, 500 ohms at 40 °C) is in series with a 1000 ohm fixed resistor and a 6.0 V supply. Find the current at each temperature.
steps: Higher temperature -> lower thermistor resistance -> larger current.
worked.ans: 0.002 A at 10 °C and 0.004 A at 40 °C: the current doubles as the thermistor warms.

worked.q: Model answer: explain how an automatic night light uses an LDR.
steps: As it gets dark, light intensity on the LDR decreases.
So the resistance of the LDR increases.
This changes the current/p.d. in the sensing circuit (p.d. across the LDR rises).
The circuit uses this change to switch the lamp on; in daylight the opposite happens and the lamp switches off.
worked.ans: Dark -> LDR resistance up -> circuit switches lamp on automatically.

phy_edx.9.9.summary: Whenever there is an electric current in a resistor, energy is transferred that **heats the resistor**. This happens because the current does **work against electrical resistance**: electrons **collide with the ions in the metal lattice**, making the ions vibrate more, so electrical energy is **dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings**. To reduce this unwanted energy transfer we use **low resistance wires** (thick wires made of good conductors such as copper), and keep currents low.

core.p: 10.22: recall that a current in a resistor causes an energy transfer which heats the resistor. 10.23: explain that electrical energy is **dissipated as thermal energy in the surroundings** when a current **does work against electrical resistance**. 10.24: explain this energy transfer as the result of **collisions between electrons and the ions in the lattice**. 10.25: explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfer through **low resistance wires**.
bullets: This is called the **heating effect of an electric current**.
It happens in **every** component that has resistance, including connecting wires.
Sometimes the heating is **useful** (kettles, toasters); sometimes it is **wasted** energy.
The advantages and disadvantages of this heating are a separate point (10.26).

callouts.p: When there is an electric current in a resistor, there is an energy transfer which **heats the resistor**.

core.p: The power supply transfers energy to the charges (p.d. is energy per unit charge). As charge passes through a resistor, that energy is transferred **electrically** into the **thermal energy store** of the resistor, which then heats the surroundings.
bullets: Energy store at start: chemical store of the battery (or energy from the mains).
Pathway: **electrical working** (current).
Energy store at end: **thermal store** of the resistor, then the **thermal store of the surroundings**.
The resistor's temperature rises until it loses energy to the surroundings as fast as it gains it.
Energy is **conserved**: it is not destroyed, only spread out (dissipated).

core.p: Resistance opposes the flow of charge. To keep a current flowing the supply has to push the charges through the resistance, so **work is done**. Work done means energy transferred, and here it ends up as heating.
bullets: **Work done = energy transferred**.
The bigger the resistance, the more work is done per coulomb of charge for a given current.
The energy is **dissipated**: spread out into the surroundings as thermal energy, where it is much less useful.
Mark schemes reward the phrase **'work is done against (electrical) resistance'**.

callouts.p: Electrical energy is **dissipated as thermal energy in the surroundings** when an electrical current **does work against electrical resistance**.

core.p: A metal is made of a regular arrangement (a **lattice**) of **positive metal ions**, with **free (delocalised) electrons** that can move between them. The current is the flow of these free electrons.
bullets: Ions are fixed in position but **vibrate** about their positions.
Free electrons drift through the lattice when a p.d. is applied.
The electrons are negative; they move from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal (opposite to conventional current).
The hotter the metal, the more the ions vibrate.

core.p: This is the key explanation for 10.24. As the electrons are pushed through the wire they **collide with the ions in the lattice**. In each collision, energy is transferred from the electrons to the ions.
bullets: Electrons gain kinetic energy from the p.d. (electric field) as they move.
They **collide with the lattice ions** and transfer energy to them.
The ions **vibrate more** (with greater amplitude), so the **temperature of the resistor increases**.
The hot resistor transfers energy to the **surroundings** by heating.
The collisions also **impede the flow of electrons**: this is what resistance is.

callouts.p: electrons collide with ions -> energy transferred to ions -> ions vibrate more -> temperature of resistor increases -> energy dissipated to surroundings.
Do not write 'electrons collide with atoms/protons/each other'. The mark scheme wants **ions** (in the lattice).

core.h: Why hotter wires have more resistance
core.p: The heating effect feeds back on resistance. In a metal, hotter ions vibrate more, so electrons collide with them **more often**, which increases resistance.
bullets: More vibration -> more frequent collisions -> **higher resistance**.
This is why a **filament lamp's** resistance increases as the current increases.
Higher resistance at a fixed p.d. means a smaller current (I = V / R).
(Thermistors are semiconductors and behave the other way; that is a separate point.)

core.h: What decides how much heating there is
core.p: The rate of heating depends on the **current** and the **resistance**. More current means more electrons colliding each second; more resistance means more energy transferred per electron.
bullets: Bigger current -> more heating (heating depends on I squared, so doubling current gives four times the heating).
Bigger resistance -> more heating for the same current.
Longer time -> more total energy transferred.
The equations (E = IVt, P = I squared R) belong to 10.27 to 10.31, but the idea links here: **reduce I or R to reduce heating**.

callouts.t: Two ways to reduce wasted heating
callouts.p: Reduce the **resistance** of the wires, or reduce the **current** in them.

core.p: In most circuits the heating in connecting wires and cables is **wasted energy**: it is not doing the job we want and it reduces efficiency. It can also be dangerous if wires overheat.
bullets: Wasted energy increases electricity cost.
Hot cables can **melt insulation** and cause **fires**.
Heating in electronic devices (phones, computers) can damage components, so they need cooling.
Energy lost in cables means less reaches the appliance.

core.h: Reducing unwanted energy transfer: low resistance wires
core.p: The main method in the spec is to use **low resistance wires**. With lower resistance, less work is done against resistance, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy.
bullets: Use **thicker wires** (larger cross-sectional area): more room for electrons to flow, so fewer collisions per electron and lower resistance.
Use **shorter wires**: resistance is proportional to length.
Use a **good conductor** such as **copper** (or aluminium in overhead cables) which has low resistance.
Keep wires **cool**: a metal's resistance is lower at lower temperature.
Appliances that draw large currents (cookers, showers) use **thick cables**.

fig.cap: For the same current, a thin wire has higher resistance and heats up more than a thick wire of the same metal and length, so thick wires reduce unwanted energy transfer.

core.h: Reducing current: the National Grid idea
core.p: Heating also depends strongly on the current. For a given power, transmitting at a **high voltage** means a **low current**, which greatly reduces heating in cables. This is why the National Grid uses step-up transformers.
bullets: Same power, higher p.d. -> lower current (P = IV).
Lower current -> fewer charges colliding each second -> much less heating.
Combined with thick, low resistance cables, this makes transmission efficient.
Transformers and the National Grid are covered in more detail elsewhere; here, just link low current with less heating.

callouts.p: If a question asks about **wires**, talk about low resistance (thick, short, copper). Only bring in high voltage/low current if the question is about transmission.

core.h: Other ways to cut wasted thermal energy
core.p: Beyond wire choice, designers reduce the effects of unwanted heating in other ways.
bullets: Use **efficient components** (e.g. LEDs instead of filament lamps) that waste less energy by heating.
Use **heat sinks** and fans to remove thermal energy from electronic components so they do not overheat.
Switch devices off when not in use so no current flows.

callouts.p: Thermal insulation keeps heat in; it does not reduce the electrical heating in a wire. For 10.25 the answer is **low resistance wires**.

core.p: Most marks on this point come from a clear explanation using the right particles and words.
bullets: Current in a resistor -> energy transfer -> resistor heats up.
Work is done against resistance; energy is dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings.
Electrons collide with lattice ions; ions vibrate more; temperature rises.
Reduce wasted energy with low resistance wires: thick, short, copper.

analogy.t: Running through a crowded dance floor
analogy.p: Electrons are like people trying to run through a crowded dance floor where the dancers (ions) stay in their places. Every time a runner bumps into a dancer, the dancer jiggles more: energy has gone from the runner to the dancer, and the room gets hotter. A wider dance floor (thicker wire) gives runners more room, so there are fewer bumps per runner, just as a thick wire has less resistance. Where it breaks down: real electrons drift very slowly overall and the 'bumps' are interactions with the electric fields of ions, not people literally hitting each other.

terms.d: The energy transfer that heats a resistor when there is a current in it.
Opposition to the flow of charge; caused by collisions between electrons and ions; measured in ohms.
A component that opposes current; any conductor with resistance heats up when a current flows.
Energy transferred when a force moves something; here, energy transferred pushing charge through resistance.
Energy that has spread out into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, so it is less useful.
Energy stored in an object due to its temperature; increases when the object heats up.
The regular arrangement of positive metal ions in a metal.
A charged particle; in a metal, the positive ions are atoms that have lost outer electrons.
Electrons in a metal that are not bound to one atom and can move to carry a current.
An electron interacting with a lattice ion and transferring energy to it.
Energy transferred to stores that are not useful, often thermal energy in the surroundings.
Useful energy output divided by total energy input; reduced by unwanted heating.
The area of the end face of a wire; larger area means lower resistance.
A wire that is thick, short and made of a good conductor such as copper, so little energy is wasted.
A piece of metal with fins attached to a component to transfer thermal energy away to the surroundings.

mistakes.w: Electrons collide with atoms / protons / each other.
mistakes.r: Electrons collide with the (positive) ions in the lattice.

mistakes.w: The resistor makes heat / heat energy is created.
mistakes.r: Electrical energy is transferred to the thermal store of the resistor and dissipated to the surroundings; energy is conserved.

mistakes.w: The ions start to move along the wire.
mistakes.r: The ions stay in place but vibrate more (with greater amplitude).

mistakes.w: Use thinner wires to reduce resistance.
mistakes.r: Use thicker wires: larger cross-sectional area gives lower resistance.

mistakes.w: Insulate the wires to stop energy being lost.
mistakes.r: Use low resistance wires (thick, short, copper) so less work is done against resistance.

mistakes.w: Use higher current so energy gets through faster.
mistakes.r: Lower current reduces heating; heating increases strongly with current.

mistakes.w: Resistance makes electrons lose charge.
mistakes.r: Electrons keep their charge; they transfer energy to the lattice ions in collisions.

mistakes.w: Only special heaters get hot.
mistakes.r: Every component with resistance, including wires, is heated by a current.

exam.q: State what happens to a resistor when there is an electric current in it.
model: It heats up / its temperature increases (energy is transferred to its thermal store).
exam.tip: Straight recall of 10.22.

exam.q: Name the particles in a metal wire that the electrons collide with.
model: (Positive metal) ions (in the lattice).
exam.tip: Not atoms, not protons.

exam.q: Give one way of reducing the unwanted energy transfer in connecting wires.
model: Use low resistance wires, e.g. thicker / shorter / copper wires.
exam.tip: Thicker is the most common accepted answer.

exam.q: Complete the sentence: electrical energy is dissipated as ______ energy in the surroundings when a current does ______ against electrical resistance.
model: thermal
work
exam.tip: Learn the spec sentence word for word.

exam.q: Explain why using thick cables reduces wasted energy in a cooker circuit.
model: Thick cables have lower resistance
so less work is done against resistance / less energy dissipated as thermal energy.
exam.tip: Link 'thick' to 'lower resistance' and then to 'less heating'.

exam.q: Explain why the energy transferred to the surroundings by a current is described as wasted.
model: The thermal energy is dissipated / spread out to the surroundings
it is not used for the intended purpose (cannot easily be used again).
exam.tip: Use the word dissipated.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of electrons and ions, why a wire gets hot when a current flows through it.
model: Electrons (gain energy and) move through the metal lattice
electrons collide with the (positive) ions
energy is transferred to the ions so they vibrate more
so the temperature of the wire increases (and energy is transferred to the surroundings).
exam.tip: This is the most commonly examined part of this point; give each step.

exam.q: Explain why the resistance of a metal wire increases as it heats up.
model: The ions vibrate more
electrons collide with the ions more often
so the flow of electrons is opposed more / resistance increases.
exam.tip: Links to the filament lamp I-V graph.

exam.q: A student says 'wrapping wires in thermal insulation will reduce the energy wasted by heating'. Evaluate this statement.
model: Insulation does not reduce resistance, so the same energy is still transferred by heating
it could make the wire hotter (increasing resistance and fire risk)
better to use low resistance wires (thicker/shorter/copper).
exam.tip: Evaluate means give a judgement with a reason.

exam.q: Explain how the heating effect of an electric current arises and describe how unwanted energy transfer in cables can be reduced.
model: Current is a flow of (free) electrons through a metal lattice
work is done against resistance as electrons collide with lattice ions
energy transferred to ions which vibrate more; temperature of wire rises
energy dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings (wasted)
reduce by using low resistance wires: thick (large cross-section), short, made of copper
reducing the current (e.g. transmitting at high p.d.) also reduces heating.
exam.tip: Structure: cause, mechanism, consequence, then solutions with reasons.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a toaster element glows red hot when switched on.
steps: A current flows: free electrons move through the metal element.
The electrons collide with the positive ions in the lattice.
Energy is transferred to the ions, which vibrate more.
The temperature of the element rises until it glows and heats the bread and surroundings.
worked.ans: Electron-ion collisions transfer energy to the lattice, raising the element's temperature: the heating effect of a current.

worked.q: A cable carries a current of 10 A. Cable X has resistance 0.20 ohms and cable Y (thicker) has resistance 0.05 ohms. Using P = I squared x R, compare the power wasted as heat in each.
steps: Cable X: P = 10 squared x 0.20 = 100 x 0.20 = 20 W
Cable Y: P = 10 squared x 0.05 = 100 x 0.05 = 5 W
Cable Y wastes 15 W less: four times less heating.
Lower resistance wire -> less work done against resistance -> less energy dissipated.
worked.ans: 20 W in X, 5 W in Y: the thicker, lower resistance cable wastes a quarter of the energy.

worked.q: Applied example: why do electric shower cables need to be much thicker than lamp cables?
steps: A shower draws a very large current (tens of amps); a lamp draws less than 1 A.
Heating in a cable increases greatly with current.
A thin cable would have too high a resistance, waste energy and could overheat, melting insulation.
A thick copper cable has low resistance, so heating is kept small and safe.
worked.ans: Thick, low resistance cables keep wasted heating low for large currents and prevent overheating.
